turns.content: Hi, I hope this is the right place to start. My name is Kenta Morishita. I'm 34 years old, and I've been sitting with this idea for a long time — maybe too long. I've been working at Marubeni Corporation for 11 years now, mostly in the food and agribusiness division, and lately I've been thinking seriously about leaving to open a restaurant. I know that probably sounds crazy, and I know the statistics on restaurant failures. But I feel like if I don't at least try to plan this out properly, I'm going to regret it for the rest of my life. I guess I'm looking for help thinking through whether this is even remotely viable, and if so, what I should actually be doing to make it happen.

Kenta, thank you for sharing something this personal — and no, it doesn't sound crazy at all. The fact that you're approaching it with eyes open about the statistics already puts you ahead of a lot of people who walk into restaurant ventures with pure enthusiasm and not much else. Eleven years at Marubeni Corporation in food and agribusiness is actually an unusually strong foundation for this kind of move. You've been operating inside the supply chain, which means you understand margins, sourcing, and the industrial reality of food at a level that most aspiring restaurateurs simply don't have.

Before we get into the mechanics of planning, I want to understand the idea itself a bit better, because the concept you're building around will shape every practical decision downstream — location, staffing, capital requirements, target customers, everything.

So let me ask a few things to start:

What kind of restaurant are you imagining? Is there a specific cuisine, format, or dining experience that's been living in your head? And is this something rooted in a personal passion — a trip you took, a meal that changed your perspective, a style of cooking you've been practicing at home — or is it more of a market opportunity you've spotted through your work at Marubeni?

Also, at this stage, are you thinking about this as a solo venture, or is there a partner — a chef, a business partner, perhaps your wife Ayako Morishita — who might be involved in the picture?

Take your time. I want to understand the shape of the dream before we start pressure-testing it.

Those are exactly the right questions. Let me try to explain the origin of all this, because I think it matters.

In 2019, Marubeni sent me on a sourcing trip to northern Italy — Emilia-Romagna region. I ended up spending time in Bologna, and honestly it changed something in me. I've traveled a lot for work, but Bologna was different. The way food functions in that city — it's not performative, it's not for Instagram, it's just deeply woven into how people live. I ate at places that had been serving the same handmade pasta for forty years and the room was packed every single night because the food was genuinely extraordinary and the experience felt completely human. I got so obsessed that I actually enrolled in a short program at the Hotel School of Bologna — just 3 weeks, but it covered the fundamentals of Italian culinary tradition, regional ingredients, the philosophy behind cucina povera. It was one of the most formative experiences of my professional life, even though it had nothing to do with my job.

What I want to open is a small Italian trattoria. Specifically something in the spirit of what I experienced in Bologna — unpretentious, focused on handmade pasta and seasonal ingredients, genuine hospitality, nothing too theatrical. I've been calling it "Ginza Trattoria" in my head, mostly as a placeholder name, because I think the Ginza area — or somewhere near it — is probably where I want to be in terms of the clientele I'm hoping to attract. I'm thinking 20-25 seats, deliberately small, so I can maintain quality and not spread the kitchen too thin.

My wife Ayako Morishita is supportive, which matters enormously to me. She's not planning to be directly involved in the restaurant, but she's a realist and she's been my sounding board for months. She has a stable job, which gives us a bit of breathing room on household income if things get tight.

The Bologna origin story is meaningful — not as sentimentality, but as a signal of something durable. People who open restaurants out of a vague passion for food often discover they were actually in love with the idea of a restaurant, not the work of running one. But what you're describing is different: you went to Bologna for work, got pulled in by something you didn't expect, and then invested your own time and money to study it formally at the Hotel School of Bologna. That's not a whim. That's a genuine gravitational pull, and it's the kind of origin story that tends to sustain a person through the very hard years that restaurant ownership involves.

Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I want to make sure I have the concept clearly: a small, honest Italian trattoria — 20-25 seats — anchored in the Emilia-Romagna tradition, with handmade pasta as the centerpiece, seasonal ingredients, and a dining room atmosphere that feels warm and human rather than high-concept. The working name is Ginza Trattoria, and you're orienting toward the Ginza area for its customer profile. That's a well-defined concept. It has coherence.

Now, a few things I want to explore with you, because they'll shape the plan significantly:

First, on the Ginza location instinct — I think you're right that the neighborhood fits the clientele you're imagining, but Ginza rents are among the highest in Tokyo, and for a 20-25 seat restaurant operating in a trattoria format — which typically doesn't push extremely high per-cover prices — the margin math can get very tight very fast. Have you thought at all about whether a slightly adjacent area, like Shimbashi, Higashi-Ginza, or even Toranomon, might let you capture a similar customer base while materially reducing your fixed cost structure? Or is the Ginza address itself part of the positioning you feel strongly about?

Second, on the chef question — you've studied at the Hotel School of Bologna and you clearly have a deep intellectual and emotional relationship with this cuisine. But the practical question for a restaurant of this kind is: do you see yourself as the chef-owner in the kitchen, or are you planning to find a professional chef and operate as the owner-manager? This is one of the most consequential decisions you'll make, and there's no wrong answer, but each path implies a very different set of risks and capabilities to build.

Third — and I'll ask this gently but directly — what does your capital situation look like? You don't need to share numbers if you'd rather not, but understanding the financial foundation will determine how aggressive or conservative the planning needs to be from the start.

All three of those questions are things I've been wrestling with, so let me try to answer them honestly.

On location: you're right that pure Ginza is probably not realistic for a first restaurant at the scale I'm describing. I've been looking at the side streets between Ginza and Higashi-Ginza station, maybe even the Tsukiji fringe area, partly because the foot traffic profile isn't that different from central Ginza for an evening-focused restaurant, and the rents are considerably more manageable. The name "Ginza Trattoria" might stick even if the physical address ends up being slightly off-center — I've seen that work for other places.

On the chef question: this is where I feel least certain. I can cook. I'm not embarrassed about my level — I've spent years cooking Italian food at home and I did genuinely learn things in Bologna. But I'm realistic enough to know that cooking for 25 covers every night, maintaining consistency, managing a kitchen team, and also running the front of house and the business is probably too much for one person without serious professional kitchen experience. My honest instinct is that I want to be the owner-operator — managing the business, the customer relationships, the sourcing (which is actually where my Marubeni background is most directly useful) — and find a skilled chef who shares the philosophy. Someone who's maybe worked in Italian cuisine and is looking for the freedom of a smaller, concept-driven kitchen. But finding that person is something I genuinely don't know how to do yet.

On capital: I'll be direct. We have 28 million yen in savings that I could realistically put toward this. Ayako and I have talked about it carefully — that's money we've accumulated over many years and it's the sum total of what we'd be willing to risk. I know that's a significant amount but I also know that restaurant startup costs in Tokyo can eat that up faster than you'd expect, especially with the kind of fit-out that a trattoria concept would need to feel right.

Your self-assessment here is unusually clear-eyed, and that matters. Let me work through each piece.

On the location adjustment — the Ginza-Higashi-Ginza-Tsukiji fringe is actually a smart move, not a compromise. Some of Tokyo's most respected smaller restaurants have built their reputations in exactly that corridor. The evening customer coming to a well-executed trattoria in that area is largely the same person who'd visit central Ginza, but you're not paying the address premium. Keeping the Ginza Trattoria name with a slightly off-center address is entirely workable — the name functions as an aspiration and a positioning signal, not a literal GPS coordinate.

On the chef partnership — your instinct is the right one for where you are. The owner-sourcing-front-of-house model with a skilled chef-partner is a legitimate and often successful division of labor, particularly for concept-driven small restaurants where the owner has a strong vision but isn't a trained professional cook. Your Marubeni background in food and agribusiness sourcing is genuinely valuable here — the ability to build direct relationships with importers of Italian ingredients, to understand quality signals in supply chains, to negotiate intelligently — that's a real operational advantage that many restaurant owners don't have. The challenge is finding the right chef, which I'll come back to.

On capital: 28 million yen is a meaningful number and I want to be honest with you about what it means in context. For a 20-25 seat restaurant in the Ginza-adjacent area, a realistic cost breakdown for an opening might look something like this — and these are rough Tokyo market figures that you'd want to validate with actual quotes:

Tenant deposit and key money: typically 6 to 10 months of rent. For a small space in that corridor, monthly rent for something suitable might run 400,000 to 600,000 yen. So just to secure the lease, you could be looking at 4 to 6 million yen before you've bought a single piece of equipment.

Fit-out and construction: a trattoria needs to feel warm, textured, lived-in — not expensive, but intentional. A responsible fit-out for 25 seats, including kitchen renovation, flooring, lighting, furniture, and the small details that make the atmosphere work, typically runs 8 to 15 million yen depending on the condition of the space you're taking on.

Kitchen equipment: professional pasta-focused kitchen with appropriate refrigeration, pasta machines, plating equipment — budget 3 to 5 million yen depending on new versus used.

Pre-opening expenses — menu development, staff hiring, training, initial inventory, licensing, signage, a modest marketing push: another 1.5 to 3 million yen.

Operating reserve: this is the one that catches people. You need enough cash to cover operating losses for the first 4 to 6 months while you build your customer base. For a restaurant at your scale, that might mean having 3 to 5 million yen untouched as a buffer.

Adding the conservative end of those ranges: you're at roughly 20 to 22 million yen to open. The 28 million yen gives you a margin, but it's not a wide one. You would not be starting this with significant financial cushion after opening day. That's not a reason not to do it — it's a reason to be disciplined about the space you select and the fit-out decisions you make.

One thing I'd want to understand better: are you planning to leave Marubeni before you open, or is there a scenario where you do the planning and early groundwork while still employed, and only resign when you're close to signing a lease? The timing of that decision has real implications for both your financial position and your personal risk exposure.

That breakdown is really useful and honestly a bit sobering — in a good way. It makes the numbers feel real rather than abstract.

On timing: I've thought about this a lot. My honest preference would be to resign from Marubeni sooner rather than later — not because I'm impatient, but because I think trying to do serious restaurant planning on top of a demanding full-time job in the food trade is going to result in doing both things poorly. Marubeni is not a company where you can quietly phone it in while building a side project. The work is genuinely demanding and the culture expects full commitment. So my inclination is to resign, give myself 6 to 9 months of serious planning and preparation time, and open sometime in late 2025 or early 2026.

That said, Ayako and I have also talked about whether there's a softer version — maybe I do the bulk of the planning while still employed and only resign when I'm within 2 or 3 months of signing a lease. I see the logic of that, but I'm honestly worried it compromises both things.

The other thing I haven't mentioned yet is the chef question in more detail. I don't have a candidate in mind. I know there are Italian restaurants in Tokyo where skilled people work who might be interested in something like this, but I have no network in the professional kitchen world. My connections are all in food trade, supply chains, import-export. I've been wondering whether I should spend some of my pre-opening time doing stage work in a restaurant kitchen somewhere — not to become a professional cook, but to understand the operational reality and maybe meet people in that world. Is that a reasonable idea, or does it sound naive?

The staging idea is not naive at all — it's actually one of the smarter things you could do, and I'd encourage you to think seriously about it. Let me explain why, and also be honest about what it will and won't give you.

What a stage will give you: operational fluency. Right now, you understand restaurants as a diner and as someone who has studied the culinary tradition academically and personally. What you don't yet have is the embodied knowledge of what a service actually feels like from the inside — the rhythm of a kitchen at full capacity, how tickets flow, how a chef communicates under pressure, what mise en place really means in practice when you're doing it for forty covers. As an owner-operator who is going to be working alongside a chef, that fluency matters enormously. It's the difference between giving your chef a direction and giving them a direction that reveals you have no idea what you're asking.

What a stage will also give you: exactly the network access you're describing. The professional kitchen world in Tokyo is small and connected. If you spend two or three months working in a well-regarded Italian restaurant kitchen — even in a very junior capacity, washing vegetables, doing prep work, observing — you will meet people. Chefs talk to each other. They know who's looking for something different, who's ready to take a step into a smaller more autonomous kitchen. That's where your chef search should actually happen, not through a job posting.

A few honest caveats: stage positions are unpaid or very low paid, and they can be physically grueling in a way that's genuinely different from office work. At 34, coming from a corporate environment, the adjustment is real. You should go in without ego and prepared to be the least experienced person in the room by a significant margin. Also, it won't make you a professional chef — three months of staging, on top of your home cooking background and your time at the Hotel School of Bologna, is not a culinary career. It's an orientation, and you should frame it as such to yourself and to the kitchens you approach.

On the Marubeni timing question — I think your instinct is correct, actually. You're describing a company with a genuine full-commitment culture, and you know it better than I do. Half-measures in both directions often produce poor results in both. If you're going to plan a restaurant seriously — scout locations, do a proper chef search, do staging, develop the menu, work through the financial model in detail — that is genuinely a full-time occupation for six to nine months. The cleaner path is probably to make the decision to resign, set a departure date, and then execute the pre-opening period with real focus.

The risk I'd want you to name explicitly though: if you resign from Marubeni and then spend 28 million yen opening a restaurant that doesn't work, what does that scenario look like for you and Ayako? I'm not asking because I think that's the likely outcome — I actually think you're approaching this with more seriousness and preparation than most. But the plan should be built with that scenario modeled, not suppressed. Do you two have a shared understanding of what the failure scenario looks like, and is it one you can both live with?

Yes. We've talked about it explicitly. Ayako asked me directly to walk through what happens if it fails within two years, which is the kind of question I'm grateful she asked because it forced me to think it through rather than avoid it.

Here's where we landed: if the restaurant fails within two years and we lose most of the 28 million yen, we're not destitute. Ayako's income covers our household expenses without my salary. We own the apartment we live in — it's not large, but it's paid off. I would need to return to the workforce, and I think honestly my 11 years at Marubeni in food and agribusiness would make that not impossible. I might not get a position at the same level immediately, but I have real skills and real relationships in that industry. I'd probably be able to find work within six months. We wouldn't be comfortable — we'd have lost a significant portion of our savings — but we'd be okay.

What I told Ayako is that I think the cost of not trying, in terms of what it would do to my sense of self over the next thirty years, is actually comparable to the cost of trying and failing. She accepted that, though I know she's hoping very much that it doesn't come to that.

I guess what I'm asking now, having laid all that out, is: what do you actually think? Not as a cheerleader, but as someone who has heard what I've said. Is this a sensible enough foundation to proceed with serious planning? Or are there things you're hearing that concern you that I haven't addressed?

I appreciate you asking for a direct answer, so here it is: yes, I think the foundation is sensible enough to proceed with serious planning. But I want to be specific about what I find solid and what I find genuinely uncertain, because you deserve both.

What I find solid:

The concept has real coherence. A small, honest, pasta-focused trattoria in the Emilia-Romagna tradition is not a trend play. It's a durable format with a clear value proposition, and the 20-25 seat scale is actually protective — it allows for quality control and creates the intimacy that makes that kind of restaurant work. You're not trying to open a hundred-seat izakaya or chase some novelty concept. You know what you're building and why.

Your background is genuinely relevant. Eleven years in food and agribusiness at Marubeni is not a generic corporate background — it's directly applicable to restaurant sourcing, supplier relationships, cost management, and understanding the industrial reality of ingredients. Most first-time restaurateurs come in blind on the supply side. You don't. The time at the Hotel School of Bologna adds a layer of culinary seriousness that many owner-operators lack. And the personal failure analysis you just walked me through — the explicit conversation with Ayako Morishita about the downside scenario — reflects a kind of emotional preparation that is genuinely more mature than most people attempting this.

The capital position is workable. 28 million yen is not a lavish budget for Tokyo, but it's not reckless either, especially with Ayako's income providing household stability. You're not betting money you can't afford to lose in a meaningful sense.

What I find genuinely uncertain:

The chef dependency. Everything about this concept works if you find the right chef. It becomes extremely difficult if you don't. The chef is not a hire you can afford to get wrong or rush. I'd want to see the chef search treated as the highest-priority item in your pre-opening period — not something you start after you've found a location, but something you pursue in parallel from day one, if not ahead of everything else.

The staging gap. Your culinary knowledge is real but it's theoretical and personal, not professional. The staging path you're considering is the right corrective, but it needs to actually happen — not as a brief orientation but as a genuine immersion. Three months minimum, I'd argue, in a kitchen where the standards are high.

The margin math in a trattoria format. This is the one I want you to go back to with a spreadsheet. A 20-25 seat restaurant doing two seatings per evening, five to six nights a week, at an average spend you'd need to project honestly — does that revenue model, at Ginza-adjacent rents, actually produce a path to profitability within twelve to eighteen months? I want you to build that model with real numbers before you commit to a lease. Not because I think the answer is no, but because you should know what the answer is before you're in it.

None of these concerns are dealbreakers. They're the specific things that need serious work in the planning period. If you resolve them — find the chef, complete the staging, build the financial model and stress-test it — you'll be in a genuinely strong position to open something that has a real chance.

So where do you want to go from here? We could start working on what the pre-opening planning calendar should actually look like — a sequenced plan for the next six to nine months if you were to resign soon. Or we could go deeper on any one of the areas I've flagged. What feels most pressing to you right now?

I think the pre-opening planning calendar is exactly what I need. I feel like I have a lot of parallel threads — the chef search, the staging, the location scouting, the financial modeling, actually resigning from Marubeni — and I don't have a sense of what order to do things in, or what depends on what. If I resigned in, say, April — so about four weeks from now — what would the first ninety days look like? What should I actually be doing, week by week or month by month?

Also, one thing I haven't mentioned yet: I have a friend from university who's a commercial real estate broker in Tokyo. He's told me informally that there are spaces in the Higashi-Ginza and Tsukiji area that come available fairly regularly, and he's offered to alert me when something suitable appears. I haven't told him I'm actually serious yet — I've kept this close — but I think he'd be useful. Should I be looping him in now, or waiting until I'm further along?

Loop your broker friend in now. Not fully, not with a detailed brief, but enough to activate him. Tell him you're getting serious about a 20-25 seat restaurant space in the Higashi-Ginza or Tsukiji fringe, that you're looking at a timeline of roughly 6 to 9 months from now for signing a lease, and that you want to understand what's realistic on rent and availability in that corridor before you get further along. That's all. You don't need to have resigned from Marubeni, you don't need a business plan, you don't need a name. What you need from him right now is market intelligence — what spaces typically look like, what the range of rents actually is, what condition spaces tend to be in when they come available, and whether there's anything he'd flag as particularly suitable for a small restaurant concept that needs a real kitchen. That information will feed directly into your financial modeling, and it costs you nothing to ask.

Keeping him uninformed longer only means you go into your financial modeling with less accurate inputs. The restaurant world is not so small and so networked in commercial real estate that telling one broker friend you're thinking seriously about a restaurant will somehow create complications. Tell him.

Now, the ninety-day calendar. If you resign in April and your first day of focus is May 1, here is how I would structure the first three months:

Month one — May. This month is entirely about foundation. Your three priorities are: financial modeling, market intelligence, and staging arrangements.

On financial modeling: spend the first two weeks building a proper operating model. Revenue assumptions based on seats, covers per night, average check, operating days per week. Cost assumptions broken into fixed costs — rent, labor, utilities, insurance — and variable costs, primarily food cost, which in an Italian trattoria format you'd want to target around 28 to 32 percent of revenue. Build the model conservatively and stress-test it. What does breakeven look like? At what utilization rate do you stop losing money? How many months of losses does your capital cover before you run out of operating reserve? You should be able to answer these questions with actual numbers by the end of May.

On market intelligence: have the substantive conversation with your broker friend in the first week of May. Visit three to five spaces, even if none of them are right, just to calibrate your sense of what you're looking at. Understand what a kitchen-ready space costs versus a shell space that requires full construction. This shapes everything downstream.

On staging: start making contacts. Identify four or five Italian restaurants in Tokyo where the kitchen standards are genuinely high and the food is in the spirit of what you want to build. Reach out in the first two weeks of May. Be honest about who you are and what you're doing — aspiring restaurateur, not a career cook, wants to learn operational reality and spend time in a serious kitchen. Some will say no. One or two will likely say yes. Your goal is to have a staging commitment confirmed by the end of May.

Month two — June. This month is split: you begin staging while simultaneously advancing the chef search and deepening the location work.

On staging: aim for three to four days per week in the kitchen, primarily evenings. You will be physically exhausted. That is the point. You'll learn the most in the state of exhaustion because that's the state in which restaurants actually operate. Pay attention to everything — not just technique, but communication, management, how the chef handles a table that sends something back, how the kitchen handles a supplier delivery that's wrong. You're gathering knowledge that no book or study program can give you.

On the chef search: this doesn't mean posting a job listing. It means having conversations. Through the staging connection, through introductions from people you meet in those kitchens, through any Italian restaurant community connections you can develop. You're looking for someone who is technically skilled, philosophically aligned with what you're trying to build, and at a point in their career where the autonomy of a small, concept-driven kitchen is more appealing than the scale of a larger operation. That person exists. Finding them requires exposure and word-of-mouth.

On location: by June you should have enough market intelligence to have defined your target parameters precisely — size range, rent ceiling, neighborhood, minimum kitchen requirements. If your broker friend alerts you to something that fits, you should be ready to evaluate it seriously, not just flag it for later.

Month three — July. This is the month where the parallel threads need to start converging.

Ideally by July you have: a financial model you have confidence in, at least one to two serious chef conversations underway, a clear picture of the real estate market, and a staging experience that has given you operational grounding. At that point you're in a position to make the first major commitment — either a letter of intent on a space, or a formal agreement with a chef, or both. The order matters less than the substance: by the end of July, you should have moved from planning to commitment on at least one of the major structural decisions.

The thing I'd say most firmly about this calendar: the chef search cannot be left to month three. It has to be running actively in month one, even if it's just the first exploratory conversations. The chef is the hardest variable to control and the longest lead-time item. If you find the right person, everything accelerates. If you don't, everything waits.

Does this structure feel workable? And is there any piece of it you want to go deeper on before we close out today?

This has been incredibly useful. I feel like I came in here with a vague dream and I'm leaving with something that actually feels like a plan. The ninety-day structure in particular gives me something concrete to hold onto.

One last thing I want to ask: I haven't told anyone at Marubeni what I'm thinking, obviously. And I haven't really told anyone outside of Ayako. Part of me wonders whether I should start talking to other people who've made similar transitions — people who've left corporate roles to open restaurants — just to get a sense of the reality from people who've done it. Is that something I should be actively seeking out? And if so, how would you even find those people in Japan, where there's still a fairly strong social norm against being open about career pivots of this kind?

Yes, you should seek those conversations out, and I'd argue they're more valuable than almost any other single thing you could do in the next few months. Here's why: every piece of advice I can offer you is structurally sound but it's also general. The person who left a trading company after twelve years to open a ramen shop in Nakameguro, or the woman who came out of a finance career to run a wine bar in Shibuya — those people have specific, granular, lived knowledge that no planning framework can substitute for. They know which things they worried about that turned out not to matter, and which things blindsided them that nobody warned them about. That asymmetry of knowledge is exactly what you need right now.

On how to find those people in Japan without violating the social norms around career disclosure: the good news is that the context in which you approach this matters more than the disclosure itself. There are a few paths that work naturally.

The first is through food and restaurant industry events. Tokyo has a reasonably active community around food entrepreneurship — trade events, natural wine fairs, artisan food markets, culinary industry nights. These are places where owner-operators show up in a professional capacity, which means the conversation about what they do and how they got there is entirely normal. You're not asking someone in a corporate elevator about their life choices. You're talking to a restaurateur at an event oriented around what they do.

The second is through the staging connections you'll be building. Kitchens talk. When you're in a kitchen in June and you mention that you're planning to open your own place, people will tell you stories. They'll mention a friend who did it, a chef who left a hotel kitchen to open something small, a former colleague who burned out on corporate life and built something. Ask those follow-on questions. Write down the names you hear. Follow up.

The third, which is underused and underrated in Japan, is simply reaching out directly to owners of small restaurants you admire — not the famous chefs at famous restaurants, but the people running 25-seat places in Higashi-Ginza or Shirokane who are doing interesting, honest work and probably don't get asked about their journey very often. A handwritten note, or even a carefully worded message through a restaurant's contact form, explaining that you're planning to open a restaurant and deeply admire what they've built and would be grateful for 30 minutes of their time over coffee — that works more often than people expect. Restaurant owners at that scale are often isolated. They didn't go to business school together, they don't have a peer group in the way that corporate professionals do. Being asked thoughtfully by someone serious is often welcome.

On the social norm concern: I think you're right that Japan still carries some stigma around visible career pivots, particularly leaving a company like Marubeni. But that stigma applies most strongly within the corporate context itself — among colleagues, at industry events, in conversations that could circle back to your current employer. The restaurant world is a different social context entirely. Among people who have already made that jump, your situation is not unusual or embarrassing — it's familiar. They've been where you are. The norm you're navigating is specific to the world you're leaving, not the world you're entering.

One more thing worth saying as we wrap up today: what you're attempting is genuinely hard, and the planning work you're about to undertake over the next six to nine months will be demanding in ways that are different from what's demanded of you at Marubeni. But the clarity you've shown today — about what you want to build, why you want to build it, what the risks are, and what you're willing to stake — is a real asset. Most people planning restaurants are much fuzzier on all of those things at this stage. You're not. That matters.

I'd encourage you to keep this conversation going as the planning progresses. The questions will change as you get further in, and some of what seems clear right now will get complicated when it meets reality. That's normal and workable. But come back when you have specifics — a space you're evaluating, a chef candidate you're considering, a financial model you've built and want to stress-test. The more concrete the question, the more useful the conversation can be.

Good luck, Kenta. I think you're starting this the right way.

Good evening. I've been out almost every night for the past two weeks doing field research — visiting restaurants, taking notes, eating way more pasta than I probably should. It was exhausting but I think genuinely necessary. I wanted to come back to you before I started drawing any real conclusions, because I find that talking through what I've seen helps me separate what's actually signal from what's just my own preferences showing up in the data. Are you ready to hear the debrief?

Absolutely — this is exactly the kind of groundwork that separates well-positioned restaurants from the ones that open with a compelling concept and close within eighteen months. There's no substitute for primary research at this stage, and the fact that you've been systematic about it rather than just revisiting places you already liked puts you ahead of most first-time restaurateurs. Please go ahead and walk me through it in whatever order feels natural to you. I'll ask questions as we go, push back where I think something warrants scrutiny, and help you build a clearer picture of where the competitive landscape actually stands. If you have your spreadsheet nearby, even better — specific observations are always more useful than general impressions at this stage.

Good, yes, I do have the spreadsheet open. So in total I visited 14 Italian restaurants across Tokyo over those two weeks. I deliberately tried to cover a real range — different neighborhoods, different price points, different service philosophies, different ways of communicating about Italian cuisine. I was tracking things like the menu structure and how it was described, the wine list approach and depth, the service style and whether the floor staff were trained to talk about the food's origins, the rough average check size I could estimate from observing other tables, and how the restaurant described its own identity — both on the menu itself and on any signage or materials I could look at. It was genuinely intense but I feel like I have a real picture now rather than just impressions from a handful of places I happened to know from before.

Fourteen restaurants in two weeks is serious commitment — that's essentially a restaurant a day on average, and doing it with structured observation criteria rather than just eating and forming impressions puts you in a completely different position analytically. I want to understand your methodology a bit before we get into specifics, because the methodology shapes what we can conclude. When you say you covered different price points, what range are we actually talking about — what was the floor and the ceiling? And were you eating dinner, lunch, or both at these places? The distinction matters quite a bit because the competitive dynamics in Tokyo Italian dining can look quite different between those two dayparts. The margin structures are different, the customer profiles shift, and importantly, how restaurants choose to communicate their regional Italian identity — if they bother at all — can vary significantly between a weekday lunch set and a full dinner service. I want to make sure we're comparing the right things when we eventually map where you want to position Ginza Trattoria.

Good question. I did both — about nine dinners and five lunches, which felt like the right proportion since dinner is where the real positioning and identity work happens. You can get away with a lot less specificity at lunch because people are there on a tighter schedule and often a budget, but dinner is where a restaurant declares what it actually believes about Italian food. So that's where I focused most of the research energy. Price range went from casual trattorias in Ebisu and Nakameguro — we're talking 4,000 to 6,000 yen dinner tickets — all the way up to the higher-end places. I visited Ristorante Aso in Daikanyama, which is consistently ranked among the top Italian restaurants in Japan and probably the most respected name in the category in terms of pure culinary seriousness. Then on the quite premium end I went to Faro in Ginza, which is the Shiseido-operated restaurant — very polished, contemporary, strong sustainability messaging, beautiful room. And I also went to Heinz Beck in Marunouchi, obviously the most decorated of the three given his three Michelin stars at La Pergola in Rome and the reputation that name carries internationally. Those three were the anchors for understanding the upper range of the market, the ceiling of what's being done in Italian dining in Tokyo right now.

Those three are excellent benchmarks to work from because each represents a distinctly different proposition even within the premium tier — the same price range but genuinely different strategic logics underneath. Ristorante Aso in Daikanyama is built on deep personal culinary craft and a very specific biographical authenticity. Hiroyuki Aso trained extensively in Italy, and the restaurant's reputation is rooted in that story and in his ongoing relationships with Italian producers and regions. The identity comes from the chef's perspective, not from institutional backing or brand architecture. Faro in Ginza takes an almost opposite approach in terms of where the credibility comes from — it's the Shiseido house, so there's institutional weight, a strong visual identity, the Ginza address as a signal of seriousness, and a conceptual frame around sustainability and the intersection of Japanese and Italian ingredients. The restaurant's identity is partly about being a Shiseido cultural statement as much as it is about Italian cuisine specifically. And Heinz Beck in Marunouchi is essentially an imported European name — the restaurant trades on a globally recognized chef identity, which gives it a kind of instant credibility with certain audiences, particularly international visitors or Japanese diners who follow the international restaurant world closely. So you've got three different theories of how to earn the right to charge premium prices. What did you actually notice about how they differentiated themselves at the level of the food and the menu? Specifically, did any of them lean heavily into regional Italian identity — particular provinces or cooking traditions — or was the positioning more about chef philosophy and technique in general terms?

That's exactly what I was paying most careful attention to, because it goes directly to the question I'm trying to answer about my own positioning. So here's what I found. Ristorante Aso felt the most personally rooted — the menu clearly reflected Aso-san's relationships with specific Italian producers and regions, but it wasn't marketed in a didactic way as 'this is northern Italian cuisine, here is a map.' It was more like his perspective filtered through genuine knowledge and love. You could feel the geographic specificity in the ingredients and preparations without it being explained at you. Faro in Ginza was much more Tokyo-contemporary in its framing — the menu talks about Japanese and Italian ingredients in dialogue, sustainability, seasonality, the relationship between Japanese craft and Italian culinary philosophy. Very beautiful conceptually but you wouldn't really call it regionally specific to any part of Italy; it's almost post-regional. Heinz Beck is obviously Roman and Lazio-influenced, Mediterranean in its sensibility, and you feel that very clearly in the menu — but it's filtered through his very personal and quite technical style of cooking. Then when I looked at the eleven other places I visited, most of them were what I'd call 'Italian in general.' Lots of carbonara and tiramisu and arrabbiata and burrata, which is fine and clearly what sells to the broadest audience, but there's no geographic specificity to speak of. You could be in any Italian restaurant in the world. And here's the finding I kept writing down in my spreadsheet, across multiple visits: not a single restaurant I visited was clearly and primarily positioning itself around Emilia-Romagna cuisine. That felt like a genuinely significant gap.

That's a significant observation, and I want to make sure we think about it carefully rather than just treating it as straightforwardly good news, because 'no one is doing this' can mean two quite different things depending on the situation. The first interpretation is that there's an underserved audience waiting to be captured — a genuine gap in supply relative to what I'd call latent demand. People who would genuinely value a restaurant specifically focused on Emilia-Romagna cuisine exist in Tokyo, but they currently have nowhere to go that satisfies that specific want, so the gap represents opportunity. The second interpretation is that the market has already made a judgment through the collective behavior of operators and investors over time — that previous attempts to build something specifically around northern regional Italian identity either failed commercially or succeeded only by broadening out to 'Italian in general,' and that the absence of Emilia-Romagna focused restaurants reflects accumulated market knowledge rather than an oversight. Neither interpretation is obviously correct without more information. So before we treat the Emilia-Romagna gap as pure opportunity, I want to push you on three things. First, did you come across any evidence — from talking to people in the industry, from reading about Tokyo's restaurant history — of restaurants that had tried to position specifically around northern Italian or Emilian cuisine in the past and either closed or pivoted away from that framing? Second, among the fourteen places you visited, how did guests actually respond to regional specificity when it was present — did you observe people at neighboring tables engaging with the provenance storytelling, asking questions, leaning in, or did it seem to largely go over their heads as an abstract concept? And third, how did the places doing 'Italian in general' seem to be performing commercially, as best you could judge from observable signals like occupancy, table turns, and the general energy in the room?

Really fair challenges, and they're pushing on the right things. Let me take them in order. On your first question — I didn't find direct evidence of places that had tried Emilia-Romagna as an explicit positioning and then walked it back or closed. But you're right that I wasn't specifically looking for that, and I probably should have been. That's a genuine research gap I need to fill before I'm too confident. I could probably get at it through some combination of industry contacts, old restaurant review archives, and maybe reaching out to importers of Italian ingredients who would know which restaurants were serious buyers of regional Emilian products over the years. On your second question — at Ristorante Aso in Daikanyama specifically, the tables around me were definitely engaged with the regional dimension in a way that felt real rather than performative. There was a couple next to me who spent probably ten minutes asking the sommelier detailed questions about which region a particular wine came from, the specific producer, the vintage philosophy — and the sommelier gave genuinely knowledgeable, enthusiastic answers. The whole table dynamic shifted, they were leaning in, it became part of the evening rather than background. That felt like a meaningful signal that there's a real audience in Tokyo who actively wants that depth and comes specifically looking for it. At the more generic Italian places, guests seemed to be enjoying themselves but the food was functioning as a background to the social occasion — which is a completely legitimate restaurant experience and probably represents the majority of restaurant visits everywhere, but those customers aren't choosing a restaurant because it's Emilian rather than Sicilian or generically Italian. On your third question — the mid-range generic places looked commercially solid. Decent occupancy on weeknights, reasonable table turns, no obvious distress signals. But they didn't feel like destination restaurants. They felt like reliable neighborhood options, which is a perfectly sustainable business and maybe a happier one than the high-stakes destination model in some ways — but it's not the restaurant I'm trying to build.

Good, and that last distinction you're drawing — between 'destination restaurant' and 'neighborhood reliable option' — is one of the most important strategic choices in this entire venture. It should probably govern every subsequent decision you make about location, price, staffing, menu complexity, and how you communicate the concept publicly. You've essentially identified two different business models that both go by the name 'Italian restaurant' but operate on completely different logics. The neighborhood reliable option succeeds through frequency and loyalty within a defined catchment area: the same thirty or forty tables coming back once or twice a month, low customer acquisition cost, high repeat rate, sustainable occupancy even in competitive environments. The margin per cover is lower but the operational risk is lower too — you're not dependent on every table being a motivated pilgrim who made a reservation three weeks in advance specifically to experience your food. The destination restaurant succeeds by drawing customers who are willing to plan ahead, travel across the city, spend substantially more per visit, and make the evening itself feel like an event rather than a meal. You need to be remarkable enough and specific enough that the word spreads, that critics and serious food people engage with what you're doing, that the reservation becomes a small ritual. The two models require quite different real estate strategies, different labor cost structures, different assumptions about how long it takes to reach breakeven, and different marketing approaches. Based on everything you've described so far, you're clearly aiming at the destination model with Emilia-Romagna regional identity as the differentiating core. Let's connect that conceptual positioning to the actual numbers, because the gap between a compelling concept and a viable business is where most serious restaurant projects either get validated or fall apart. Last time we spoke, you mentioned a 20 to 25 seat room. Have you started forming a clear view on where the check average needs to land to make the economics work at that scale?

Yes, and this is something I've been running numbers on in parallel with the market research, trying to calibrate against what I was actually seeing in the field. My current thinking is an 8,500 yen dinner ticket as the average spend per person, excluding drinks — so the actual total check with wine pairings, digestivi, and service would be meaningfully higher, probably pushing toward 14,000 or 15,000 yen all-in per person at the high end. For lunch I'm thinking a set menu format at 1,800 yen — probably a two or three course structure, a pasta or antipasto choice followed by a pasta main and a small dessert or coffee — that lets us showcase what Emilia-Romagna cuisine actually is without the full commitment of a dinner reservation. The logic is that it acts as a lower-barrier entry point for new guests. Does that positioning make sense given everything I've described about the competitive landscape?

Let me think through both numbers carefully. The 8,500 yen dinner ticket places you in what I'd call the 'serious trattoria' tier — above the casual 4,000 to 6,000 yen range in Ebisu and Nakameguro, but well below the premium anchors. Faro in Ginza and Heinz Beck in Marunouchi are almost certainly running dinner tickets north of 20,000 yen before drinks, and Ristorante Aso in Daikanyama is probably in the 18,000 to 25,000 yen territory. At 8,500 yen you'd be distinctive enough to have an identity worth seeking out without inviting direct comparison with the Michelin universe. On the economics: 20 to 25 seats at two turns on a strong night is roughly 340,000 to 425,000 yen in food revenue before drinks. A beverage multiple of 0.5 to 0.7 is realistic at this tier, so total revenue per dinner service might be 510,000 to 720,000 yen. Meaningful — but it means consistently strong occupancy is essential; you can't absorb many half-empty nights at this room size. On the 1,800 yen lunch — I want to flag that number specifically. For a restaurant with genuine Emilia-Romagna product commitments — handmade pasta, quality charcuterie, regional cheeses — the food cost at 1,800 yen creates real pressure. Either you cut corners on those commitments and undermine the identity, or you subsidize lunch from dinner revenue, which changes the whole economic model. Why 1,800 yen specifically? How did you land on that number?

The 1,800 yen was a number I observed in the field during the lunch visits — several of the mid-range places I visited, including one in Hiroo and one near Shimbashi, were running lunch sets at that price point as an explicit foot-traffic driver and customer acquisition strategy. The front-of-house manager at one of them actually mentioned it to me directly when I was chatting with him — he said lunch at that price point is basically a loss leader that they use to introduce the restaurant to new guests who then come back for dinner. The conversion rate he described wasn't specific but he made it sound like a meaningful portion of their dinner regulars had originally come in for a cheap lunch. So the logic I'm working from is: set the barrier very low at lunch, showcase the concept as honestly as I can at that price point, and use it to build the pool of guests who've already experienced what Ginza Trattoria is about before asking them to commit to a full dinner. But you're right that the food cost math could be uncomfortable, so I need to design the lunch menu very carefully. The other thing I should mention — I'm still using the working name Ginza Trattoria, though I know I need to make a final decision on that eventually. The location question is still genuinely open, and whether Ginza actually makes sense for the concept is part of what I'm trying to figure out.

The customer acquisition logic is sound, and hearing it described in explicit strategic terms by someone actually running one of those restaurants gives it more credibility than a theoretical argument would. The key design challenge is exactly what you've identified: you need a lunch menu that feels authentically Emilian without straining food cost. Building heavily around fresh handmade pasta makes sense — tagliatelle al ragu, tortellini in brodo, something genuinely Emilian rather than generic — because handmade pasta is relatively efficient to produce once the rhythm is established and carries enormous perceived value. A small salumi selection, a pasta main, and a coffee probably works at 1,800 yen if you're disciplined about portion size. On Ginza Trattoria as a working name — the word 'trattoria' is doing real positioning work: it signals warmth and informality that distinguishes you from the ristorante register of Heinz Beck or Ristorante Aso, while still anchoring you in genuine Italian identity. If you land in Ginza the name works perfectly. But if you open in Azabu-Juban or Shirokane instead, 'Ginza' in the name creates a dissonance — guests who know Tokyo would wonder why a Ginza restaurant is somewhere else. Have you started forming a real view on location candidates, or is that being held as a separate phase?

It's been deliberately separate, yes. I made a conscious choice at the beginning of these two weeks to not let my location preferences contaminate the market research. I wanted to first understand the competitive landscape clearly, on its own terms, and then figure out where I fit into it geographically — rather than starting with 'I like Daikanyama' and then interpreting everything I saw through that lens. But I do have intuitions forming now that the research is mostly done. Ginza is hard for two reasons: the rents are extraordinarily brutal for a 20 to 25 seat room trying to hit an 8,500 yen dinner ticket, and the competition there is well-resourced — Faro in Ginza specifically is backed by Shiseido and doesn't need to be profitable in the way an independent restaurant does, so it's almost unfair competition at the neighborhood level. Daikanyama is interesting to me personally but Ristorante Aso essentially owns the Italian category there to a significant degree; opening in the same neighborhood at a lower price point risks being perceived as a lesser version of something that already exists, and that's not the story I want to tell. Azabu-Juban has the residential affluence and the concentration of foreign residents with genuine European culinary experience — people who've actually been to Bologna, who know what tortellini in brodo is supposed to taste like — and that audience feels very naturally suited to what I want to do with Emilia-Romagna cuisine. And Shirokane-Takanawa is interesting as an emerging option as that area continues to develop, though the discovery risk is higher. What I keep coming back to is the question of whether identity can substitute for location. If the Emilia-Romagna positioning is strong enough, distinctive enough, does it draw people to wherever you are?

You're not wrong to think that way, but I'd frame the relationship between identity and location slightly differently: a strong identity is a necessary condition for a destination restaurant, but it's not sufficient on its own to overcome a genuine location problem. The destination model works when the identity is compelling enough that a meaningful number of people make a plan specifically to experience it — they look up your restaurant, they put it in their calendar, they bring someone they want to impress. That behavior can overcome a lot of geographic inconvenience, and there are destination restaurants all over Tokyo in neighborhoods you wouldn't necessarily expect that succeed precisely because they've built that kind of intentional following. But there's still a threshold of accessibility and basic discoverability below which even a very compelling identity can't pull customers reliably enough to sustain the economics. If you're in a location where the walk from the station is confusing, or there's no natural foot traffic at all, or the neighborhood itself sends a signal that conflicts with the concept, you're fighting gravity on multiple fronts simultaneously. Azabu-Juban is genuinely worth taking seriously as a primary candidate for the reasons you mentioned, and I'd add a couple of things to your analysis. The foreign resident concentration there does skew toward people with real European cultural exposure — not Italy-as-a-category in the abstract, but people who've actually traveled, who've eaten at genuine trattorias in Bologna or Parma or Modena, who understand what makes the cooking of Emilia-Romagna different from the rest of Italy. That's a built-in audience for the kind of specificity and depth you're proposing, and they're more likely to become vocal advocates — the kind of early guests who tell five friends — because they have a reference point to recognize what you're doing. It's also a neighborhood where an 8,500 yen dinner ticket doesn't require justification; it fits the local context without friction. The Daikanyama analysis is astute and I agree with the logic — you don't want to open in the same neighborhood as the strongest player in your category even if you're not directly competing at the same price tier, because the comparison is forced on you by geography and you're unlikely to win it. For the next session, I'd suggest we build a structured location evaluation framework — something that weights rent-to-revenue ratios against each other, catchment demographics, proximity to category competitors, foot traffic patterns, and visibility from the street. That would give you a way to compare the candidates rigorously rather than going on intuition alone, which is important when you're about to make a commitment of the size and duration a restaurant lease represents. But before we close tonight — stepping back from location for a moment — given everything you've actually seen and experienced across those 14 Italian restaurants over two weeks, what's your current conviction level on the Emilia-Romagna positioning? Is it stronger now than when you started the research, weaker, or roughly the same?

Honestly? Much stronger. I went in with a hypothesis and hoping to find a gap, and I found it — but what I didn't expect was that the evidence would be as clear as it was. Not a single one of the 14 restaurants I visited was doing what I want to do with Emilia-Romagna cuisine in a serious, sustained way. More than that, I found that the places doing the most rigorous work on Italian regional identity were the ones that felt the most alive as restaurants — the ones where the guests were genuinely engaged rather than just eating and talking about something else. That couple at Ristorante Aso asking the sommelier about the wine's regional origin for ten minutes — that's exactly the table I want to be running. And seeing that the Emilia-Romagna gap was real, that no one was flying that flag specifically, felt less like a warning sign and more like an invitation. I know there are still risks I need to stress-test. I know I need to do much more work on the location question and on the financial model before this is anything more than a concept with good market research behind it. But the two weeks of field work made me more confident in the direction, not less, and the confidence is coming from evidence rather than from just wanting it to be true. I think that distinction matters.

It does matter, and it's the right distinction to be drawing. The difference between conviction that comes from evidence and conviction that comes from desire is the difference between a well-calibrated business judgment and a motivated belief — and in a venture of this scale, those two things lead to very different outcomes. What you've done over these two weeks isn't just confirm a preference. You visited 14 Italian restaurants with a structured observation framework, you anchored your analysis against the top of the market at Ristorante Aso in Daikanyama, Faro in Ginza, and Heinz Beck in Marunouchi, you identified a specific and nameable gap in Emilia-Romagna positioning, and you watched how real customers in real restaurants responded to regional specificity versus generic Italian. That's a genuine evidentiary foundation. The Emilia-Romagna gap held up under serious scrutiny. Here is where I'd suggest focusing your energy before we meet again. First, fill the one research gap you identified yourself: look specifically for any historical cases of Emilia-Romagna focused restaurants in Tokyo that didn't survive, or that survived by abandoning that specific framing. That's the counter-evidence that's currently missing from your picture, and until you've looked for it and either found it or not found it, there's a small but real risk that you're benefiting from a survivor bias in your research. Talk to importers of Italian products, read old restaurant columns, ask anyone you know with roots in the Italian food business in Japan. Second, start building a rough but honest financial model around the 8,500 yen dinner ticket and the 1,800 yen lunch set — even estimates of rent at 300 to 400 yen per square meter per month in Azabu-Juban, labor as a percentage of revenue, and food cost percentage will tell you quickly whether those price points are viable at 20 to 25 seats or whether you need to go higher on the dinner ticket. The numbers don't need to be precise at this stage but they need to be honest. Third, start the location research in earnest, with Azabu-Juban as your first serious candidate to evaluate. The Emilia-Romagna identity is clear. The two weeks of research have validated that there's a gap worth pursuing. The next phase is proving that the economics can actually support the concept you've built in your head — and that work is just as important as anything you did in the field. You've done the hardest part of the strategic thinking. Now it needs to survive contact with the numbers.

Hey, it's been a busy couple of weeks. I've been heads-down drafting the business plan and I finally got to sit down with my accountant for a full working session yesterday. I walked in with a rough spreadsheet and we spent about three hours going through it together. I feel like I have a much clearer picture of the numbers now, but I want to talk through them because there are a few things I'm still not sure I fully believe. Can I walk you through what we built?

Please do. The move from concept to an actual financial model is one of the most clarifying — and sometimes humbling — steps in this whole process. Who are you working with on the accounting side? That context helps me understand whether to trust the framework or probe it.

His name is Hiroshi Tanabe — he runs a boutique firm called Tanabe & Partners. Their office is at 2-7-3 Shibuya, Daiichi-Bunko Building 5F. A friend from my Marubeni days introduced me. Tanabe-san has done the accounting and business plan work for three other restaurant startups in Tokyo, which was the main reason I chose him over a larger firm. He knows the specific cost structure for F&B businesses, which I figured mattered more than general credentials.

That's the right call. Restaurant accounting has genuine domain specifics — the timing of prepaid deposits, pre-opening inventory builds, how to model beverage attach rates, the way tip and service charge accounting intersects with labor calculations in Japan. A generalist will get the math right but miss the nuances that matter most when you're pitching a loan officer or projecting cash flow for an unfamiliar format.

So walk me through it. What's the headline revenue figure he landed on?

The projected monthly revenue at full capacity is 4.2 million yen. That's based on 24 seats — we've firmed up on 24 rather than the 20 to 25 range I was floating earlier — running dinner Tuesday through Sunday, and adding lunch service on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Tanabe-san modeled an average dinner ticket of 8,500 yen per person all-in, food and drinks combined, and lunch at 1,800 yen. Full capacity means every seat filled at every service. He was clear that's a theoretical ceiling, not an operating expectation, but it's the reference point the whole model is anchored to.

The 4.2 million yen full-capacity figure is reasonable as a ceiling anchor, and it's useful that the 8,500 yen dinner average includes beverages — that's an important distinction. If it were food-only, you'd be leaving a meaningful revenue line off the projection entirely, since wine at a northern Italian trattoria can add 2,500 to 4,000 yen per person easily. At 8,500 yen all-in with a quality wine program, that's an attainable number but not a padded one — the reference restaurants you visited during your research were in the 7,500 to 12,000 yen range, so you're positioned toward the accessible end of that spread.

A few things I'd probe before accepting the model. First, what seat turn rate is baked in for dinner? Two seatings on 24 covers gives you 48 dinner covers per night maximum, but that assumes clean back-to-back timing. If your first seating runs long or your second seating arrives early, you lose the gap and the second seating becomes chaotic. Tanabe-san's model may be assuming cleaner turn discipline than you'll actually have in the first months of operation.

Second, what utilization rate did he use for the working projection — the number he actually expects rather than the ceiling?

He used 70% as the medium-term utilization assumption. He said that's typical for a new restaurant that's settled in, maybe month three or four of operation. So the working monthly projection for month three is around 2.94 million yen — which is 70% of the 4.2 million yen ceiling. On the cost side we mapped out food cost at 30% of revenue, labor at 35%, rent and utilities at 18%, and a catch-all for admin, supplies, insurance, and depreciation at about 12%. That totals 95%, leaving a 5% operating margin at the 70% scenario. Tanabe-san said 5% is thin but typical for year one in Tokyo, and that it should improve as we move up the utilization curve.

Five percent at 70% utilization is thin but not unrealistic, and Tanabe-san is right that it tends to improve as volume increases — fixed costs don't scale with revenue, so every incremental cover above breakeven contributes more to margin than the average. That said, I want to flag two specific risk areas in that cost structure.

Food cost at 30% is achievable if your menu is pasta and vegetable-forward, which northern Italian naturally is. But it's highly sensitive to your protein mix. Imported Italian ingredients — Parmigiano-Reggiano, prosciutto di Parma, high-quality bresaola — can push individual dish food costs well above 40%. The blended average of 30% works if your high-margin pasta and vegetable dishes carry enough of the volume. Worth asking Tanabe-san whether that 30% was derived from a menu cost build or is a rule of thumb from his other restaurant clients.

Labor at 35% is honest for a startup that intends to execute well. Kitchen wages in Tokyo are competitive right now, and if you want a skilled head chef capable of executing Emilia-Romagna cuisine properly, you're going to pay for it. That 35% may actually run higher in the first six months if you're staffing full during low-volume lunch services.

The 18% rent-and-utilities line is the one I can't evaluate yet. That has to be anchored to an actual lease number. Once you sign a lease, that percentage either holds or it doesn't — and if rent comes in higher than the model implies, the 5% margin disappears fast. What's the actual monthly rent figure Tanabe-san is working with, or is he still using a placeholder?

It's still a placeholder — we haven't signed a lease yet, so he used a percentage assumption that he calibrated from his other restaurant clients in similar Tokyo neighborhoods. He's planning to revise the entire model once we lock in a property. He wanted to get the structural logic right first, then update the inputs. That makes sense to me, but I know it means the 5% margin could shift significantly depending on where we land.

The thing I most wanted to walk through with you is the breakeven analysis. Tanabe-san calculated that we need 38 covers per day average to break even — that's across all services, dinner and lunch combined, averaged over the operating month. When he showed me that number I wasn't immediately sure whether it was achievable or whether it was too optimistic. What do you think?

Let me work through the math with you. In a typical operating month you'd have around 26 days open — Tuesday through Sunday. You have 6 lunch services in that window and 24 dinner services, so about 30 total services. At 38 covers per day average, your monthly total is roughly 988 covers. If dinner covers outnumber lunch covers at approximately a 3-to-1 ratio given the frequency difference, and you weight them at 8,500 yen dinner and 1,800 yen lunch respectively, the implied monthly revenue at breakeven lands somewhere around 2.6 to 2.8 million yen. That's about 62 to 67 percent of your 4.2 million yen full-capacity ceiling.

Hitting breakeven at 65% of capacity is a structurally sound position. You have genuine upside if the restaurant fills above that, and you don't need a perfect restaurant to stop burning cash. The question is how long it takes to reach 65% — and that's where the ramp-up assumptions matter more than the breakeven figure itself.

The other thing worth sitting with is that 38 covers per day average is a blended number that can mask very uneven distribution. A slow Tuesday dinner might produce 10 covers. A Saturday with both lunch and dinner might produce 60. The monthly average can look fine while you're hemorrhaging cash on every Tuesday and Wednesday. Does the model have any day-of-week granularity, or is it purely a monthly average?

It's a monthly average — no day-of-week breakdown. I noticed the same thing you're pointing at when I was doing research visits. The mid-range Italian restaurants I went to over the past two weeks were noticeably quieter on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, even at places that seemed to be doing well overall. The ones with steady weeknight numbers all seemed to have either strong repeat regulars or a corporate clientele coming in on expense accounts.

On the ramp-up, Tanabe-san modeled it in three stages: month one at 40% utilization, month two at 55%, month three at 70%. He calculated the cumulative cash burn from those three months — the operating shortfall before you get to breakeven — at about 3.5 million yen. That's what drove the loan discussion. We're planning to borrow from Japan Finance Corporation. The application is for 15 million yen at 1.85% interest. That's meant to cover the ramp-up shortfall and also fund a meaningful portion of the fit-out and equipment.

Japan Finance Corporation is the right institutional choice for this type of startup, and 1.85% is a favorable rate. The JFC's new enterprise loan programs are specifically structured for small business founders without an operating track record — that's exactly your situation. A commercial bank would almost certainly want collateral, a guarantor, and two to three years of business tax returns before lending 15 million yen to a first-time restaurateur. JFC's underwriting logic is different: they're evaluating the credibility of the plan and the character of the applicant, which is why Tanabe-san's experience preparing those applications matters.

At 15 million yen and 1.85% over a typical seven-year term, your monthly debt service would run roughly 200,000 to 210,000 yen. At your month-three projected revenue of 2.94 million yen, that's about 7% of revenue going to debt service — manageable but not invisible. It does compress the already-thin 5% operating margin, so you'll likely be running near breakeven at 70% utilization even after you stabilize, at least until revenue grows further.

One thing I want to flag on the ramp-up projection: 40% utilization in month one assumes you're at meaningful volume essentially from day one. For a restaurant positioning at 8,500 yen average ticket, word-of-mouth and early press coverage typically take time to build. A 40% fill rate in week two of operation is aggressive unless you have a deliberate pre-launch strategy — a guest list for early seatings, a relationship with someone who can generate early Tabelog reviews, or a soft opening event that primes the room before you open to the public. Does Tanabe-san's model account for any dead time in the literal first two weeks?

He acknowledged that the first two weeks are probably optimistic in the model. His suggestion was to add 500,000 yen to the contingency buffer to absorb that, which means in practice the 15 million yen loan request from Japan Finance Corporation is sized to cover the ramp-up shortfall, the extra contingency, and leave roughly 4 to 5 million yen in unallocated reserve after all startup costs are paid. The personal savings contribution is going toward the bulk of the fit-out and equipment spend.

He also ran a downside scenario — what happens if the ramp-up is slower than expected and we're only at 50% utilization through month four. In that case the reserve gets eroded by month seven or eight, and we'd need to either find additional capital or make significant cost cuts. That scenario is uncomfortable but it's not impossible, especially if we're in a competitive location or if something goes wrong in the kitchen in the early weeks. I'd rather know that now than discover it in month six.

Running that downside scenario proactively is exactly what you should be doing. Month seven or eight with an exhausted reserve is a genuinely difficult position — you're too far in to walk away, but you haven't yet built the reputation and repeat customer base that would let you raise prices or reliably fill the room. The restaurants that fail at that stage usually do so because they had no visibility into the problem until it was already urgent.

The critical thing to work out now, while the numbers are theoretical, is what your action triggers are. If by the end of month two you're tracking at 35% utilization instead of 55%, what specific action do you take? Cut a lunch service? Reduce kitchen staffing on quiet nights? Run a promotional evening for the first seating? None of those decisions are obvious in the moment unless you've pre-committed to a response framework. I'd encourage you to build one of those with Tanabe-san — not just the scenario model, but the explicit decision rules that go with it.

I also want to make sure I understand the full capital picture. You mentioned the 15 million yen loan from Japan Finance Corporation covers the ramp-up and reserve. What is your total pre-opening spend projected at — fit-out, equipment, key money, deposits, licensing, pre-opening inventory — and how does your personal savings contribution cover that alongside the loan?

Total pre-opening outlay is estimated at 22 to 25 million yen, depending heavily on how the fit-out bids come in. Tanabe-san said renovation and equipment usually account for the biggest variance. My plan is to put in 12 to 13 million yen from personal savings toward the pre-opening spend, and the 15 million yen from Japan Finance Corporation covers the remainder of the startup costs plus the ramp-up operating shortfall and reserve we discussed. Total available capital between loan and savings is roughly 27 to 28 million yen. Against a 22 to 25 million yen burn to reach opening day, that leaves somewhere between 3 and 6 million yen as working capital depending on how the fit-out goes.

Tanabe-san said he'd feel more comfortable if the working capital floor were at least 6 million yen. We might increase the personal contribution slightly to ensure that, but I want to see the fit-out bids before committing to anything. The whole structure feels directionally right to me, but I'm aware there's a lot of uncertainty in the cost inputs still.

The capital structure is directionally sound. Twenty-seven to twenty-eight million yen against a 22 to 25 million yen pre-opening spend leaves real margin for error, and Tanabe-san's instinct to want a 6 million yen working capital floor is well-calibrated — it gives you roughly two to three months of operating costs as a buffer even if the ramp-up is slower than the base case.

The area I'd keep pressure on is the fit-out cost range. A 3 million yen spread between your low and high pre-opening estimates is significant when working capital is the variable that adjusts. Renovation bids for restaurant spaces in Tokyo can vary enormously depending on the condition of the existing build-out, what the previous tenant left behind, and whether you need significant electrical or ventilation work. When you go into the location scouting phase, it's worth asking whether properties have any usable kitchen infrastructure remaining — that alone can be worth 2 to 4 million yen in renovation savings.

On the JFC application specifically: Tanabe-san mentioned that the interview runs 60 to 90 minutes and that the number one rejection reason is applicants who can't speak fluently to their own cost structure. You're in a good position there because you've been working through these numbers actively. But I'd suggest one specific preparation exercise before the interview. Take the two headline figures — the 4.2 million yen full-capacity revenue and the 38 covers per day average breakeven — and practice deriving them from first principles out loud. Not reciting them, but building them from the inputs: seats, ticket, services, cost structure. If you can walk an interviewer through that arithmetic naturally, it signals you own the model rather than just presenting it.

That's really useful framing. Tanabe-san is targeting the end of April for the JFC application submission, which gives us about four weeks. He'll handle the financial modeling section and the loan narrative, but I need to write the market research section and a personal background statement. He said the JFC reviewer will spend significant time on both, because the market research section is where they evaluate whether the applicant actually understands their competitive environment — not just the internal financials. The personal background statement is where they form a view on whether the founder has the judgment to run the business through difficulty.

Honestly I feel more prepared than I expected after going through all this. The market research I have is solid — 14 restaurants visited, clear positioning rationale, price comparisons.
