The numbers I can speak to. The thing I want to make sure I can do is connect them in a way that's internally consistent rather than just answering individual questions in isolation.

That internal consistency is exactly what distinguishes a fundable application from a collection of plausible-sounding numbers. The JFC reviewer has seen hundreds of business plans. They know when someone is reciting projected figures versus when they understand why those figures are what they are. The connection you need to make — and to be able to make conversationally, not just on paper — is the through-line from your market positioning to your revenue assumptions to your cost structure to your capital requirements.

Here is that through-line stated plainly: northern Italian cuisine in the Emilia-Romagna tradition is underrepresented in the Tokyo market relative to demand, as evidenced by the price premiums at the small number of operators doing it well. Your 8,500 yen average dinner ticket is attainable because comparable restaurants in that segment operate at 8,000 to 12,000 yen and sustain strong occupancy. Your food cost can hold at 30% because the menu is pasta and grain-forward, which has structurally lower ingredient cost than protein-heavy French or contemporary Japanese cuisines. Your labor at 35% is honest because executing this cuisine well requires trained kitchen talent. And the 15 million yen loan from Japan Finance Corporation at 1.85% is sized to bridge the ramp-up period before the 38 covers per day average breakeven becomes self-sustaining — not to fund the core startup, which your personal savings contribution covers.

If you can speak that narrative clearly, you'll be fine in the interview. The numbers you have — the 4.2 million yen capacity ceiling, the breakeven cover count, the loan terms — are all defensible. The job between now and the JFC application is to make sure you can tell the story that connects them.

Hey, good to connect again. So I've been on the ground for the past three weeks doing location scouting — basically living out of Hamada's car at this point — and I finally feel like I have a real, empirical picture of the market instead of just assumptions based on places I've eaten at over the years. I wanted to walk you through everything I found and get your perspective on how each neighborhood fits with what Ginza Trattoria is trying to be. It's a lot of material, so I want to be organized about it. Would you prefer I go neighborhood by neighborhood, or would it be more useful to hit the strongest candidates first and then work backward through the runners-up?

Great to hear you've been doing the legwork seriously — three weeks on the ground will teach you things that no amount of desk research or market reports can capture, because you're reading the actual energy of those streets at different times of day, in different weather, on weekdays and weekends. That texture matters enormously for a restaurant concept.

I'd say let's go neighborhood by neighborhood rather than starting with the top candidates. Here's the reasoning: if we jump straight to your favorites, we lose the comparative framing. Part of what makes a location decision good is understanding what you're not choosing and why — it keeps the logic honest and it also helps us spot whether your top pick is genuinely right or whether it's just the best of a flawed shortlist. We also might find that a neighborhood you're currently ranking lower has a specific attribute that addresses a concern you haven't articulated yet.

As you go through each area, I want to hear about: the physical spaces themselves, the street-level feel at the times when dinner service would be running, the demographic you actually observed rather than assumed, the rent range, and any landlord or lease dynamics that came up. We can map each of those against the Ginza Trattoria concept as we go — the mid-to-upscale northern Italian positioning, the 40-to-55-seat target, the wine program, the occasion-dining frame. Ready when you are — where did you start?

Alright, let me set the stage first. The broker I've been working with is Yusuke Hamada from Plaza Homes Commercial. He was introduced to me by my college friend Daichi Sasaki — Daichi opened a wine bar in Ebisu about two years ago and used Hamada for that search, and he said Hamada was the only broker he met who actually understood hospitality spaces as opposed to just treating them like generic retail boxes. That recommendation turned out to be well-founded. Hamada has been incredibly thorough and proactive throughout this whole process.

What he did was pull together a comprehensive initial list of 23 properties spread across five neighborhoods, and over the past three weeks we physically walked every single one of them together. Not just looked at photos or floor plans — actually walked in, measured, looked at the exhaust routing, checked the electrical panels, stood outside for twenty minutes watching foot traffic. That's why I feel confident we're not missing anything obvious in these five areas. The neighborhoods are Nishi-Azabu, Higashi-Azabu, Hiroo, Yoyogi-Uehara, and Kagurazaka. Very different vibes, and honestly some of them surprised me in ways I didn't expect going in.

Shall I start with Nishi-Azabu? That was the first area we covered, and because it was first it became my mental benchmark for comparing everything else.

That context about Yusuke Hamada from Plaza Homes Commercial is genuinely reassuring. The distinction you're describing — a broker who understands hospitality spaces rather than treating them like standard retail — is not a small thing. Restaurant spaces have specific requirements around ventilation and exhaust systems, electrical load capacity for kitchen equipment, structural tolerance for grease traps, floor-load bearing for walk-in coolers, and sometimes acoustic isolation concerns depending on the building type. A broker who has placed food-and-beverage tenants before knows to look at all of that during the walkthrough rather than leaving it for the tenant to discover post-signing. The fact that your college friend Daichi Sasaki vouched for Hamada based on an actual successful opening is also meaningful — it's real-world validation, not just a reputation.

Walking all 23 properties physically across five neighborhoods is the right approach. You cannot evaluate a restaurant location from a floor plan. The sight lines from the street, the quality of natural light, the ambient noise level from neighboring tenants, the slope of the entryway, the dimensions of the service corridor — all of those are things you need your body in the space to understand. So you've done this correctly.

Nishi-Azabu as your benchmark makes complete sense. It's one of the most established and legible upscale-dining corridors in central Tokyo, which means it gives you a clear reference point for everything else. Walk me through what you found there — the spaces, the street atmosphere, and especially the economics, because Nishi-Azabu rents are the number I'm most curious about.

Nishi-Azabu was exactly what I expected in some ways and significantly more complicated in others. The three spaces Hamada showed me there were all roughly the right footprint — we're looking at 40 to 55 tsubo of net floor area, which is what the kitchen layout requires to give us the service flow we want without cramping the dining room. Two of the three had previous restaurant tenants, which meant the basic infrastructure — exhaust ducting, grease traps, gas routing — was already in place. That saves real time and money on the fit-out, and Hamada estimated the pre-existing infrastructure was worth somewhere between 3 and 5 million yen in avoided construction costs depending on how much we'd need to modify it.

The street feel in Nishi-Azabu at dinner time is genuinely strong. I went back on a Wednesday evening and a Saturday evening to compare, and the Saturday experience was particularly convincing. At 7pm on a Saturday the foot traffic on the main corridor is dense and the demographic walking past is clearly the one we're after: couples in their late thirties and forties dressed for a proper evening out, small expense-account groups of four and five, a real mix of Japanese professionals and foreign residents, very few large families or teenagers. It felt exactly like the customer base Ginza Trattoria is designed for.

The problem, and it's a real one, is the rent. Hamada put together a detailed comparison sheet for all the Nishi-Azabu units and the range was coming in between 85,000 and 105,000 yen per tsubo per month. I brought those numbers to Hiroshi Tanabe, my accountant, and he ran them through the unit economics model we built in Session 3. His conclusion was that we shouldn't go above 95,000 yen per tsubo in Ginza-level locations, and even that figure he described as aggressive for a first opening with no proven track record at this address. So Nishi-Azabu puts us right at or above that ceiling depending on which unit you're looking at. I loved the feel of the area, but I'm not sure the math supports it without a very aggressive negotiation on the lower-priced unit.

The tension you're describing — strong concept-fit but rent economics that are right at the edge — is probably the most common trap in premium Tokyo restaurant location searches, and the fact that you caught it analytically rather than emotionally is important. Many operators fall in love with a neighborhood and then try to make the numbers work afterward, which is when you start seeing optimistic covers-per-night assumptions and revenue projections that assume 90% occupancy from month two. That's how restaurants fail even when the food is excellent.

Hiroshi Tanabe's ceiling of 95,000 yen per tsubo is not arbitrary conservatism. Let me put some texture on why that number matters. At a 45-tsubo footprint — splitting the difference on your target range — the gap between an 85,000 yen per tsubo unit and a 105,000 yen per tsubo unit is 900,000 yen per month in base rent, before any common area maintenance charges or administrative fees. That's 10.8 million yen per year. To service that additional rent purely from food and beverage revenue, assuming a 35% rent-to-revenue ratio, you'd need to add roughly 30 million yen in annual revenue — which at an average check of 15,000 yen per person translates to roughly 2,000 additional covers per year, or about six additional fully-seated tables per week. In the first year, when you're still building the reservation base and word-of-mouth hasn't fully activated yet, that gap is genuine operational risk, not just a line item.

That said, I wouldn't close the door on Nishi-Azabu quite yet. The range you quoted — 85,000 to 105,000 — tells us there's real variance within that corridor, which means something is driving the spread. Age and condition of the building, landlord motivation, vacancy duration — any of those could explain a 20,000 yen per tsubo gap. You mentioned the corner unit has been sitting empty for about eight months. That's potentially meaningful. A landlord who has been carrying a vacant restaurant space for eight months, paying property taxes and building maintenance with zero rent income, is in a different negotiating posture than one who just received their first inquiry on a unit that came to market last week. Did Hamada have any intelligence on the landlord situation for the corner unit specifically — whether it's individual ownership or a property management company, and whether there's any flexibility on free-rent periods or fit-out contribution?

On the corner unit — Hamada said the owner is an individual, older gentleman, probably late sixties, who inherited the building from his father. He's not a professional property manager. Hamada's read is that he's been holding out for a certain rent number because that's what his last tenant paid, but he's starting to feel the vacancy pain. There might be room to have a real conversation there, especially if we come in with a credible business plan and a strong personal presentation. Hamada actually suggested that the right move might be to request a meeting with the owner directly rather than negotiating through the agent layer, because that kind of landlord tends to make decisions based on trust in the person rather than purely on the numbers. I thought that was an interesting piece of advice.

Let me move to Higashi-Azabu, because I want to get through all five before we start ranking. Higashi-Azabu was interesting and honestly a bit of a surprise. I went in expecting it to feel like a diminished version of Nishi-Azabu — same general area, slightly less premium — but it really doesn't read that way at all. It has its own distinct identity. The streets are quieter, much more residential in character, and there are almost no chain establishments of any kind. What you find instead is a cluster of what I'd describe as serious, intentional restaurants that seem to operate entirely on reservations and word of mouth. They're not depending on walk-in traffic at all, and some of them appear to be thriving.

The rents in Higashi-Azabu were noticeably lower than Nishi-Azabu. Hamada quoted 68,000 to 78,000 yen per tsubo for the units we looked at, so we're comfortably under Tanabe's ceiling across the board. The spaces themselves varied more in quality. One was excellent — a second-floor unit with a proper staircase entry, good ceiling height, and an exhaust system that was already spec'd for a serious kitchen. The other two were more raw and would need meaningful construction investment.

Here's my concern about Higashi-Azabu. Ginza Trattoria isn't going to open with a built-in reservation list. We don't have a celebrity chef with an existing Tokyo following or a PR agency running a six-month pre-launch media campaign. We need to earn our customer base from scratch over the first twelve months, and that means early foot traffic for awareness-building is genuinely important. My worry is that Higashi-Azabu rewards restaurants that already have a reputation, and isn't particularly forgiving of newcomers who need discovery traffic to build one. Does that concern make sense, or am I being too pessimistic about our ability to drive early reservations through other means?

Your concern is legitimate, and it maps onto a real structural dynamic in how Higashi-Azabu restaurants build their customer base. The ones that thrive there — and I think you've accurately read the neighborhood — tend to arrive with at least one of three things already in place: a chef who has a reputation that travels independently of the location, a built-in private client network from a previous restaurant or catering relationship, or a pre-launch PR campaign that puts the reservation list at 60% before the doors open. You're right that opening without any of those things into a discovery-poor environment is a harder path in the first six to twelve months.

The second-floor unit you described is genuinely interesting, though, and I want to push back slightly on one point. Second-floor restaurant entries in Tokyo function as a filter in both directions. Yes, they eliminate casual walk-ins — but you'd lose most of that traffic in Higashi-Azabu anyway, so the cost of the filter is lower than it would be in Nishi-Azabu or Hiroo. What the second-floor entry gives you in return is a sense of arrival and occasion that is very difficult to manufacture in a ground-floor street-level space. The act of climbing a staircase, seeing the room open up above you — that primes the guest for an experience. At the price point Ginza Trattoria is targeting, that psychological framing has real value.

The practical question for Higashi-Azabu is whether you have any levers to drive the first 500 covers. Do you have a corporate network — companies who might book private dinners or wine-pairing events in the first few months? Are you planning to join any reservation platforms at launch, and do you have a relationship with any food media or hospitality press contacts who might cover the opening? The answers to those questions change the risk calculation meaningfully. A restaurant that can fill 70% of its tables through advance reservations from day one can survive in Higashi-Azabu. One that depends on street-level discovery to hit that number is in trouble there.

I'll flag the second-floor unit as worth keeping on the shortlist even if Higashi-Azabu doesn't end up being the winner. Now tell me about Hiroo — that one I'm particularly curious about because the foreign resident density there is genuinely among the highest in the city, and for a northern Italian concept that leans heavily on wine, that demographic can be very valuable.

Hiroo was one of the more interesting and in some ways most legible stops. The international community there is real and highly visible — you notice it immediately just walking the streets, which have a character unlike any other residential area in central Tokyo. The French school generates a lot of family traffic in the afternoon, and there are several embassies within walking distance, which brings an international professional population that tends to have genuine cultural familiarity with European food and wine. These are people who've lived in Milan or Lyon or Madrid, who understand the difference between a Barolo and a Barbera, who have strong opinions about pasta al dente. That demographic aligns well with the northern Italian positioning — better, honestly, than almost any other neighborhood in the city.

Hamada showed me four properties in Hiroo. The rents ranged from 72,000 to 82,000 yen per tsubo — better than Nishi-Azabu, comfortably under Tanabe's ceiling at the upper end. The spaces themselves were a mixed bag. One ground-floor unit on a reasonably trafficked street was very promising in terms of size and infrastructure; it had a previous food-and-beverage tenant and the extraction system was already in and functioning. A second-floor unit similar to the Higashi-Azabu one was also worth noting — smaller, 38 tsubo, which is slightly under our target range, but with a nice intimate quality that might work if the kitchen layout could be compressed.

The challenge in Hiroo that I haven't fully worked out is parking. The area isn't good for street parking and none of the four units we looked at came with dedicated parking spaces. For a mid-to-upscale dinner restaurant, that's a real consideration — especially for longer multicourse evenings where guests might want to drive home rather than taking a taxi late at night with a few glasses of wine in them. Hamada suggested we could negotiate a block of monthly reserved spaces at a nearby parking structure, maybe four or five spots, and position them as a guest amenity. But that adds a cost line. How important do you think parking actually is for this kind of concept in central Tokyo?

Parking is a real consideration but I think it's probably lower in the decision hierarchy than you're currently weighing it, and here's why. The behavioral pattern for this kind of concept in central Tokyo — mid-to-upscale dinner restaurant, two-to-three-hour multicourse experience, alcohol program as a significant revenue driver — skews very strongly toward train, taxi, and now ride-share for arrival and departure. The guests you're targeting are sophisticated urban consumers who have internalized that driving to dinner means not drinking at dinner, and at a restaurant where a well-chosen wine pairing is part of the appeal, most of them will make the calculation to leave the car at home without needing to be told.

That's not to say parking is irrelevant — some guests will drive, particularly those coming from further residential areas like Setagaya or Meguro where train connections to Hiroo require a transfer, and for that group, a confirmed parking arrangement at a nearby structure genuinely removes friction. Hamada's suggestion of four or five contracted spaces presented as a guest amenity is actually the right answer. You offer it at reservation confirmation: 'We have a small number of reserved spaces at the structure two minutes' walk away; please let us know when you book if you'd like us to reserve one.' It turns what could be a negative into a service point.

The monthly cost will likely be in the range of 30,000 to 40,000 yen per space at a Hiroo-area structure, so call it 150,000 to 200,000 yen per month for five spaces. That's real money, but if you're already under Tanabe's ceiling on the base rent, the parking cost doesn't push you over the threshold on the overall occupancy cost calculation. It becomes a line item in the operating budget rather than a deal-breaker on the location.

Hiroo's international resident base is genuinely one of the strongest assets in your shortlist. The French school families and embassy communities develop strong restaurant loyalties, and they refer aggressively within their own networks once they trust a place. You can realistically envision a scenario where two or three embassy families become regulars in the first six months and introduce Ginza Trattoria to forty or fifty other households through dinner party recommendations. That kind of network-driven growth is much faster and more capital-efficient than building a following from zero through advertising.

What did you find at Yoyogi-Uehara? I know that one was Hamada's addition and might have seemed like a stretch geographically — I'm curious what changed your view when you actually walked it.

Yoyogi-Uehara was the one I was most skeptical about before the visit, and it ended up being one of the more thought-provoking stops, even if my conclusion is complicated. Hamada included it based on his read of where the dining culture in Tokyo is moving over the next five years rather than where it is right now, which I thought was an interesting framing from a broker.

Walking the neighborhood absolutely changes the picture. It has evolved meaningfully over the last five or six years. There's a genuine food culture that's developed there, not manufactured or themed but organic — chef-owner places, natural wine bars, small producers doing interesting things with Japanese ingredients. The residents skew younger than Hiroo or Nishi-Azabu, probably late twenties to early forties on average, but they are food-literate and willing to spend on quality in a way that's different from status-driven spending. They care about provenance and craft. A Barolo matters to them because of what it is, not because of what it signals.

The economics in Yoyogi-Uehara are the most attractive we saw across all five areas. Hamada quoted rents of 55,000 to 68,000 yen per tsubo, which is far enough under Tanabe's ceiling that it meaningfully changes the break-even picture. The spaces themselves were some of the more architecturally interesting ones in the whole 23-property search — more character, better natural light in a couple of them, and because fewer had pre-existing restaurant buildouts we'd actually have more freedom on the kitchen layout rather than being constrained by an inherited infrastructure that doesn't quite fit what we want to do.

But here's where I get stuck. Ginza Trattoria, as a concept name and a brand positioning, implies something central and establishment-facing. When I imagine our ideal customer searching for an occasion dinner and encountering the name Ginza Trattoria, I think they're mentally placing us somewhere between Roppongi and Ginza — not in Yoyogi-Uehara. There might be a brand dissonance that actually works against us in that neighborhood, not because the food culture there is wrong, but because the name and the neighborhood tell different stories. Would we be fighting our own positioning just by being there? I haven't resolved that in my head.

I'll save Kagurazaka for last because honestly it might be my top pick right now, and I have the most to say about it.

The brand dissonance question you're raising about Yoyogi-Uehara is real and it's the right thing to be articulating. Let me try to be precise about what the problem actually is, because I think it's slightly different from what you've described.

The issue isn't just that 'Ginza Trattoria' implies a geographic location and Yoyogi-Uehara isn't it. Restaurant names regularly depart from literal geographic accuracy and guests accept that quickly once the experience justifies the name. The deeper issue is register. 'Ginza Trattoria' signals a particular mode of dining — formal enough to be an occasion, central enough to be a destination, establishment-facing enough to be appropriate for business entertainment and significant anniversaries. The Yoyogi-Uehara food culture you've described — chef-owner, natural wine, craft-focused, organically developed — operates in a fundamentally different register. It's anti-establishment in its appeal. It rewards people who found the place before it was known. The restaurant that works in Yoyogi-Uehara is one that leans into discovery, not one that positions itself as a destination you're supposed to know about.

What this means practically is that the Yoyogi-Uehara economics, attractive as they are at 55,000 to 68,000 yen per tsubo, belong to a different concept than Ginza Trattoria. If you were opening something called Osteria Qualcosa — or really any name that didn't invoke a formal city-center frame — Yoyogi-Uehara would be a compelling answer. As it stands, you'd be swimming against your own positioning from the first Google search result. I'd put Yoyogi-Uehara low in the current ranking unless you're genuinely open to revisiting the brand name and concept register, which is a much larger conversation.

Now I'm genuinely curious about Kagurazaka. It's the one area on your list with a pre-existing European culinary identity — the French restaurant heritage, the cobblestone alleys, the ryotei tradition sitting alongside Western dining in an unusual coexistence. It pulls both destination tourists and strong local residents. But the landlord culture there is famously idiosyncratic, especially in the older buildings on the narrow lanes, and some of those structures have basement kitchens that create real ventilation challenges. Tell me what you found and what's moved it to the top of your list — I want to understand whether you're reading the upside accurately or whether something about the visit created a halo effect that's worth questioning.

I signed the lease this morning. I just got back from the notary's office with Hamada-san from Plaza Homes Commercial — it was nearly a two-hour process between the initial document review, the countersignatures on the main agreement and the build-out rider, the seal registration confirmation, and then the landlord's representative doing a brief walkthrough formality before the formal handover of the keys. I am still a little bit in shock, honestly. I can barely sit still. After four months of thinking about this, talking about it, running projections with Tanabe-san, doing multiple walk-throughs in different neighborhoods with Hamada-san, and honestly some nights lying awake wondering whether I was making the biggest mistake of my life or whether I was finally doing the thing I should have started five years ago — it feels almost surreal to have an actual physical set of keys in my hand and a signed paper saying the space is mine to build in. I took a photograph of the signed page before I handed my copy to Hamada-san for scanning. I'm not sure why. Maybe just to have something that felt real. I called my mother from the sidewalk outside the notary and she cried a little. I may have too. Don't tell anyone.

Congratulations, Kenta — that is a genuinely significant moment, and you've earned it. Four months of serious groundwork is not nothing. A lot of people with a restaurant idea never get past the spreadsheet phase, and a meaningful number who do get past it stall out at the location search because the gap between what they can afford and what they can envision turns out to be unbridgeable. The fact that you navigated the market research, built a financial model rigorous enough to take to Japan Finance Corporation, engaged Hamada-san, did multiple walk-throughs across different Minato-ku sub-neighborhoods, and got all the way to an actual signed lease means you've already cleared the filter that stops most would-be restaurateurs before they ever face a real rent obligation. That is not a small thing. The call to your mother sounds exactly right for the moment. Now — tell me everything about the property. Which space did you end up going with, and what were the final terms? I want to make sure I'm working from the actual signed details, not the estimates and projections we'd been using in earlier sessions.

It's the space Hamada-san first showed me about three weeks ago, the one in Higashi-Azabu that I told you I kept coming back to mentally even when I was trying to evaluate the other two candidates in Toranomon and Azabujuban. The official address on the lease agreement is 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, Minato-ku. The building name is Azabu Heights Building. I walked through it one final time this morning before we went to the notary, and I'll say again what I said the first time I saw it — there's something about that space that just feels like the restaurant I've been building in my head. The afternoon light through the west-facing windows is genuinely beautiful. The previous tenant had put in a brick accent wall along the north side of the dining area and it gives the room a textural warmth that would cost serious money to fabricate from scratch. I stood in the middle of the empty room before Hamada-san arrived and tried to imagine it with covers laid and candles lit and a pasta course going out, and I didn't have to try very hard. It was already there.

Higashi-Azabu is a well-considered choice for the concept you're building. It has the residential-adjacent character that works well for a neighborhood trattoria positioning — close enough to the business density of Roppongi and the money of Azabu proper, but with a slightly lower-key street presence that suits a restaurant that wants to be discovered rather than simply stumbled into by foot traffic. Minato-ku addresses carry a certain weight without announcing it too loudly, which fits a northern Italian concept that's trying to signal seriousness and intention rather than spectacle. The brick accent wall sounds like a genuine stroke of luck and I'd encourage you to treat it as the anchor of the room's identity rather than a background detail. Authentic industrial texture is one of those things that photographs as either beautiful or unconvincing depending entirely on whether it's real, and guests who eat out regularly can feel the difference even if they can't articulate it. The fact that it was left by the previous tenant rather than commissioned as a design decision actually makes it more valuable — it has earned-in character that no interior designer can manufacture on a deadline. Now let me ask you the practical questions, because the aesthetic can follow once we know the financial foundation is solid: what are the core numbers on the lease? Floor area, monthly rent, deposit structure, term?

I have the summary sheet right in front of me, I actually photographed it and sent it to Tanabe-san before I even left the notary's lobby. Floor area is 64.5 square meters, which is 19.5 tsubo — Hamada-san made sure to note both on the summary because my contractor friends still think entirely in tsubo and I knew I'd have to translate it for them eventually. Monthly base rent is 487,000 yen. On top of that there's a common area fee of 73,000 yen per month, so the all-in occupancy cost before utilities is 560,000 yen per month. The key money came out to 2,922,000 yen, which is exactly six months of base rent, and I had Tanabe-san verify that figure against comparable Minato-ku commercial leases before I agreed to it. He said it was solidly within the normal range, maybe even slightly favorable given the building's location and condition. The lease term is 4 years renewable. Signing all of those numbers into reality this morning was its own kind of ceremony, honestly. Writing my seal next to 2,922,000 yen is a very clarifying experience.

Let me work through those numbers carefully, because they're the foundation everything else will rest on. 64.5 square meters, or 19.5 tsubo, at a monthly base rent of 487,000 yen plus a common area fee of 73,000 yen — so 560,000 yen all-in per month — with key money of 2,922,000 yen already committed, on a 4 years renewable term. The per-tsubo rent works out to roughly 25,000 yen per tsubo per month, which is reasonable for a well-located Minato-ku ground-floor commercial space. The key money at six months is standard; I've seen up to eight months in parts of Azabu proper so you're not in bad territory. The 560,000 yen monthly all-in number is the one I want to pressure-test against your revenue model. If I remember your projections from the session with Tanabe-san, you were modeling somewhere around 30 covers per service and two services on peak nights. Has any of that changed now that you have the confirmed floor area? And critically — does the JFC loan application still reflect the right figures, or does anything need to be revised before the decision comes back?

The loan application is fine as-is. The 15 million yen we applied for at Japan Finance Corporation was sized against a target space in this general range — we didn't have the confirmed address at the time of submission, but Tanabe-san and I had been conservative enough in our space-cost assumptions that the confirmed numbers for Azabu Heights Building fall comfortably within what the model was built on. I'm still waiting on the JFC decision; Tanabe-san says to expect it within two to three weeks from now, possibly faster since our application file was apparently reasonably clean. What I will say is that the build-out cost estimate has come in slightly higher than the rough figure we were using in the original projections, but there's an important offset that actually makes the overall position better than I expected. Hamada-san negotiated with the landlord to absorb the cost of completing the HVAC pre-duct work. The tenant who was in the space before us — a French bistro that closed in October 2024 — had gotten roughly 60 percent of the way through their ducting installation before they ran into their own difficulties and shut down. The landlord agreed, as a condition of our signing, to finish that work at his expense. Suzuki-san, my contractor, estimated that piece of the work would have cost us between 400,000 and 500,000 yen. Having it handed over to us already done is a meaningful offset against the higher-than-projected build-out line.

That's a genuinely useful concession that Hamada-san pulled out of the negotiation, and it tells you something interesting about the state of the space and the landlord's position. The French bistro that closed in October 2024 going under at 60 percent through their build-out is a somewhat unusual situation — most tenants either pull out before they've invested much in a fit-out, or they go far enough that they're trying to sell the fit-out to the incoming tenant as an asset rather than just abandoning it in place. The fact that they got to 60 percent on HVAC specifically and then shut down suggests they ran into cash flow problems mid-construction, which is one of the more common failure modes for first-time restaurant operators who underestimate how long a build-out actually takes and what the carry costs look like during a period when you're paying rent and getting no revenue. It's a sobering data point for you to keep in mind as you manage your own build schedule. The landlord agreeing to complete that work at his own expense — rather than just marketing the space as-is with 60 percent of the ducting done and calling it a selling point — tells you he was motivated to get the space re-let quickly and on good terms, which in turn suggests Hamada-san's introduction and your application made a strong impression. That's actually a good foundation for the landlord relationship going forward. The 400,000 to 500,000 yen saving is real and material at your budget scale. What else did Suzuki-san observe about the general condition of the space? Have you done a full contractor walk-through yet, or is that still ahead of you?

That walk-through is this afternoon — I have Suzuki-san meeting me at the Azabu Heights Building at three o'clock, which gives me just enough time to eat something and mentally organize my questions for him. From my own observations this morning, the grease trap looks like it's in at least reasonable condition, which I was relieved about because replacing or relocating a grease trap in a multi-tenant building is one of those jobs that can spiral very quickly once you're dealing with building management associations and shared drainage infrastructure. There are gas stub-outs in what looks like approximately the right positions for the kitchen footprint I have in mind, though Suzuki-san will need to verify the line sizing and pressure specs before I know whether I can run the burner configuration I want. The extraction fan housing is still mounted on the kitchen side of the north wall — the French bistro's kitchen was at the north end too, which is good for us because it means the general infrastructure logic of the space maps onto our layout intent. Whether the extraction motor itself is still in spec, I genuinely don't know. That's on Suzuki-san's assessment list. The question I care about most going into this afternoon's walk-through is whether we can shift the pass-through position laterally by about a meter and a half without running into anything structural on the west wall. I have a layout concept in my head that I think would work really well for us, but it depends on that wall being non-structural, or at least modifiable within the lease's build-out restrictions.

The pass-through position is actually the most consequential single decision you'll make about the interior, and I'm glad you're leading with it when you sit down with Suzuki-san this afternoon. In a space this size — 64.5 square meters, 19.5 tsubo — the spatial relationship between the kitchen threshold and the dining floor isn't just an operational question about plate flow, it's the thing that determines whether guests feel connected to the kitchen energy or isolated from it. A meter and a half shift sounds incremental but it can be the difference between a counter seat at the bar that looks straight into the kitchen and feels exciting, versus a counter seat that looks at a wall with a small window. Before we get into the structural question, I want to understand the layout you have in mind. Where is the entrance relative to the long axis of the space? And where are you thinking of positioning the bar versus the kitchen versus the main dining floor? Walk me through it as you imagine it.

Alright, so the entrance comes in from the south face of the building. There's a small vestibule area that's probably four square meters of the total 64.5 square meters — it's partially enclosed by what looks like an original partition wall and a glass panel that I think the French bistro added. I want to keep that as a coats-and-waiting zone because it gives you a proper threshold between the street and the restaurant, which matters to me atmospherically. You don't just walk in and immediately feel like you're in someone's living room; there's a moment of transition. Beyond the vestibule, the main floor opens up with the long axis running north-south. My plan is to put the bar and a short counter section immediately to the right as you come through from the vestibule — that puts it along the east wall of the main floor. The bar becomes a visual anchor and also a functional landing pad: solo diners can sit there comfortably, early-arriving guests can wait with an Aperol Spritz instead of standing in the vestibule, and during quieter services it creates a sense of activity and energy even when the dining floor isn't fully covered. The kitchen occupies the northern third of the space — probably somewhere around 18 to 20 square meters — and I want a low partition between the kitchen and the dining floor with the pass-through roughly centered on that partition. The remaining middle section is the main dining floor. If the layout comes together the way I'm imagining, I think I can seat 28 covers comfortably — that means tables with proper elbow room, nothing crammed. Maybe 32 if I add two bar stools along the counter, but I'd rather open at 28 and feel spacious than open at 32 and feel like a conveyor belt. Tanabe-san's model was based on 30 covers, so 28 is within a margin that doesn't break anything.

The logic of this layout is sounder than it might seem at first pass. You're essentially using the bar not as a destination in its own right — the way a cocktail-forward restaurant would — but as a spatial transition element and a hospitality buffer. That's the right call for a trattoria positioning where the main event is at the table and the bar is a tool for managing arrival rhythm and keeping the energy visible even on a quiet Tuesday. The vestibule as a threshold is also genuinely important for the atmosphere you're describing. Northern Italian restaurants at the level you're aiming for tend to have a quality of enclosure — you feel like you've arrived somewhere specific, not that you've walked off the street into an open room. That glass panel and partition might be worth keeping even if they need refinishing. Twenty-eight covers is the right number to open with in 64.5 square meters. At that density you're probably looking at somewhere between 8 and 10 tables depending on your mix of twos, fours, and the bar counter. At an average spend of 12,000 to 15,000 yen per head — which is where a serious northern Italian with a wine focus should be positioning in Minato-ku — 28 covers at one full turn gives you 336,000 to 420,000 yen in revenue per service. Two services on a Friday or Saturday gets you close to or past the 800,000 yen daily revenue threshold that would sustain a 560,000 yen monthly occupancy cost. The structural question I want to flag for your Suzuki-san conversation: in a mid-rise commercial building in Minato-ku from that era, the structural spine tends to run through the interior rather than along the perimeter walls. If that's true here, your west wall might be a curtain wall — meaning your meter-and-a-half shift is entirely feasible — but your north wall, where the kitchen is anchored and where the extraction housing is already mounted, could be where the column grid runs. Make sure Suzuki-san checks not just the wall itself but whether there's a column embedded in or near the north partition that would constrain your kitchen depth. And separately — what do the lease build-out restrictions say? The rider Hamada-san reviewed with you, does it specify any structural no-go zones?

Actually, before you answer that — I also want to ask about the wood-fired oven question, because I know that was part of your original concept and I'm curious where you've landed on it. In a space this size, with a 4 years renewable lease and a landlord relationship you're going to need to maintain, the fire safety certification process for a live-fire installation in Tokyo is not trivial. Has that come up yet in your conversations with Suzuki-san, or is that still a decision point ahead of you?

There are two things, so let me take them in order. On the lease rider: yes, Hamada-san walked me through the two-page build-out restriction addendum at the notary this morning. The main restrictions are that we cannot modify the shared corridor wall on the east side of the building without written landlord consent, we cannot alter the electrical panel without a licensed electrician filing a separate notification with the building, and any floor penetrations for plumbing work need written pre-approval from the landlord before we proceed. None of those feel like showstoppers — they're basically standard landlord protections, and Suzuki-san told me last week that he deals with this kind of addendum on every commercial restaurant restoration he does in Minato-ku. The one that requires the most coordination is the floor penetration clause, because there's a reasonable chance we'll need to adjust one of the existing drain positions depending on where we end up placing the prep station. But that's a matter of paperwork and timing, not a fundamental obstacle. On the wood-fired oven: I've been going back and forth on this genuinely, and I think I'm landing on not doing it. The ventilation certification process in Tokyo for a live-fire installation is legitimately complex — Suzuki-san mentioned that the Tokyo Fire Department inspection and the additional structural sign-offs on the extraction system can add two to three months to an already tight build schedule, and potentially significant cost for reinforced fire suppression equipment. More practically, I've been asking myself honestly whether the wood fire is actually essential to the food I want to cook, or whether it's an ego statement I'm making at the expense of the project's timeline and budget. The answer, if I'm being rigorous about it, is that a high-quality gas-fired stone deck oven will give me results on the bread and the pizze al taglio I want to run that guests will not be able to distinguish from live fire — provided my dough development and fermentation process are right, which they will be. The romance of the wood fire matters to me personally, but the guest's experience at the table is what the restaurant is for, not my personal satisfaction in the kitchen. So: gas deck oven, better timeline, cleaner budget, same quality on the plate. That feels like the right call.

That's a well-reasoned decision and I think you've thought about it the right way — by asking whether the wood fire is serving the guest or serving your own aesthetic preference. The answer you've arrived at, that a properly executed gas deck oven with serious fermentation discipline produces a result the guest cannot distinguish at the table, is correct. The live-fire romance is most visible in a fully open kitchen where the fire itself is part of the show, and while your layout has an open-kitchen quality, the pass-through partition means the oven isn't necessarily the theatrical centerpiece. You're better off directing that visual energy toward something guests will actually see — the counter, the bar setup, the pasta station if you're doing fresh pasta to order. What I'd suggest, if the gas deck oven ends up well-positioned on the kitchen's east wall, is that you think about the pasta preparation happening somewhere with line-of-sight from the dining floor. Watching someone roll and cut fresh pasta is one of those elemental restaurant moments that communicates everything you want guests to understand about the quality of your food without you having to explain it. That's the kind of visual theater that earns you word-of-mouth. For now though — you have a signed lease on a space at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, Minato-ku, in the Azabu Heights Building. You have Suzuki-san walking through it at three o'clock today. You have a JFC loan decision expected in two to three weeks. You have a layout concept that's coherent and build-ready once you know the structural answer on the west wall. What's the thing you most want to get clarity on before our next session?

Honestly, the thing I most want going into the next couple of weeks is resolution on two fronts simultaneously: the JFC loan decision and Suzuki-san's full condition report with a revised build-out cost estimate. Both of those need to land before I can finalize the budget and set a firm opening target date. My working assumption is somewhere in late autumn — September or October at the optimistic end, November if things take longer than expected — but I haven't committed to any of that publicly yet because I don't want to be in a position where I've told people a date and then have to walk it back. The other thing I'm holding is the conversation with Fujita-san, my candidate for head chef. She trained for four years at a Michelin-starred trattoria in Torino and came back to Tokyo last autumn, and I've been having periodic coffee conversations with her to keep the relationship warm without making a formal offer I'm not yet in a position to commit to. She knows Ginza Trattoria is moving forward and that I'm serious, but I haven't given her a start date or a salary offer because I didn't want to do that until I had a signed lease and a realistic build-out timeline. Now I have the lease. So the next step with her is probably a more formal conversation about terms — but that feels like Session 6 material. Today I just want to sit with what happened this morning. I have a lease. I have an address. I have a building name on a key fob in my pocket. Ginza Trattoria has a location. After four months of working toward this, that feels like enough for one day.

Good evening. I finally have all three renovation quotes in hand and I've been going back and forth on this all week, so I'd really like to work through it carefully with you tonight if that's okay. This decision feels bigger than I expected it to — signing the lease was exciting, but now I'm actually committing to spending a large chunk of money with a specific contractor, and once construction starts there's no easy reversal. The space is the one we've been discussing: 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, Azabu Heights Building, sixty-four and a half square meters on the ground floor.

Good evening, Kenta. That sense of weight is completely appropriate — contractor selection is one of the most consequential decisions in the entire project lifecycle, arguably more consequential than the lease negotiation itself, because a contractor's competence, communication style, and financial discipline will shape everything that happens between now and opening day. A beautiful concept can be ruined by poor execution, and conversely the right contractor can surface ideas and solutions you hadn't considered. The good news is that you now have concrete proposals to work from rather than abstract impressions. So let's go through each bid methodically. You said you have three quotes — tell me who the firms are and give me the headline numbers first, before we get into the details of what each one proposed.

Right, three bids. The first is from a company called Kenchiku Plus — they're a mid-size general contractor based in Minato-ku, fairly well known for commercial fit-outs. They came in at 9.6 million yen. The second is from Yamamoto Koumuten, which is a smaller specialized firm with a focus on restaurant interiors. The owner is a man named Tetsuo Yamamoto and he came highly recommended by my real estate agent, who has worked with him on several past projects. Their bid came in at 8.2 million yen. The third is Sasaki Design Build — they're the most design-forward of the three, and they've done a few restaurant projects I've seen photos of online that are genuinely impressive visually. They came in at 11.1 million yen. So there's a pretty wide spread.

That is a meaningful spread. You're looking at roughly a 2.9 million yen gap between the lowest bid and the highest, which on a project of this size — a 64.5 square meter restaurant fit-out — represents a very significant percentage difference. Before we go firm by firm, I need to ask two foundational questions. First: what is your actual renovation budget? That context is essential because it immediately tells us who is in the game and who is not. Second: did all three firms bid on an identical set of specifications that you gave them, or did each one interpret the brief somewhat differently? When comparing bids, apples-to-apples alignment matters enormously — a lower bid that cuts scope you actually need is not cheaper, and a higher bid that includes things you didn't ask for isn't necessarily more expensive on the things you do need.

My renovation budget is 8.4 million yen. That's the number I communicated clearly to all three firms upfront, in writing, when I sent them the project brief. I told them it was a hard ceiling and I needed them to come in at or under that figure. So as you can see, Kenchiku Plus is already 1.2 million yen over budget, and Sasaki Design Build is nearly 2.7 million yen over. Yamamoto Koumuten is the only firm that actually came in under the ceiling, at 8.2 million yen. On your second question — they mostly bid on the same core specifications, but each firm exercised different degrees of creative interpretation. Kenchiku Plus followed my original brief very closely, almost to the letter. Sasaki Design Build departed significantly from my brief in two specific areas that we can get into. Yamamoto Koumuten also proposed some changes to the original spec, but their changes stayed within the budget envelope.

That renovation budget figure of 8.4 million yen is actually the most important piece of information in this conversation, because it immediately restructures the analysis. With a hard ceiling stated upfront in writing, Kenchiku Plus and Sasaki Design Build have both demonstrated that they either couldn't or didn't take your constraint seriously. Kenchiku Plus came in 14 percent over budget. Sasaki Design Build came in 32 percent over. These aren't rounding errors — these are fundamental misalignments with the project parameters you gave them. Even if you tried to negotiate either of them down to 8.4 million, you'd be starting from a position of weakness: you'd be asking them to reduce by amounts that force painful scope cuts or margin compression on their side, and that creates its own risks during construction. Yamamoto Koumuten being the only firm to actually honor your constraint is itself a meaningful signal about how they run their business. Let's go through each proposal in detail, though. Start with Kenchiku Plus — what did their proposal actually contain, and what's your read on them beyond the number?

Kenchiku Plus was very professional in their presentation. Thick bound document, detailed line items, every element broken out clearly. From a technical competence standpoint I have no serious concerns — they've done a lot of commercial restaurant fit-outs and their references checked out. But the actual proposal was underwhelming in terms of vision. Their kitchen layout was competent but completely conventional — they essentially replicated my original brief without any creative interpretation at all. The finishes they specified were generic: standard subway tile, off-the-shelf millwork, nothing that would create a strong or distinctive visual identity for the space. They proposed a fairly standard semi-open kitchen with a pass-through counter, which is fine, but it creates no memorable moment for guests when they walk in. The proposal read like something they pull from a template for any restaurant client. I don't have concerns about their execution quality, but I also have zero excitement about working with them. And then, of course, there's the budget problem — 9.6 million yen against a renovation budget of 8.4 million yen is a non-starter unless they can shave 1.2 million off, which feels like asking a lot.

Your read on Kenchiku Plus sounds accurate and I think appropriately skeptical. The combination of uninspired design and budget overage is a double flag. Let's address the budget issue directly: getting a contractor to reduce a bid by 1.2 million yen — roughly 12.5 percent — is not impossible, but it almost always means one of three things: cutting scope you actually wanted, substituting lower-quality materials that will disappoint you later, or compressing their labor margin to a point where they start making corners-cutting decisions on-site that you won't discover until something fails during service. When a contractor comes in over a clearly stated ceiling, it signals either that they didn't take the constraint seriously or that their genuine cost structure can't reach it. Neither scenario is particularly reassuring as the basis for a working relationship. The lack of design ambition compounds this — you'd be paying over budget for a restaurant interior that gives guests no particular reason to take a photograph or return. For a new restaurant in Higashi-Azabu trying to establish an identity, that's a real cost even if it doesn't appear on the invoice. I'd keep Kenchiku Plus as a reserve option in case the preferred firms fall through for some reason, but I wouldn't lead with them. Tell me about Sasaki Design Build — you mentioned they departed from your brief in two significant ways.

Sasaki Design Build produced the most visually stunning proposal of the three, by a significant margin. The renderings were beautiful — polished stone surfaces, warm lighting design, a refined northern Italian aesthetic that genuinely matched the mood I'm trying to create for Ginza Trattoria. Looking at those images, I could actually see the finished restaurant. But they made two major unilateral changes to my brief that I hadn't asked for. First, they completely reconfigured the kitchen layout in a way that would require relocating the main drain line — that's a structurally complex and expensive piece of work that wasn't in my original spec and that they just decided was necessary without consulting me first. Second, they specified imported Italian stone for the bar counter and dining surfaces, which I had not requested — and that stone alone accounts for nearly 800,000 yen of their overage above the 8.4 million yen ceiling I had set. When I pushed back on both of those items in our follow-up meeting, their project manager told me the Italian stone was integral to their design vision and that relocating the drain was 'the right thing to do structurally.' That answer made me genuinely uneasy.

That response from Sasaki Design Build's project manager is a red flag that I'd take very seriously. Let me explain why specifically. When a contractor tells you that an 800,000 yen material upgrade is 'integral to their design vision' — on a project where they've already come in 2.7 million yen over your stated hard ceiling — what they're actually telling you is that their aesthetic preferences take priority over your financial constraints. That is a fundamental misalignment in how they see the client relationship. And when they tell you that an unplanned drain relocation is 'the right thing to do structurally,' without having been asked to assess the structure in the first place, they're inserting their judgment in a way that conveniently expands scope and cost. These are patterns, not one-off miscommunications. Design-forward firms that blend their own creative vision with client work can produce extraordinary results — but they can also be the most difficult contractors to manage under construction pressure, precisely because every scope dispute becomes an argument about artistic integrity rather than a straightforward conversation about what was agreed and what it costs. The 11.1 million yen figure is almost secondary to the attitudinal problem. If you engaged Sasaki Design Build, you'd be entering a relationship where their opening position, before construction even starts, is that they know better than you what your restaurant should look like and what it should cost. That dynamic almost never improves once you're on-site and the contractor has leverage. I'd treat their proposal as a valuable visual reference for the design direction you want to communicate to your chosen contractor, but not as a viable path for this project. Now tell me about Yamamoto Koumuten in detail, because based on what you've said, that's where this decision is actually headed.

You're reading the situation correctly. I've been leaning toward Yamamoto Koumuten since the second site visit, and I want to talk through why I feel good about them but also what gives me some hesitation. The positive case starts with Tetsuo Yamamoto himself. He came to the Higashi-Azabu space twice. The second visit, he brought a junior site manager with him and the two of them spent about two full hours going through the ceiling structure, the existing drainage runs, and the HVAC situation in detail. He knows the Azabu Heights Building — apparently Yamamoto Koumuten had done previous work in the building on a different tenant space, so he was already familiar with the building's infrastructure in ways that a contractor seeing it fresh wouldn't be. He also picked up on something important that I would not have caught on my own. He noticed that the existing electrical panel is undersized for a commercial restaurant kitchen and flagged it early as something we needed to budget for explicitly. And then he made a design recommendation that I found genuinely exciting — he proposed an open kitchen with a brick-faced pizza oven facing dining room as the central visual feature of the space. He said it would anchor the entire dining room, create theater for guests, and give the restaurant a focal point that would photograph well for social media. It's the kind of idea that came from someone who was actually thinking about what this restaurant needs to be, not just executing a generic brief.

Everything you've described about Tetsuo Yamamoto's approach is the profile of an engaged, experienced contractor who invests real intellectual effort in a project before the contract is signed — and that diligence during the proposal phase is one of the most reliable predictors of how a contractor will behave once they're on-site. Let me unpack a few specific things you mentioned, because I think their significance is worth making explicit. The prior experience in Azabu Heights Building is a practically underrated advantage. Building-specific knowledge about drainage routing, structural elements, HVAC paths, and electrical infrastructure means fewer costly surprises mid-construction. When a contractor who doesn't know the building encounters an unexpected condition — a drainage run that doesn't go where the plans suggest, a structural member in an inconvenient location — that becomes a change order that costs you money and time. Tetsuo Yamamoto already knowing the building reduces that risk materially. The electrical panel observation is exactly the kind of thing that can become a 400,000 to 600,000 yen surprise change order if it's discovered after construction starts. The fact that he surfaced it proactively, before the contract, and incorporated it into the budget tells you that his 8.2 million yen number reflects actual understanding of the project rather than a low-ball estimate designed to win the job and expand later. On the design recommendation — the open kitchen with the brick-faced pizza oven facing dining room is a strong concept for northern Italian, both from a guest experience standpoint and an operational one. It creates immediate visual legibility: a guest walks in and within seconds understands the restaurant's identity and cooking philosophy. It also creates the kind of ambient theater — watching dough go into a fire-lit oven — that justifies premium pricing and generates the word-of-mouth that a new restaurant needs in its first months. What did Yamamoto say about where the oven would be sourced, and how that fits within the 8.2 million yen figure?

He was very specific on that point, which I appreciated. He recommended sourcing the wood-fired oven through a supplier called Forno Bravo Japan. He explained that they distribute Italian-manufactured ovens domestically and provide local installation support and service — which matters because if something goes wrong with the oven during the first year of operation, you want someone in Japan who can actually respond. He told me he's worked with Forno Bravo Japan on two previous restaurant projects and has confidence in both the product and their installation team. He walked me through the oven he had in mind — a mid-range model that's appropriate for the volume I'm projecting, neither underpowered nor oversized for the space — and said the installed cost would land somewhere in the range of 1.2 to 1.4 million yen. And critically, that figure is already included within his overall 8.2 million yen bid. He didn't present the oven as a separate line item to be decided later; he had already done the specification work, priced it out with Forno Bravo Japan directly, and built it into the total. He also walked me through the ventilation requirements for the wood-fired oven, the floor load implications given that a masonry oven at that scale is genuinely heavy, and the fire suppression coordination requirements. He clearly knew the product well and had thought through the installation dependencies before our meeting.

That depth of pre-contract homework is genuinely unusual and tells you a great deal about how Yamamoto Koumuten operates. The fact that Tetsuo Yamamoto had already contacted Forno Bravo Japan, selected an appropriate model for your volume, understood the installation requirements, and baked the installed cost into the bid means that his 8.2 million yen number is grounded in real pricing rather than estimates. Contractors who leave equipment specifications vague — who say 'we'll sort out the oven separately' or 'that will depend on what you select' — are essentially carrying placeholder costs in their bids that become change order opportunities later. Yamamoto eliminated that ambiguity upfront, which is a mark of professional discipline. I also want to flag the wood-fired oven question as something worth thinking through carefully on the operational side, because it affects your restaurant in ways beyond the renovation scope. A wood-fired oven is a genuine differentiator — it creates flavor characteristics and visual drama that a gas oven simply cannot replicate, and for northern Italian where wood-roasted meats, focaccia, and pizza are central to the menu, it is authentically appropriate. But it comes with operational commitments. Wood storage requires physical space and a reliable supply chain. Ash management is a daily task that requires trained staff. Temperature regulation in a wood-fired oven is a skill — you can't just turn a dial — so your kitchen team will need either to hire someone who knows the equipment or to train. Fire code compliance for wood-burning equipment in Tokyo is more involved than gas. For a restaurant where the oven is the visual centerpiece and the focal point of the dining experience, I would argue those commitments are worth accepting. But you should staff and plan for them from the beginning rather than discovering them six months into operation. Has Yamamoto discussed any of the building management coordination for fire suppression, and are there any aspects of his proposal that gave you pause?

On fire suppression — he mentioned specifically that the building management coordination is something Yamamoto Koumuten has handled before in Azabu Heights Building, which is reassuring since that's a conversation that apparently requires knowing who to talk to in the building management office. He also included a dedicated commercial hood system in his spec, rated appropriately for the oven output. So the ventilation and suppression side seems well considered. The areas where I have hesitation are two things. First, timeline: Yamamoto Koumuten is estimating fourteen weeks of construction from permit issuance. I've been hoping to open by early October, and depending on how long the permit process takes, that timeline is potentially tight. For comparison, Kenchiku Plus estimated twelve weeks, though obviously they have the budget problem. Sasaki Design Build estimated sixteen weeks. So Yamamoto Koumuten is in the middle. Second, and this is more of a psychological concern than a practical one — Yamamoto Koumuten is a small firm. Tetsuo Yamamoto runs a total team of twelve people. Part of me worries about whether that's enough capacity to execute reliably on a project like this.

Let me address both hesitations directly. On the timeline question: the twelve-week estimate from Kenchiku Plus is almost certainly the least reliable number of the three, and I'd encourage you to discount it. A contractor who came in 1.2 million yen over a clearly stated renovation budget of 8.4 million yen, without creative justification for doing so, is also likely to have been optimistic about timeline in order to present a competitive picture. Contractors who underprice to win work frequently also underestimate duration. The fourteen-week estimate from Yamamoto Koumuten, backed by someone with direct knowledge of Azabu Heights Building's infrastructure and a clear understanding of what the project actually involves — including the wood-fired oven installation, the electrical panel upgrade, and the open kitchen configuration — is almost certainly a more honest number. As for the math: if permits issue in late June, which is achievable if you move quickly on the application, fourteen construction weeks takes you to late September to early October. That is actually quite close to your target opening window. The real variable is permit timing, and that's outside any contractor's control. What I'd recommend is pressing Yamamoto Koumuten specifically on two things: first, what the permit dependencies are and which elements have the longest lead time; second, whether there is meaningful pre-permit work — material procurement, detailed drawings, equipment ordering — that can begin before permit issuance so that the fourteen weeks can start from the strongest possible position. On the team size concern: twelve people for a 64.5 square meter restaurant fit-out is genuinely sufficient capacity, and I'd argue that a small specialized firm where the owner is personally engaged in the project often delivers better outcomes than a larger generalist firm where your job is handed to a junior project manager after the contract is signed. Everything you've described about Tetsuo Yamamoto — the two site visits, the electrical panel catch, the Forno Bravo Japan specification, the open kitchen concept — points to someone who will be personally invested in your project's success. Personal owner engagement is worth more than headcount for a project at this scale. I think you've already made your decision, Kenta. Tell me if I'm wrong.

You're not wrong. I'm going to go with Yamamoto Koumuten. I've been leaning that way since the second site visit, but I wanted to articulate the reasoning carefully so I could feel genuinely confident rather than just going on instinct. The budget fit is obviously the primary factor — they're the only firm that actually came in under my renovation budget of 8.4 million yen, and they did so while proposing more, not less. But what really clinches it is the combination of Tetsuo Yamamoto's personal involvement from the beginning, the fact that Yamamoto Koumuten already knows the Azabu Heights Building, the proactive catch on the electrical panel, the Forno Bravo Japan oven sourcing, and most of all the open kitchen with the brick-faced pizza oven facing dining room — that concept is exactly the restaurant I want to build. That's the image I've had in my mind of what Ginza Trattoria should feel like when you walk in the door. Kenchiku Plus gave me nothing to be excited about. Sasaki Design Build showed me something beautiful on paper but gave me serious doubts about the working relationship. Yamamoto Koumuten showed me both competence and vision, and stayed within the budget doing it. What do I need to do next?

That's a well-reasoned decision and I think it's the right one. Congratulations — this is a significant step forward. Here is what your immediate next steps should look like, ordered by priority. First and most urgently, contact Yamamoto Koumuten this week — ideally within the next two to three days — to communicate your selection and request a formal contract draft. Do not let this drift into next week. Good specialized contractors with strong reputations, especially smaller firms like Yamamoto Koumuten where Tetsuo Yamamoto's own capacity is the limiting resource, get picked up by other projects. Your verbal or written selection will effectively hold his calendar, but formalize it quickly. Second, before you sign the contract, make sure it contains four things explicitly. One: a detailed payment schedule tied to construction milestones rather than calendar dates — you want payments to correspond to verified completed work, not to dates that could slip for any reason. Two: a written scope of work that specifies the open kitchen, the brick-faced pizza oven facing dining room using the Forno Bravo Japan unit with model number confirmed, the electrical panel upgrade, and any other specific elements discussed in your meetings. Three: a change order clause requiring your written approval for any scope or cost change above a threshold — I'd suggest 50,000 yen — so that no surprises accumulate without your explicit authorization. Four: a timeline commitment with a realistic float provision that both sides agree to upfront. Third, notify Kenchiku Plus and Sasaki Design Build promptly. You don't need to explain your reasoning in detail — a professional, courteous decline is sufficient and is the right thing to do, since they invested real time in preparing proposals. It also preserves those relationships in case you ever need them for a future project. Fourth, begin the permit application process as soon as possible in parallel with the contract finalization. Every week saved on permits is a direct week saved on your October opening timeline, and permits in Tokyo for commercial restaurant fit-outs, particularly ones involving a wood-fired oven and ventilation modifications, are not trivial. Ask Yamamoto Koumuten specifically whether they handle permit coordination in-house or use an expediter, and whether their prior experience in Azabu Heights Building has any bearing on that process. This is a genuinely good outcome. You found a contractor who knows your building, respects your budget, proactively surfaced a real problem before the contract was signed, and came with a design vision — the open kitchen and brick-faced pizza oven as the focal point — that serves the restaurant you are actually trying to build. Ginza Trattoria is becoming real.

Good morning. I have some news — big news, actually — and I've been sitting with it since yesterday afternoon trying to figure out exactly how I feel about it. The loan decision came in from Japan Finance Corporation. I finally got the call from my loan officer around 3 PM yesterday. I was honestly expecting to either be thrilled or devastated, and instead I'm sitting here in this weird middle space where it's genuinely good news on one level and genuinely frustrating on another.

Good morning, Kenta. I've been wondering when you'd hear back — you mentioned a few sessions ago that Japan Finance Corporation was taking longer than the initial estimate they gave you, and I know that uncertainty has been hanging over a lot of our planning conversations. The fact that you're in a 'middle space' rather than one extreme or the other actually tells me something before you've even given me the details. Tell me exactly what they said. What was the approval, and what are the terms?

So here's where I am. Japan Finance Corporation did approve the loan, which is the unambiguously good part. But the approved amount came in at 12 million yen — not the 15 million I applied for. That's a 3 million yen shortfall against what I was counting on in my financial model. And then on top of that, the final interest rate is 1.95%, which is meaningfully higher than what they originally quoted me during the preliminary consultation phase. At that early stage they were describing something in the range of 1.6 to 1.7 percent. I remember writing that number down and building my debt service projections around it. So the final number being 1.95% caught me off guard. I understand that preliminary quotes are not commitments, but it's still a recalibration I have to absorb. So: approved, but lower principal, higher rate. That's where I am.

Okay. Let me work through this with you carefully, because there are actually several distinct things happening here and it's worth separating them before you decide how worried to be.

The first thing I want to say is that an approval from Japan Finance Corporation, at any amount, represents a meaningful validation of your plan. They are not a lender that approves restaurant loans as a formality — they assess cash flow projections, the business concept, the borrower's background, and the specific market context. Getting the 12 million yen approved means they looked at your application and concluded that your restaurant concept at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, run by you, with your plan, has a fundable business case. That matters and it should not get lost in the frustration about the shortfall.

Now, the shortfall. Twelve million yen versus fifteen million yen is a 20% reduction from what you requested. That is not trivial and I don't want to minimize it. But the impact depends entirely on what that 3 million yen was earmarked for in your original plan. Before we talk about solutions, I need to understand the internal breakdown of that 15 million. Was it all construction and fit-out, or did it include working capital and pre-opening costs as well? Because the answer determines where the pain is and what the options are.

On the interest rate: the jump from roughly 1.65% to 1.95% is real but let me put it in perspective for you. On a 12 million yen loan amortized over, say, seven years, the difference between 1.7% and 1.95% in monthly debt service is roughly 2,500 to 3,500 yen per month. Over the full term that adds up to something, but on a month-to-month cash flow basis running a restaurant with your rent load, it is not the number that should be keeping you up at night. The 3 million yen principal gap is the operative problem. Walk me through the breakdown.

You're right that the rate is less of an operational issue than I was making it. Let me walk you through the 15 million yen breakdown as I had it structured. Approximately 10 million was for construction — and within that, the signed contract with Yamamoto Koumuten, with Tetsuo Yamamoto, was 8.4 million for the base scope. The remaining 1.6 million within that construction envelope was a contingency buffer I was holding explicitly for overruns, last-minute scope additions, or unexpected conditions that came up once they opened walls and started the actual build. That contingency felt responsible to me given that we're doing a full restaurant conversion on a space that was previously an office. Then the remaining 5 million was split among three buckets: equipment purchases not covered by the leasing arrangement I have in place for the main kitchen equipment, pre-opening costs which includes staff recruitment and training, menu development, the initial liquor license and health inspection fees, and then working capital to carry the business through the ramp-up period — probably three months of operating losses before we stabilize.
