Olive oil quality varies year to year similarly to wine — drought years, excessive heat during flowering, irregular rainfall, disease pressure — all of these affect the final oil character and sometimes the polyphenol levels significantly. Solleone Japan told me they send tasting samples from each new harvest before they ask restaurant clients to commit to a seasonal order, so if in a given year the Frantoio Franci quality doesn't meet my standard, I'm not stuck with inventory. They maintain relationships with two or three backup Tuscan producers for exactly that reason, so the supply chain doesn't break even if I need to switch in a given season. On the delivery side, the minimum order is six bottles per delivery, which is perfectly calibrated to my usage — six bottles is roughly three weeks of inventory, so I'm ordering approximately every three weeks. They operate a Tokyo delivery route twice a month, and for restaurant clients in the 23 wards they do direct delivery. The detail I was most pleased about is that they use a climate-controlled vehicle for summer deliveries — they told me they maintain below 20 degrees Celsius in transit even in July and August in Tokyo. That's critical. An oil like Frantoio Franci that you're paying 4,200 yen per 500ml for should not be riding around in an uninsulated delivery van in 35-degree heat.

The climate-controlled transit detail is exactly the right thing to have pressed them on, and the fact that they proactively maintain below 20 degrees in summer is a meaningful operational commitment. A lot of importers who sell you on premium positioning then put the product in a van that reaches ambient temperature in July, and you lose a significant fraction of the oil's character before it even arrives at your kitchen. The vintage flexibility policy also tells you something important about how Solleone Japan thinks about their restaurant relationships — they're not trying to lock you into quantity commitments and move product regardless of quality; they're structured around keeping the restaurant satisfied, which is what you want in a long-term supplier. The six-bottle minimum per delivery fitting naturally into your usage rhythm is also a good sign that they've structured their minimum orders around realistic restaurant consumption patterns rather than their own logistics convenience. Now let me ask about flour, because for a northern Italian kitchen doing fresh pasta daily, your flour sourcing is just as consequential as your oil. Have you worked that out?

Flour was actually more straightforward than the oil search, in retrospect, because the answer was obvious from the start — for fresh pasta at a serious Italian restaurant you use Caputo 00, full stop. Caputo is the Naples mill, they've been milling specialty flours for over a century, and the 00 designation for pasta specifically is calibrated for the protein content and granularity you need to get proper gluten development in fresh pasta without overworking the dough. I've used Caputo in other kitchen contexts and I wasn't going to experiment with a Japanese domestic substitute or a different Italian brand when Caputo is the established standard. The question was which importer to use, and after a few conversations I went with Suzuki Foods. They're a mid-sized food importer based in Osaka with a Tokyo distribution hub in Koto-ku. They're not a single-category specialist the way Solleone Japan is, but they have a strong Italian pantry dry goods division — pasta, flour, specialty ingredients — and they've been importing Caputo specifically for about fifteen years, which means their supply chain and quality management for that product line is mature. The pricing they quoted me is 3,800 yen per 25kg sack, which I benchmarked against a reference from a chef colleague of mine who runs a Neapolitan pizza operation in Shibuya and was paying 4,100 yen per 25kg sack through a different importer for the same product. So I feel confident that the Suzuki Foods pricing is genuinely competitive.

Caputo 00 is the correct answer for fresh pasta and I'd agree that experimenting with alternatives when you have a proven standard available introduces unnecessary risk, especially in the pre-opening period when you're trying to stabilize your kitchen processes rather than troubleshoot flour variables. The 300-yen-per-sack difference between your price at 3,800 yen per 25kg sack and what your colleague is paying at 4,100 is meaningful at volume — if you're going through one sack every ten to fourteen days, that's a saving of somewhere between 600 and 900 yen per month, which isn't transformative but it's real money for the same product. Koto-ku is a reasonable location for a Tokyo distribution hub serving central Tokyo restaurants, it's a standard freight corridor and the logistics to Higashi-Azabu are workable. Did you ask Suzuki Foods about delivery frequency and minimum order quantities, and did you check into their lot documentation practices? With flour, especially 00 for daily pasta production, you want to know you're working with product that was milled recently, not flour that's been sitting in a warehouse since the previous season.

Yes, I pushed them on both points. On delivery frequency, Suzuki Foods runs a delivery schedule to central Tokyo three times a week — Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays — and the account rep confirmed that same-week orders are accommodated as long as I place the order by noon the day before the delivery. That level of flexibility is important for a small restaurant operation where I don't want to be carrying more than three weeks of inventory at a time. The minimum order is two sacks per delivery, which fits my usage. At my anticipated pasta output for a dinner service of 30 to 40 covers, I estimate going through roughly one sack of Caputo 00 every ten to fourteen days, so two sacks per order gives me approximately three to four weeks of inventory. I have a dedicated dry goods room in the basement that the renovation included specifically for this kind of storage — temperature controlled, properly shelved, designed to keep flour in optimal condition. On lot documentation, I did ask specifically, and this was a slightly more involved conversation because initially the account rep was giving me best-before dates, which aren't what I want. I want milling dates. I explained that for fresh pasta production where you're working with the flour every day, the milling date tells you much more than a best-before — it tells you how far into the shelf life you are and whether the hydration behavior you calibrated at the beginning of the month is still going to hold as the batch ages. They came back to me after checking with their operations team and confirmed they can provide milling date documentation on request for each lot. I'll be asking for that every delivery.

Pushing for milling dates rather than best-before dates is exactly the right ask — it tells you how far into the shelf life you are and whether your hydration calibration will hold as the batch ages. The fact that Suzuki Foods could accommodate it after checking internally suggests the data exists; they just don't surface it proactively. Tuesday-Thursday-Saturday delivery with a same-day noon cutoff gives you real operational flexibility. Between the Caputo 00 from Suzuki Foods and the Frantoio Franci from Solleone Japan, your dry pantry backbone is solid. Now tell me about produce — I have a feeling that's where the story gets more interesting.

Yes, the produce story is the most interesting one. I have to start with the origin of the connection, because it's one of those things where the value of a trusted network reveals itself in unexpected ways. You know I've been working with my accountant, Hiroshi Tanabe — he's been handling all the financial structure for this project, we've talked about him in previous sessions. I didn't know until about six weeks ago that Tanabe's wife runs a catering business. It came up completely offhand in a call where we were reviewing the equipment budget — he mentioned that she had recently switched her produce sourcing contact for her catering business and her ingredient costs for Italian-style vegetables had dropped noticeably while the quality had gone up. I asked him what had changed, and he said she'd started working with a produce broker who specializes in European-style vegetables for Western cuisine restaurants. I asked him if he could make an introduction, and he was happy to — he actually seemed pleased that a contact through his wife's business world might be useful to me. He introduced me to a man named Kenji Ueno, who operates as a produce broker out of a firm called Ueno Seika. Ueno Seika works specifically with Tsukiji-Ota Market — that's the main wholesale produce market that absorbed the trading relationships and many of the vendors from the original Tsukiji inner market after the move to Toyosu — and Kenji Ueno is specifically known among his restaurant clients for sourcing European-style vegetables and specialty Italian produce items that don't flow easily through general wholesale channels.

That connection is a good illustration of why the professional network around a project matters beyond its obvious functions. Tanabe is there to manage your accounting, but a good accountant who's been close to a project often makes lateral connections instinctively. His wife's catering business having a prior working relationship with Kenji Ueno at Ueno Seika gives you a real-world operational reference — she's been placing orders, receiving produce, dealing with the day-to-day reality of working with him. That's far more meaningful than anything from a cold introduction. The specialization in Tsukiji-Ota Market is also significant: after the Tsukiji move, that market became the real center of gravity for specialty produce in Tokyo, and a broker with deep relationships there is in a completely different position from someone working through general wholesale channels. What was your first meeting with Kenji Ueno like, and how did you structure the arrangement?

The first meeting was very good. We met in person at a coffee place in Tsukishima, which is geographically close to the market area — he'd been at Tsukiji-Ota Market from around three AM that morning and Tsukishima was convenient. He's in his mid-fifties, calm, very direct, with the kind of unhurried confidence that you see in people who are genuinely expert in their domain and don't feel any need to sell themselves. Within about ten minutes of talking, he was describing which farms in Nagano are currently growing radicchio this season, which prefecture is producing the best cavolo nero right now, what the supply situation on cardoons looks like for autumn — all of this from memory, no notes, with the specificity of someone who is in daily contact with these supply chains. That kind of market knowledge is not something you can fake and it's not something you get from a product catalog. It comes from twenty-plus years of being at the market every morning and building relationships with every layer of the supply chain. The arrangement we settled on is spec-based sourcing. I provide him with a seasonal produce list at the start of each month — the kinds of items I'm planning to work with, the quantities I anticipate, the quality thresholds I need. For a northern Italian kitchen that means things like radicchio, cavolo nero, castelfranco, treviso, fennel, cardoons when they're available in autumn, different varieties of winter squash, fresh peas in spring, and so on. He sources to those specs, but he also proactively contacts me when something exceptional comes through Tsukiji-Ota Market that he thinks I'd want to know about — a particularly beautiful batch of something seasonal, or a small quantity of something unusual that he knows fits my menu direction. That proactive intelligence function is, honestly, probably the most valuable part of the arrangement.

The way you're describing Kenji Ueno matches what you want in a produce broker at this level. The best brokers at Tsukiji-Ota Market are market people who happen to also sell to restaurants — the relationship dynamic is somewhat reversed from a typical supplier interaction. The spec-based structure with proactive intelligence is exactly the right framework for a northern Italian kitchen. Radicchio, castelfranco, treviso, cavolo nero, cardoons — these are items that a generalist Tokyo supplier either won't carry or will carry past their peak. Having a broker at Tsukiji-Ota Market every morning sourcing to your specification is what makes those varieties viable as consistent menu elements rather than lucky-day specials. What's the pricing structure, and how does delivery work in practice?

The pricing structure is a broker margin on top of market rate, which is standard for this kind of arrangement — Kenji Ueno is not a wholesaler, he's a broker, so he's not marking up on an inventory he holds; he's charging a margin for the sourcing service and the quality filtering he applies at the market. I've done some benchmarking on a few test items — comparing what he quoted me against the general wholesale prices I could find from publicly available references for those product categories — and his margin is in the range of 8 to 12 percent above the market rate depending on the item. For the sourcing service he provides, and particularly for the quality filtering and specialty expertise, I think that's very fair. Some items where he's doing more active sourcing work might be at the higher end of that range, more commodified items might be closer to 8 percent. I'm comfortable with the overall cost structure. On delivery: Ueno Seika operates a small refrigerated van, and for restaurant clients in central Tokyo, Kenji Ueno does a morning delivery run himself. The schedule for Higashi-Azabu would put my delivery as the second or third stop on his Minato-ku route, arriving somewhere between five-thirty and seven AM. That timing is ideal for a dinner-only kitchen — the produce arrives right at the beginning of kitchen prep, which means by the time my team is doing the detailed prep work for evening service, everything is already on site and has been inspected. I place the order by eight PM the evening before, he's at Tsukiji-Ota Market from around three AM, sources what I need, and delivers by mid-morning at the latest. The lead time is as tight as it can possibly be while still going through the market sourcing step. And he's agreed to send me a weekly text briefing on Sunday evenings — a short summary of what looks exceptional for the coming week and what's likely to be scarce or priced high due to weather, seasonal pressures, or supply disruptions. That forward intelligence on the market is very useful for menu planning.

Eight to twelve percent over market rate for a specialist produce broker with Kenji Ueno's depth of market access and the sourcing service he provides is very reasonable — you're paying for daily expertise, quality filtering, and relationship access, not just a logistics markup, and the alternative of sourcing that category of specialty Italian vegetables yourself through general wholesale channels would either cost more, deliver lower quality, or both. The five-thirty to seven AM delivery to Higashi-Azabu fitting naturally into his existing Minato-ku route is logistically clean — you're not paying a premium for an out-of-the-way detour, and the timing is perfectly matched to a dinner-only kitchen's prep schedule. The eight PM order cutoff the evening before is a tight cadence but it becomes natural once your team has rhythm, and the benefit is that you're receiving produce purchased at market that same morning rather than something redistributed from a warehouse. The Sunday evening market briefing is worth calling out specifically — that weekly forward read on scarcity and exceptional product is the kind of intelligence that lets you write your weekly menu with real market awareness rather than working backwards from what you were able to get. It's a qualitatively different way of planning a menu. I want to ask about one more dimension: how are you thinking about formalizing these three supplier relationships? You have Solleone Japan, Suzuki Foods, and Ueno Seika — are any of these on written contracts, and have you thought about what level of documentation makes sense for each one given how differently they're structured?

Good question, and this is actually something I've been thinking about in the context of Tanabe's role specifically. Since Tanabe is my accountant and he's tracking all of the business expenditures for this project, he has a legitimate professional interest in understanding the supplier arrangements at some level of detail. And since it was Tanabe who introduced me to Ueno through his wife's catering connection, he has a bit of a different relationship to that particular supplier arrangement than he does to the others — there's a personal network element there that makes it feel right to loop him in more deliberately. For the Solleone Japan and Suzuki Foods relationships, those are both operating under standard vendor purchase order terms — their standard business terms, nothing bespoke. I've reviewed both sets of terms and they're clean. No unusual exclusivity clauses, no onerous liability provisions, standard delivery and payment terms. Those relationships are well-structured from a contractual standpoint and don't require anything special. The Ueno Seika arrangement is where I want to be more thoughtful, because the nature of produce brokering means you can't have a rigid contract — you can't fix pricing in advance on perishables, you can't guarantee quantity commitments when you're sourcing to market availability. But I do want a written memo of understanding that documents the terms of the relationship in a reference form: the broker margin range, the delivery timing and logistics, the Sunday briefing arrangement, the spec-based ordering process, minimum order parameters, and the general quality standards I've communicated to him. I'll ask Tanabe to review whatever we put together, partly because he knows Ueno through his wife's business and can give me a reality check on whether the terms I'm documenting reflect what the actual experience of working with Ueno Seika is like.

That's a well-calibrated approach across the three relationships. Standard vendor terms for Solleone Japan and Suzuki Foods makes sense — those are straightforward buyer-supplier arrangements where the supplier's own terms are adequate. The memo of understanding for Ueno Seika is the right call: it documents mutual expectations without trying to impose rigid contractual structure on what is inherently a market-flexible brokering relationship. Involving Tanabe in reviewing the Ueno Seika documentation is sound for multiple reasons — as your accountant he should have visibility into a recurring cost relationship that affects food cost, and his connection to Kenji Ueno through his wife's catering business gives him a practical benchmark. Whatever you document — the margin range, delivery arrangement, Sunday briefing — he can cross-reference against what she's actually experienced, which is a genuine verification rather than just a formality. Between the Frantoio Franci through Solleone Japan, the Caputo 00 through Suzuki Foods, and the specialty produce through Ueno Seika at Tsukiji-Ota Market, you've built a supply foundation that's well above average for a new opening.

Okay, so we're finally getting to the wine conversation. I've been putting this off for a few weeks because it felt like the most complicated piece to wrap my head around, but we're at the point where I need to commit. Quick status on everything else first: the contractors finished the main renovation last Thursday — the back wall came out perfectly, the wood paneling in the dining room is exactly what I wanted, very Piedmontese in feel without being kitschy. Kitchen equipment is basically installed. The pasta cooker came in two days late from the supplier, which had me stressed for a moment, but it went in without any issues and we tested it yesterday afternoon. I spent most of last week getting the pantry organized — dry goods, the basics I need to be stocked for opening month: semolina, '00' flour, a few different rices for risotto, the preserved ingredients that take time to source well. All of that is sorted. So the wine program is genuinely the last major piece before I can call ourselves ready for a September opening. I've been doing a lot of thinking about it and I've also had some very productive conversations with a supplier. I want to walk through where I've landed, get your reaction, and figure out if there are any gaps in my thinking before I finalize the opening order.

It sounds like the buildout is in really good shape — the fact that kitchen equipment is in and tested is a significant milestone, and having dry goods sorted means you've removed a lot of the operational uncertainty that tends to pile up in the final weeks before opening. Wine is absolutely the right conversation to have now. Depending on how complex the initial cellar is, you typically need three to five weeks between placing the opening order and being ready to serve the first bottle — there's receiving, inspection, entering everything into inventory, organizing the cellar by your system, and then the practical work of making sure your floor staff understands what's on the list. So the timing is right. What I'd find helpful to understand is where you're starting from: have you already identified a supplier, or is that still an open question? And do you have a rough sense of what kind of cellar you're trying to build — in terms of scale, depth, price range — or is that also still being shaped?

The supplier question is actually already settled, which is probably the most important thing I've done on the wine side so far. I went with a company called Nakata Shoji. They're a mid-size importer and distributor, headquartered in Minato-ku, been operating since the late eighties. Their reputation is strongest on Italian and French, which obviously aligns well with what I'm doing. But let me tell you how I actually found them, because the story matters. About six weeks ago I had dinner with a friend of mine named Reiko Igarashi. Reiko and I go back a long way — we trained at the same culinary school, though we went in very different directions after graduation. I went into the kitchen and spent the next decade cooking. She went the sommelier route, and she's been extraordinarily successful at it. She's currently the head sommelier at Hotel Okura, which if you know anything about the Tokyo hospitality world, is a genuinely prestigious position. The wine program at Hotel Okura is one of the most respected in the city, and the fact that she holds that role says a lot about where she is in the field. Anyway, we were at dinner — just catching up, talking about the restaurant, what I was planning — and I mentioned that the wine side of things was weighing on me. I didn't have a supplier relationship established, I wasn't sure who to approach, and I was nervous about making the wrong choice at the outset because the supplier relationship tends to set the whole tone of your program for years. Without hesitating, Reiko said 'You need to talk to Mariko Nakata.' She said Mariko is, in her view, the best account manager she has ever worked with across any supplier, and that her depth of knowledge specifically on Italian wine is exceptional. She also mentioned that the overall service level from Nakata Shoji — reliability, delivery accuracy, responsiveness — has been consistently excellent over the years of working with them for Hotel Okura. What really struck me was that Reiko wrote the introduction email right there at the dinner table, on her phone, before we'd finished our drinks. She wasn't saying 'I'll put you in touch sometime' — she just did it immediately, which told me she genuinely meant what she said. I had a meeting with Mariko Nakata the following week, and I was impressed from the first five minutes. She came in already having done homework on the restaurant — she knew it was northern Italian, she knew the Higashi-Azabu location, she had a sense of the price positioning I was targeting — and she showed up with a tasting sheet that was already pre-filtered to be relevant to my concept. That's not typical. Most reps show up with a generic catalog and let you fish. She came in with a curated starting point. I also found out at some point that her father is actually the president of Nakata Shoji, but you would never guess it from how she conducts herself. There's no sense of entitlement, no coasting. She runs her accounts with the same professionalism and attention you'd want from any senior rep.

That's a meaningful introduction to have. A recommendation from Reiko Igarashi in her position at Hotel Okura carries real weight — she's working at a level where she interacts with multiple suppliers and account managers constantly, so when she names one person as the best she's worked with, that's based on a real comparison set. The fact that she made the introduction immediately, without prompting, rather than filing it away as a vague intention, suggests the recommendation reflects something she actually feels strongly about rather than a polite social gesture. And the behavior you're describing from Mariko Nakata in that first meeting — arriving pre-briefed, bringing a tailored tasting sheet rather than a catalog, showing genuine knowledge of the Italian portfolio — is exactly what you want from an account manager at this stage. It tells you she's going to be a resource rather than just a fulfillment mechanism. The family connection to the ownership at Nakata Shoji is worth noting: it typically means she has more institutional access and more latitude to make decisions quickly than a standard rep, which can be very useful when you need something specific on short notice or want to have a real conversation about portfolio direction. It sounds like you've made a good call. How did the conversations with Mariko Nakata develop from that first meeting? What does the actual structure of the opening order look like in terms of scale?

We had three meetings in total before I felt confident enough to commit to the opening order. The first was the tasting and initial conversation I described. The second was more detailed — we went through the specific appellations I was most interested in, she brought samples of a few bottles I hadn't tried, and we started talking seriously about quantities and budget. The third meeting was basically finalizing everything and going over the logistics of the delivery and cellar organization. By the end of that process I was very clear on what the opening cellar was going to look like. In terms of total bottle count, we landed on 280 bottles for the initial order. That number was arrived at through a real conversation about the right scale for a 40-seat restaurant at our price point. Mariko had data from other comparable accounts she worked with and she made a case for starting at that level rather than going significantly smaller. My instinct at first was to start more conservatively — I'd heard horror stories from other operators about opening with overambitious wine programs and then spending the first year with dead inventory that wasn't moving and was tying up capital. Her argument was that 280 bottles with the right selection was defensible and wouldn't leave me in that position, especially given the structure of the list we were building. On the label count, we settled on 47 labels for the opening list. Mariko actually pushed me to go broader — she floated somewhere in the range of 55 to 60 labels, which she felt was more appropriate for a restaurant at our positioning. But I pushed back. For a 40-seat room in the first months of operation, 47 labels feels like the right degree of focus. You can tell a coherent story with 47 labels. If you go much beyond that without already knowing your clientele, you're guessing, and that guessing tends to show. On the financial side, the total inventory cost for the opening purchase is 1.85 million yen. That's the landed cost to us, not retail. It's a significant number, and I sat with it for a while, but relative to the overall investment in the restaurant and relative to what 280 bottles at our price positioning should be able to generate in revenue, it's proportionate. I feel good about it.

The numbers cohere well. 280 bottles across 47 labels works out to roughly six bottles per label on average, which is an important detail: you're not putting one or two bottles of anything on the list, which would mean a single enthusiastic table could wipe out a label in a night. Six bottles gives you enough of a buffer that a popular bottle can sell well for a couple of weeks before you hit a reorder point. The 1.85 million yen landing cost implies an average of about 6,600 yen per bottle at cost — if you're targeting a standard restaurant markup of roughly 2.5 to 3x for bottles, that puts your average bottle on the list somewhere in the 16,500 to 20,000 yen range, which is consistent with a mid-to-upper positioning in Higashi-Azabu. The fact that you had three structured meetings with Mariko Nakata before finalizing the order is also encouraging — it means you weren't rushed into a decision, and the selection reflects real back-and-forth rather than just accepting a first proposal. One thing I'm curious about: given that you went with Nakata Shoji specifically for their strength on Italian and French, and given that the concept is northern Italian, what does the geographic breakdown of those 47 labels and 280 bottles actually look like? I'd expect Italian to dominate, but I'm interested in how you thought about the balance.

The cellar breakdown is 60% Italian, 25% French, 15% Japanese, and I can walk through the reasoning for each tier. The Italian 60% was the one number I never seriously questioned. If you're calling yourself a northern Italian restaurant and you're serving in a neighborhood like Higashi-Azabu at a serious price point, the Italian wines need to be the heart of your list, both in volume and in quality. Within that Italian 60%, the selection is heavily concentrated in the north. Piedmont is the anchor — Barolo and Barbaresco from producers that Mariko Nakata helped me identify, some single-vineyard Nebbiolo, Dolcetto and Barbera for more accessible price points, Gavi di Gavi and Roero Arneis for whites. I also brought in some Franciacorta for sparkling — I prefer Franciacorta to Prosecco for a restaurant of this caliber, the methodology is more rigorous and the results in the glass are more interesting. There's some representation from other northern regions: a Lugana that I love, a couple of Alto Adige whites. And I do have some central Italian wines — a few Sangiovese-based bottles that I have personal feelings about — but the geographical center of gravity of the Italian tier is firmly in Piedmont and Lombardy. The French 25% was the number I debated most. My original instinct was to keep it lower — maybe 15 or 20% — because there's an argument that in a northern Italian restaurant the French wines are something of a concession to conventional expectations rather than a genuine curatorial statement. But Mariko made a very specific argument that I found convincing: at our price point, in Tokyo, a certain segment of the clientele is going to want a French option for significant occasions regardless of what food they're eating. She said from her experience managing accounts at comparable restaurants, when a table is celebrating something — an anniversary, a business success, a major birthday — the host very often reaches for Burgundy or Champagne as the prestige bottle, and if you don't have that option you're losing those sales and potentially sending a signal that the restaurant isn't quite ready to hold its own against the French-wine-dominated establishments in the neighborhood. I found that argument genuinely persuasive and adjusted my initial position. The Japanese 15% was my initiative entirely, and Mariko was actually somewhat skeptical at first. She wasn't opposed exactly, but she didn't immediately see it as a natural fit, and I think her concern was partly about whether Japanese wine would be legible to the clientele at a northern Italian restaurant in a way that felt intentional rather than accidental. But I pushed for it because I feel strongly that a restaurant in Tokyo in 2025 should be making a statement about Japanese wine at a moment when Japanese producers are doing genuinely interesting things. I'm specifically thinking about producers like Fattoria AL Fiore in Miyagi — what they're doing with Pinot Noir is remarkable, it's getting real international attention — and Grace Wine in Yamanashi, which has a level of consistency and sophistication that holds up against serious European producers. But beyond the quality argument, the Japanese tier gives the wine list a dimension of identity that I think is actually very consistent with what the restaurant is trying to do overall: there's a Japanese sensibility running through everything, even though the food is Italian. The wine list can be a place where that sensibility becomes explicit and legible rather than just implicit in the room.

The 60% Italian, 25% French, 15% Japanese breakdown is thought through in a way that goes beyond just splitting percentages on a spreadsheet. The Piedmont concentration within the Italian tier is exactly right for the concept — Barolo and Barbaresco have the stature and the food affinity for what you'll be cooking, and the range you're describing from entry-level Barbera and Dolcetto up through single-vineyard Nebbiolo gives you both accessibility and depth in a single appellation family. That's good list architecture. The French 25% will probably turn out to be right even if it doesn't feel philosophically pure, because Mariko Nakata's read on the clientele psychology at Tokyo restaurants at this price point is almost certainly accurate. The Burgundy and Champagne moment is real and you'll feel the absence of it if you've underprovided. And the Japanese tier — I think the case you're making for it is actually the strongest version of the argument. It's not tokenism, it's a genuine curatorial position, and the fact that you can name specific producers with specific reasons — Fattoria AL Fiore in Miyagi for the Pinot, Grace Wine in Yamanashi for consistency — means your floor staff can articulate it with conviction rather than stumbling through a vague answer. 

I want to shift to how this cellar functions during service. The structure of the glass program has a big operational impact on how the 280 bottles actually behave in practice — some labels will be stable bottle-only inventory, others are going to rotate quickly through the by-the-glass section and need tight reorder discipline. Can you tell me how you're thinking about the pour-by-the-glass component of the list? How many wines are you offering by the glass, and how are you deciding which labels go into that tier versus staying bottle-only?

The glass program was probably the most operationally detailed conversation I had with Mariko Nakata across all three meetings, and I want to explain both the structure and the reasoning behind it. The decision I've landed on is eight wines by the glass at any given time. That's the number. Two sparkling, three white, three red. Everything else on the list — all 47 labels minus the eight in the glass program — is bottles only. Let me explain why I landed on eight rather than a larger or smaller number. On the low end, you could argue for five or six, which keeps the program extremely tight and simple to manage. But five or six by the glass starts to feel sparse for a solo diner or a couple who want to try different things across a meal, and it doesn't give us enough variety to serve as a genuinely useful entry point for guests who aren't ready to commit to a full bottle. On the high end, some restaurants at our positioning offer twelve, fifteen, even twenty wines by the glass, and I've watched that create real operational problems: oxidation management across too many open bottles, inconsistent pour quality as the night goes on, staff who can't speak to every wine on the glass list with any depth. Eight is the number that gives real choice without those problems. The two sparkling slots are important to me — I want to have something interesting in Franciacorta by the glass, not just a generic Prosecco, and I want a second sparkler option, potentially rotating between a French Champagne and something from our Japanese tier depending on the season and what's interesting. For the three whites and three reds by the glass, the selection will reflect the geographic structure of the overall list — probably at least two of the three whites being Italian at any given time, and the reds tilted Italian as well. On the practical side, Mariko suggested using Coravin for any wine in the by-the-glass program that retails above 7,000 yen per bottle. Below that threshold we pour and manage turnover the traditional way, which means on those lower-priced pours I need to be confident we're moving at least a bottle a day on busy nights, and the selection has to reflect what I actually believe will turn over at that rate. The Coravin approach protects the higher-value bottles and lets us offer something genuinely interesting by the glass without the risk of oxidation eating into margins or quality. Mariko was also clear that the eight-glass program shouldn't be static — she recommended reviewing and rotating it every six to eight weeks based on what's selling, what's seasonal, and what's arriving new in the Nakata Shoji portfolio that might be a good fit for the glass tier. She said she'd proactively flag candidates from their incoming inventory, which is exactly the kind of ongoing dialogue I wanted when I chose to work with them. This isn't a one-time transaction where I buy the opening cellar and then call them when I run out of something. It's meant to be a genuine working relationship.

Eight by the glass is well calibrated for a 40-seat room. The two-three-three structure across sparkling, white, and red is logical and symmetrical enough that your floor staff can memorize it quickly and navigate it without hesitation, which matters in service. The 7,000-yen retail threshold for Coravin is the right kind of bright line — it's specific enough to be a rule rather than a judgment call in the moment, and it protects the bottles where oxidation risk is most economically consequential. The math on Coravin is simple: the per-use cost is real but modest relative to the waste cost of an opened 10,000-yen bottle that doesn't sell through in two days, so at and above that threshold the tool pays for itself quickly. 

The seasonal rotation cadence is something that separates wine programs that stay alive from ones that quietly stagnate. Every six to eight weeks is ambitious but achievable, especially if Mariko Nakata at Nakata Shoji is doing her part by flagging incoming arrivals proactively. The only thing I'd add is that the rotation should be data-informed as well as instinct-informed — meaning when you review the glass list, you should have a clear picture of which bottles in the glass program turned over fastest, which ones needed Coravin every time, and which ones were slow. That data is relatively easy to track and very useful for shaping the next rotation. 

I want to ask about the physical storage side of the operation. You mentioned early on that you built out a dedicated cellar space — can you describe the setup? Temperature, humidity, capacity, and how you're thinking about the organizational system within it?

The cellar space is something I'm genuinely proud of, because we designed it from the start as a real working cellar rather than an afterthought. It's a room behind the main dining room, temperature-controlled with a dedicated commercial cooling unit — not a repurposed home wine cooler, a proper commercial unit sized for the space, which runs at 13 to 14 degrees Celsius. I was specific about that temperature range because it's the sweet spot for Italian reds in particular: cold enough to keep the wines stable and slow any premature evolution, but not so cold that you're slowing down the development of anything you're holding for even a few months. Humidity is sitting at 68 to 72 percent, which is where I want it — high enough to keep corks sealed and prevent the micro-oxidation that comes from dry-shrinking corks, but below the threshold where labels start getting damp and racking hardware can corrode. The racking itself is floor-to-ceiling on the two long walls of the room, plus a central freestanding island unit. All cedar. I pushed for cedar over the alternatives because I like the way it looks and smells and because cedar is appropriately chemically inert — it's not going to off-gas anything that interacts with the wine over time. Total capacity with the current racking configuration is around 350 bottles. So when the 280 bottles from the opening order come in, I'll be at roughly 80% capacity, which feels right. I specifically did not want to be at 100% from day one because it would make receiving new stock from Mariko Nakata a logistical problem rather than a pleasure — every new arrival would mean something has to move. I want to have room to receive things. For the organizational system within the cellar, I've laid it out geographically in a sequence that mirrors how I think about Italian wine: starting with Piemonte on the left wall, moving east across northern Italy, transitioning through central Italy and then to France organized by region, and ending with the Japanese section on the island unit. Within each region, reds are racked separately from whites. This geographic logic serves a dual purpose — it helps me navigate the cellar quickly, and more importantly it helps the floor staff develop a mental map of where things live, which speeds up retrieval during service. I also have a small separate refrigerated unit behind the bar for the bottles that are in active service — meaning the bottle that's currently open or the next-in-line for a label in the glass program. Those never go back to the cellar during a service; they stay at the bar where the server can reach them without leaving the floor.

That's a well-engineered setup. The 13 to 14 Celsius range is exactly right for your Italian-dominant list — it's the professional standard for working cellars serving aged Nebbiolo-based wines, and it will also keep your whites and Franciacorta in good condition even if they sit for a few weeks before service. The 68 to 72 percent humidity is well controlled: below 75% so you're not fighting mold or label deterioration, above 60% so corks aren't drying out on the longer-hold bottles. The fact that you chose a purpose-built commercial unit rather than a converted home appliance is the kind of decision that looks boring in the planning phase and matters enormously a year in, when a home unit would be cycling on and off constantly in a commercial context and eventually failing on a Friday night in the middle of summer service. The cedar racking adds something the alternatives don't — the aesthetic is genuinely appropriate for the room, and you're right that it's inert. The geographic organization by appellation is the standard that works best operationally; the alternatives — organizing by price tier, by food pairing, by producer — all break down in practice because staff can't internalize them as a spatial map. Geography is learnable because it's stable and intuitive. The bar fridge for active-service bottles is a detail that seasoned operators often include and first-timers often skip, and the difference in service flow during a busy night is significant — you don't want your server walking the length of the restaurant to retrieve a bottle from a temperature-controlled back room in the middle of a turn. That system is sound. 

I want to close with a question about the reorder workflow, because this is where a lot of wine programs that are well-designed on opening day start to drift. How are you thinking about the mechanics of knowing when to reorder — specifically, how do you plan to track when a label is running low, and what's the trigger for contacting Mariko Nakata at Nakata Shoji to place a replenishment order?

Honestly, the reorder workflow is the piece I'm least satisfied with at the moment, and your question is exactly the right one to end on because it's the thing I need to nail down before we open. Here's where I am: the rough working principle I have right now is that when any individual label drops to two bottles remaining in the cellar, that's the signal to reorder. Two bottles gives me enough buffer that I'm not in a panic, and if I contact Mariko Nakata immediately when I hit that threshold, under normal circumstances I should be able to get a replenishment delivery in time before I'm completely out. But 'rough working principle' is not a system, and I know it. What I want to build before September is a simple weekly inventory check — probably every Monday morning, before the week's service starts — where whoever is responsible for the cellar, likely the floor manager, goes through and notes any label sitting at two bottles or under. That flags list goes to me, and I want it to also go directly to Mariko Nakata at Nakata Shoji, so she's not waiting for me to forward something to her, she's seeing the same picture I'm seeing in real time. One thing she offered during our final planning meeting that I'm going to take her up on is a standing order arrangement for what she called the 'high-velocity' labels — the bottles she predicts, based on her experience with comparable accounts, are going to turn over fastest in the first months of operation. Her thinking was that for those specific labels, rather than managing reorders reactively, we establish a standing delivery cadence so I'm never caught short on the bottles that are most likely to sell consistently. That kind of proactive thinking is exactly what I was hoping to find in a supplier when I started this process. It's one of the reasons the Nakata Shoji relationship feels right — Mariko isn't waiting to be asked, she's thinking ahead about what I'm going to need before I've identified it myself. I don't know how September is going to go. Launching a northern Italian restaurant at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu at the positioning we're targeting is not a low-risk proposition. There's genuine uncertainty. But the wine program is the one piece of the opening that I feel genuinely confident in — the cellar structure is right, the supplier relationship is right, the list reflects what I actually believe in rather than what I thought the market wanted me to offer. That's the best position you can be in at this stage of the preparation. Everything else from here is execution.

Hey, I need to have a serious conversation with you today. I've been sitting on this for a while, but I think we need to officially retire the working name 'Ginza Trattoria' and commit to something new before we go any further with signage, menus, or any other tangible deliverables. Every time I tell someone the name, I have to immediately follow it up with 'but it's actually in Azabu' — and that's just embarrassing. It kills the energy of a conversation that should be building excitement. A friend of mine who works in hospitality PR actually laughed when I told her the name and then gave her the address. She wasn't being mean about it, but she said, 'Kenta, that's going to confuse your first hundred guests before you've even served them a single plate of pasta.' And honestly, she's right. The 'Ginza Trattoria' name is confusing since the restaurant is in Azabu, not Ginza at all. I need to fix this now, before we get deeper into the branding work. We're at a stage where the signage vendor is following up on me weekly, Aiko is waiting for a revised brief, and the web developer has the domain sitting there doing nothing. Every additional week I spend under the wrong name is a week where someone could encounter the restaurant for the first time and immediately wonder whether I know what I'm doing. That's not the first impression I want to make.

You're absolutely right to address this now, and honestly, I'm glad you're pulling the trigger on it at this stage rather than six months after opening. Your friend's reaction is exactly the kind of first impression you cannot afford to let become a pattern. The name-location mismatch is a real credibility problem — not just a quirk — because Ginza and Azabu carry very different neighborhood identities in Tokyo dining culture. Ginza reads as formal, corporate-lunch, department-store adjacency, the kind of place you go for a business dinner where the bill gets expensed without any conversation about it. Higashi-Azabu reads as intimate, residential, discerning — the kind of neighborhood where people live intentionally and choose their restaurants carefully. Those aren't interchangeable connotations, and a name that points to the wrong neighborhood will actively work against the atmosphere you're trying to build before a single guest has sat down. The good news is that you've caught this before anything permanent has been installed or printed in quantity. The name exists only in documents and digital files right now, which means the cost of changing it is low and the cost of not changing it compounds every day you leave it. So let's treat this as an opportunity rather than a setback. You've been operating under a placeholder, and now it's time to make the real decision. Walk me through what you've been thinking. Do you have any candidate names already in your head, or are you starting completely fresh?

I've been scribbling things down in a notebook for the past few weeks, actually. Let me share where my head is at, because I've gone through several directions and I want to explain why I've ended up where I have. First, I thought about leaning heavily into the northern Italian regional angle — something like 'Osteria del Nord' or 'Trattoria Piemonte.' The cuisine is rooted in Piemonte and Lombardia, so there's a genuine logic to it and it would tell a guest immediately what kind of food to expect. But then I kept running into the same problem: those names feel very generic. When you search 'Osteria del Nord' in any major city, something comes up. There's one in Amsterdam, probably one in Melbourne, almost certainly one in Paris. I don't want to be fighting for SEO territory with a restaurant on the other side of the world, and I don't want guests arriving with expectations shaped by a completely different kitchen. The second direction I explored was incorporating the neighborhood — 'Azabu Cucina,' 'Higashi-Azabu Table,' 'Casa Azabu,' things like that. Those feel more grounded geographically and they at least put us in the right part of the city. But I worry they sound either too casual, like a lunch spot that does reasonable pasta for the nearby office crowd, or too real-estate-brochure, like a developer named a lobby restaurant after the neighborhood to signal that it was premium without actually committing to anything. Neither of those registers is what I'm trying to build. The third direction, and this is the one I keep coming back to, is using my own name. 'Osteria Morishita.' It's clean, it's personal, it signals ownership and personal pride, and there's a long and respected tradition in Italian dining of restaurants bearing the chef-owner's family name. Think of places like Ristorante Cracco in Milan, or Dal Pescatore up in Canneto sull'Oglio. The name doesn't describe the food; it describes the person accountable for it. Am I overthinking the regional direction, or is there a version of it I should explore further before I commit to putting my own name on the door?

You're not overthinking it at all. You've actually mapped the decision space quite clearly, and the conclusion you keep arriving at is the right one for your specific situation. Let me give you a direct read on each direction so you can move forward without second-guessing. The regional appellations like 'Osteria del Nord' and 'Trattoria Piemonte' are charming, but they carry a structural limitation: they describe the food, not the place, and more importantly they don't build any equity in you as the person behind the restaurant. If you run 'Osteria del Nord' for five years and then decide to open a second location, or start hosting private dining events at a different venue, or put your name on a wine import project, the regional name gives you nothing to work with. It's also descriptive rather than distinctive as a trademark, which matters if you ever need to protect it. The neighborhood-based names suffer from a different kind of problem. They anchor you in a very specific moment in time, and neighborhoods change. Higashi-Azabu is a particular kind of neighborhood right now, but its associations in people's minds could shift meaningfully over the next decade, and 'Higashi-Azabu Table' could read very differently in 2032 than it does today, and not necessarily in a direction you'd want. But your third instinct — 'Osteria Morishita' — is strong for several reasons that I want to state explicitly so you can use them when explaining the name to future guests and press. First, the word 'osteria' carries a more personal register than 'trattoria': an osteria traditionally implies a place driven by the owner's direct hospitality and personal wine curation, which is precisely the experience you've been describing to me from the beginning of this project. Second, your family name is genuinely distinctive in the context of Italian dining. There is no significant restaurant called 'Osteria Morishita' anywhere I'm aware of, which means you own that combination the moment you begin using it publicly and consistently. Third, and most importantly, it puts your personal reputation on the door. That is not a small statement. It tells every guest who reads it that this place exists because one person believed in it deeply enough to stake their name on it. My recommendation is clear: go with 'Osteria Morishita.'

Okay. We're doing it. Renaming from 'Ginza Trattoria' to 'Osteria Morishita' — that's the decision, and I'm not revisiting it. I feel genuinely relieved saying it out loud. It just sounds right in a way the old name never did. The working name always felt like something I had typed into a spreadsheet before I had a real answer, and now I have a real answer. Now I need to think about what this means practically, because there are several things in motion that need to be updated. The most immediate one is Aiko Fujimoto. She's a freelance logo designer I've been working with on the visual identity, and she came very highly recommended by another restaurateur I respect, someone who opened a well-regarded kaiseki restaurant in Minami-Aoyama a few years back. Aiko did the full visual identity for that place and the work held up beautifully even after they went through a renovation and refreshed a significant portion of the menu. I sent her the old brief when we were still using 'Ginza Trattoria,' so I obviously need to update everything I've sent her. But I don't want to just fire off a name-change email and call it a brief revision. Before I update that document, I want to make sure I'm giving her a genuinely coherent new direction, not just a new name pasted onto the bones of an old brief that was pointing at the wrong kind of restaurant. What should I be thinking about in terms of visual identity for 'Osteria Morishita' specifically? What are the brand signals we want to send into the world, and how do they differ from what a 'Ginza Trattoria' brief would have implied?

That's exactly the right instinct — updating Aiko Fujimoto's brief isn't just a find-and-replace exercise on the name. The name change reflects a philosophical shift in how you're positioning the restaurant, and that shift needs to run through every element of the visual brief you give her. So let me walk you through the layers of brand signal that matter most for a restaurant at your level. Starting with the core emotional register: 'Osteria Morishita' should feel warm, unhurried, and deeply personal — the aesthetic equivalent of being welcomed into someone's home in the Langhe hills, but with the discretion and refinement that Higashi-Azabu guests expect. That's a specific tension, and it's actually a productive one if you name it clearly in the brief: 'rustic soul, precise execution.' For color palette, I'd steer you toward earth tones that reference both the northern Italian landscape and the materiality of the building and tableware. Specifically, think about terracotta and ivory as your anchor colors. Terracotta connects to the fired-clay tradition of Italian ceramics and the warm ochre of Piemontese stone buildings, while ivory provides the breathing room and lightness that prevents the palette from feeling heavy or dated. Together they read as sophisticated without being cold, and they photograph beautifully in both natural light and candlelight, which matters for your social media presence. For typography, I'd pair a humanist serif — something with visible calligraphic origins — with a clean, minimal grotesque for secondary text. The serif carries the warmth and the Italian heritage; the grotesque signals that this is a contemporary operation, not a theme park. And the logo itself should probably be typographic rather than illustrative — 'Osteria Morishita' in well-chosen letterforms is more durable and more versatile than any icon or pictogram. It will work on menus, signage, a website header, a business card, and a wine label equally well.

The terracotta and ivory direction makes a lot of sense to me, and I think Aiko Fujimoto will be excited about it — she tends to work in natural, material-reference palettes anyway, so this plays to her strengths. I had a call with her last week and she gave me a rough breakdown of her process. She works in three phases: initial concept exploration where she delivers four to six distinct directions, a refinement phase where we narrow to one and develop it fully including logo lockups, color system, and typography specimens, and then a final delivery phase with all the production files, brand guidelines document, and print-ready versions for the signage vendor. Her fee for this full scope is 320,000 yen, which includes unlimited revisions within each phase but not full direction changes between phases — so I need to get the brief right the first time. Given that fee structure, is there anything specific I should absolutely nail down in the brief before I hand it off to her? I don't want to waste one of the direction slots on something obviously wrong.

A logo design fee of 320,000 yen for a three-phase process with production-ready deliverables and brand guidelines is very reasonable for a Tokyo-based freelancer of that caliber, especially if she's worked on hospitality branding before — so you're not overpaying, but you're also paying enough that you should go into the brief with real specificity. Here's what I'd lock down before you hand anything over. First, the name is now 'Osteria Morishita' — make sure this appears clearly at the top of the brief, along with a single sentence explaining the positioning: chef-owner-driven northern Italian osteria in Higashi-Azabu, opening in 2025. Don't make Aiko infer the story from scattered notes; give her the sentence you'd use to introduce the restaurant to a journalist. Second, give her the color anchors explicitly: terracotta and ivory are your primary palette, and you want her to build the concept directions around that constraint rather than exploring wildly different palettes in each of the four to six concepts. You'll still get variation in how those colors are used — proportions, textures, typography pairings — but you won't waste a direction slot on something in navy and brass that you'd never approve anyway. Third, provide reference images in two categories: restaurants or brands whose visual identity you admire (even if they're not Italian), and restaurants or brands whose identity you actively dislike and don't want to be compared to. The negative references are often more useful than the positive ones because they help the designer understand your taste at the boundary. Fourth, specify the primary applications in order of priority: exterior signage at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, the physical menu, the website header, and business cards. This tells her which formats the logo needs to perform in first, which affects decisions about line weight, legibility at small sizes, and how well it reproduces in single color for things like embossing or foil stamping on menus.

This is really helpful. I'm going to draft the updated brief this weekend. One more piece I want to lock in today is the web presence. I've been meaning to handle the domain situation for a while and I finally did it — I registered the domain osteria-morishita.tokyo earlier this week. I was actually surprised it was available; I half expected something like that to already be taken. The .tokyo TLD feels right for this — it's specific, it signals place, and honestly I think it looks elegant on print materials compared to .com or .jp. Now I need to figure out what we actually build on that domain before the opening, and I want to make sure whatever we launch is aligned with the brand work Aiko Fujimoto is doing. What's your thinking on the web strategy — specifically the pre-opening phase versus the post-opening site?

Registering osteria-morishita.tokyo was a smart move, and you're right that the .tokyo extension works particularly well for a restaurant at this address and positioning — it reads as local and intentional rather than just the default choice, and it prints beautifully on a business card or a menu footer. Now, on the web strategy: I'd think about this in two distinct phases with very different objectives, and the key is not letting phase one accidentally undermine phase two. Pre-opening, your website has one job: build anticipation while collecting something of value from interested visitors. That means a minimal but beautiful single-page site — probably live within two to three weeks of receiving Aiko Fujimoto's final logo files — that includes the restaurant name and location, a brief statement of what Osteria Morishita is about in two or three sentences, an email signup form with a compelling reason to subscribe (early reservation access is the most effective hook for a restaurant in this category), and a target opening month. No placeholder lorem ipsum, no 'coming soon' countdown clock unless it's very close to the real date, no stock photography. If you don't have your own food photography yet, use a single well-chosen color image — something in the terracotta and ivory palette — that suggests the mood without making a specific promise about the food. The goal is to have four to six hundred email addresses by the time you open, from people who are already invested in the narrative of the restaurant. Post-opening, the site expands into a proper destination: the full menu with provenance notes on key ingredients and wine producers, a reservations widget connected to whatever booking system you're using, the story of the restaurant and your background, and eventually press coverage and event listings. But here's the critical sequencing point: don't build the full post-opening site until the brand guidelines from Aiko are finalized. Use a simple, well-crafted pre-opening page as a holding pattern rather than rushing a full site that doesn't match the final visual identity.

The email list idea is something I want to take seriously. I've seen other restaurant openings in Tokyo fumble the pre-opening period by either going completely dark — no online presence at all until they open — or by oversharing, posting every construction update and every delivery of kitchen equipment as if that's inherently interesting content. I don't want to do either of those things. My thinking is that the people who sign up for a list before a restaurant exists are a self-selecting group of exactly the right kind of early guests — they're curious, they're willing to take a chance, and they're almost certainly going to come with friends who trust their recommendations. So if I can get even three hundred of the right people on that list by opening week, that's real momentum. Now, let me make sure I have the full picture of what we've decided today, because I want to send a summary to Aiko Fujimoto before the end of the week. We are: one, officially renaming from 'Ginza Trattoria' to 'Osteria Morishita'; two, briefing Aiko Fujimoto with a revised document that includes the terracotta and ivory color direction, the typographic logo approach, and the primary application hierarchy I mentioned; three, building a pre-opening page on the osteria-morishita.tokyo domain; and four, keeping the full site development on hold until Aiko's brand guidelines are in hand. Does that capture everything? Is there anything I'm missing or should be thinking about before I close out today?

That summary is accurate and well-organized — you've captured the four key decisions cleanly. Let me add a few final notes to close out today's session properly. On the renaming: when you send the update to Aiko Fujimoto, frame it not just as a name correction but as a clarification of the restaurant's identity. A single paragraph explaining that the working name 'Ginza Trattoria' was always a placeholder, that the restaurant is located at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, and that 'Osteria Morishita' better reflects the chef-owner model and the neighborhood will help her understand that this isn't an arbitrary change — it's a more informed brief. Designers work better when they understand the thinking behind a decision, not just the outcome. On the budget: the 320,000 yen fee covers logo, color system, typography, brand guidelines, and production files. Make sure you clarify with Aiko whether website asset exports — things like SVG files optimized for web, favicon versions, and any social media template sizes — are included in that scope or billed separately. It's a small conversation to have now versus a friction point later when you're trying to launch the pre-opening page. On the pre-opening page: once you have even a draft logo direction from the first concept review, you can get the page live in a simple, typographic form. You don't need the finalized brand guidelines to launch something clean and intentional at osteria-morishita.tokyo — you just need the name, the color palette, and a working email capture form. Don't wait for perfection on the site when the primary function is list-building. And one thing you didn't mention but should consider: a reservation holding system. Even before you have a booking widget, a simple reply-to email or a Google Form that collects name, party size, and preferred dates for opening week can give your most committed list subscribers a tangible reason to sign up and feel invested. You can manually manage thirty or forty opening-week requests; you cannot manually manage three hundred, so build the proper system before the list gets that large. Overall, today was a genuinely useful session — you made a decision that needed to be made, and you made it well. 'Osteria Morishita' is a name worth building toward.

Good morning. I have some significant news to share today, and honestly I have been looking forward to telling you. We have finally made a hire for the head chef position at Osteria Morishita. It took longer than I originally hoped — I would say close to six weeks from the time we first started reaching out to candidates until we actually had a signed contract in hand — but I am very confident that we found exactly the right person. The search was exhausting at moments, particularly in weeks three and four when I was starting to worry we might need to push the opening timeline back if we could not find someone who fit the concept. But we got there, and I think when I tell you the full story you will understand why I feel so settled about the decision.

Good morning, Kenta-san. That is genuinely exciting news — congratulations on closing that hire, and I can hear the relief in how you are describing it. Six weeks is a real investment of time and attention, especially when you are also managing the interior build-out, the branding transition from Ginza Trattoria to Osteria Morishita, and all the supplier relationships that need to be in place before you open. The fact that you held out rather than settling for someone who was almost right suggests you had a clear picture of what you needed, which is the first requirement for a search like this to succeed. I want to hear everything — who you hired, how the candidate pool looked across those six weeks, what the deciding factors were, and how the practical details of the contract came together. Please take it from the beginning.

His name is Marco Petrelli. He is 38 years old, which I think is actually an ideal age for this kind of role — experienced enough to command a kitchen, to have made his significant mistakes already and learned from them, but still young enough to have genuine energy and ambition rather than someone who is coasting. He is originally from Modena, which in the context of what we are building at Osteria Morishita is almost poetic. We have been very deliberate about anchoring our menu to the northern Italian regions, particularly Emilia-Romagna, Lombardy, Piemonte, and having a head chef who grew up in Modena means that sensibility is not studied or adopted — it is genuinely native to him. The pasta traditions, the slow-cooked meat dishes, the relationship with aged products, the way that cuisine thinks about fat and richness and texture — that is his mother tongue. His most recent position was at Ristorante Acqua Pazza, the Italian restaurant in Daikanyama that has a very good reputation for serious regional cooking without trying to be flashy about it. He spent 4 years there in total, the first three as sous chef and the final year as head chef when the previous head left to open his own place. We signed the contract last week and I am still a little stunned that it came together the way it did.

Marco Petrelli — I want to make sure I am tracking this correctly. Ristorante Acqua Pazza in Daikanyama is a house with a real identity, not a generic Italian operation. If I recall correctly, it has been regarded as one of the more thoughtful regional Italian kitchens in that part of Tokyo, with a wine list that takes the cuisine seriously rather than just serving what sells. Four years at a single restaurant, with an internal promotion to the top of the kitchen rather than needing to be recruited from outside — that is a meaningful signal. It tells you the people who worked alongside him most closely trusted him enough to hand him the keys when the moment came. The Modena origin is worth dwelling on for a moment because it shapes the palate in very specific ways. Emilia-Romagna is probably the most technically demanding of the northern Italian regional cuisines — the pasta work is intricate, the ragù requires patience and a particular understanding of how collagen and fat behave over long cooking times, the relationship with Parmigiano-Reggiano and aged aceto balsamico tradizionale is about restraint and timing rather than volume. A chef who grew up eating those things as home food, not as restaurant food, has a completely different reference point. Did his cooking during the trial cook actually reflect that regional depth, or did you find he had moved toward something more broadly contemporary in his style?

The trial cook was extraordinary, honestly. I set it up as a half-day event in the Osteria Morishita kitchen — we are still in the equipment-testing phase so not everything is fully calibrated, and I told him upfront that the environment would be imperfect, partly as a practical reality and partly because I wanted to see how he responded to constraints. He arrived forty minutes early, walked the kitchen slowly without saying much, asked the kitchen manager two very specific questions about the oven calibration and where the heavy copper pans were stored, and then he just began. For the trial cook he prepared three dishes. The first was a tagliatelle al ragù — classic, foundational, the kind of dish where you immediately know whether someone understands the cuisine at a structural level. He made the pasta by hand in front of the whole team, and his technique was exceptional in a way that was almost quiet. No showmanship, no commentary, just the kind of practiced confidence that comes from doing something ten thousand times. The sheet was thin without being fragile, the cut was consistent, and the ragù had clearly been developed over many hours, with a depth of flavor that you simply cannot rush. The second dish was a tortellini in brodo that he said his grandmother in Modena taught him when he was very young, and I will be completely honest with you — I nearly hired him on that dish alone. The broth was luminous and had been built from a proper mix of capon and beef with vegetables roasted to a specific shade, and the tortellini were the size of a thumb tip, the pasta thin enough to be almost translucent around the filling. It was the kind of dish that makes you feel like you are being trusted with something. The third dish was more deliberately contemporary, a roasted duck breast with a Lambrusco reduction and shaved truffle, which demonstrated that he can move beyond the canon when the context calls for it without losing the disciplined sensibility underneath. What struck me as much as the food itself was the way the kitchen staff watched him the entire time. Nobody drifted, nobody checked their phones, nobody had a side conversation. They were genuinely engaged and I think a little in awe. That told me as much about his presence as the food did.

The tortellini in brodo detail is the one I would weight most heavily out of everything you just described. That dish is almost a trap for chefs who have technique without genuine depth, because there is nowhere to hide. The broth has to be impeccably clear, properly seasoned, and built from real stock work over many hours — you cannot reduce or concentrate your way to the right result quickly. The filling inside a tortellini is compressed into a very small space, which means every component of it has to carry its own weight. The pasta itself has to be thin enough to feel delicate in the mouth but structurally sound enough to hold the filling through the cooking process. Any serious cook can learn the mechanics of assembling tortellini, but cooking them at the level you are describing — the kind of dish that makes you feel like you are being trusted with something, as you put it — requires that the person making it grew up eating the right version and has that reference point built into their body rather than learned from a recipe book. The fact that he attributed it to his grandmother in Modena rather than to a mentor chef or a culinary training program tells you something important: this is family knowledge, and people who cook from family knowledge have a completely different emotional relationship with the dish than people who cook from a plated photograph in a culinary textbook. As for the kitchen team staying engaged for the full trial — you are right that this is a significant signal. Line cooks are a brutally honest audience. They are tired, they are skeptical of outsiders, and they have no professional obligation to pretend to be interested. If they were watching, it was because he was doing something worth watching. How did the broader search unfold before Marco entered the picture? You mentioned six weeks — what did the earlier phases look like?

The early phase was honestly discouraging. We used a culinary recruitment agency for the first round, and we interviewed four candidates through them over the first three weeks. Not a single one of them was quite right, and interestingly the reasons were all different, which made it difficult to simply redefine the brief and try again. The first two candidates were technically strong — you could see that immediately — but both of them had spent the majority of their careers in Japanese-Italian fusion contexts, the kind of restaurant that uses Italian structure as a loose framework and then layers in Japanese ingredients and Japanese sensibility in ways that blur the regional character. That is a legitimate genre and there are places in Tokyo doing it beautifully, but it is not what Osteria Morishita is. We are a northern Italian restaurant, specifically and deliberately, and I did not want to hire someone whose primary creative instinct would be to reframe everything through a Japanese lens. The third candidate had a genuinely impressive CV — some years in Italy, some serious Tokyo restaurants — but when we sat in the interview I could feel something was missing. He talked about cooking in a way that had become transactional. He talked about hours as a burden, about the demands of the craft as something that had worn him down. He was a burned-out version of someone who had probably been excellent five years ago, and no salary or title was going to fix that. The fourth was probably the most painful because he had real promise — he was twenty-nine, he had done a stage in Turin and worked at two good restaurants in Tokyo — but he was genuinely not ready to head a kitchen. You could see the instincts forming, but they were not yet automatic in the way they need to be when you are responsible for the entire output of a kitchen every service. I sent his information to a colleague who runs a smaller operation and suggested they stay in touch with him in a year or two. Then came the referral that changed everything. Our wine supplier, Mariko Nakata from Nakata Shoji, mentioned she had a contact through the import trade community who might be exactly what we were looking for. Mariko has been working restaurant accounts across Tokyo for many years and she has a genuinely remarkable network in the industry. She introduced us to Marco Petrelli through those industry contacts, and from the very first phone call it was obvious we were speaking to a completely different caliber of candidate.

The way you have described those four early candidates maps almost perfectly to the four failure modes of chef hiring: technically capable but wrong concept fit, technically capable but wrong culinary DNA, technically capable but emotionally depleted, and genuinely talented but not yet ready for the scope of the role. Those are four distinct problems and you handled each of them correctly by not trying to bend the role to fit the candidate. The instinct to forward the fourth candidate's information to a colleague rather than just file it away is worth noting — that kind of practical generosity tends to come back in useful ways in a small industry. Now, the Mariko Nakata referral is interesting to me on multiple levels.
