A wine supplier representative who covers restaurant accounts across Tokyo is, in a certain sense, better positioned to know the actual state of the chef talent market than any formal recruiter. Formal recruiters see candidates who are actively looking and have chosen to engage with a process. Mariko is in the kitchen at delivery time, she is at the pass when things are calm, she sits through end-of-service conversations when people are honest and a little tired. She knows who the serious people are, who is quietly thinking about a change, who is frustrated with their current situation, and critically, who would be a meaningful fit for a particular concept because she understands the concepts intimately through the lens of building wine programs for them. A referral that arrives through industry contacts of that kind comes pre-filtered in a way that a CV submission through an agency cannot replicate. It also carries a layer of mutual accountability — Marco knows that Mariko's professional standing is in some sense attached to this introduction, which adds weight to his own seriousness about it. How did the Nakata-san conversation actually happen? Did she proactively come to you, or did it emerge from something you said?

It was almost accidental in the way that the most important things often are. Mariko was in for our monthly wine tasting — we had a long afternoon session working through the opening cellar list, going bottle by bottle through the Piemonte and Emilia-Romagna selections, deciding what would anchor the list and what would fill in around it. It was a good session but I was clearly distracted, and at some point I said something offhand about the agency candidates being a disappointment, that I was worried we might not have the right head chef in place before we needed to. She did not react visibly at the time, she did not make a promise or suggest she had anyone in mind, and we moved on and finished the tasting. But about three days later she called me directly — not through email, she actually phoned — and she said she had thought about what I mentioned and that she had spoken to someone she felt might be exactly what I had described. That was Marco Petrelli. She had seen him during a routine delivery visit to Ristorante Acqua Pazza a few weeks earlier, and he had told her during their conversation that after 4 years there he was starting to think seriously about his next step. He said he felt ready for something that would be his own project to build rather than executing someone else's established vision. She remembered that when I mentioned the search, and she made the connection. The timing was almost uncanny. I have already told her that she is getting a reservation on opening night and the best table in the room, and she laughed and said she would take it only if Marco's cooking is as good as she told me it would be. Now of course I also owe her a very good dinner once we are fully running.

The detail that Mariko called rather than emailed is small but meaningful — it signals that she was treating this as a personal matter, a careful introduction rather than a casual forwarding of contact information. People reach for the phone when they want to be present in the conversation rather than simply transmitting a message. She clearly thought about it deliberately over those three days and decided she was willing to put her own name behind this introduction in a way that carries real weight in a close-knit industry. The thing Marco said about wanting something that felt like his own project rather than someone else's established vision is worth sitting with carefully, because it is simultaneously the most compelling thing about him and the thing that will require the most thoughtful management going forward. A chef who has spent 4 years executing a kitchen's inherited identity and is hungry to build something original will bring an extraordinary level of energy, creative investment, and genuine ownership to Osteria Morishita. He will arrive early to solve problems you have not yet identified. He will think about the menu during his days off. He will care about the restaurant in the way that an employee who is merely well-compensated never quite does. All of that is enormously valuable to you. At the same time, Osteria Morishita is your concept, your address at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, your name on the door in the form of the restaurant brand you are building, your vision of what northern Italian cooking should feel like in this particular neighborhood. The key is to establish early — ideally before the first service, while everyone is still in the constructive phase — a shared language about where Marco has full creative authority over the menu, the kitchen culture, the cooking processes, and where decisions come back to you as the owner. That clarity, established when relationships are healthy and forward-looking, prevents an enormous amount of friction later when the restaurant is under pressure and both of you are tired. How did the contract negotiations go? I imagine getting the structure right there was important.

The contract negotiations were actually smoother than I expected, and I think that is in part because Marco came to them with a clear and reasonable sense of his own market value rather than either underselling himself or opening at a number designed to test my reaction. We spent most of two conversations on the structure. We agreed on a monthly salary of 720,000 yen, which I will be honest is toward the higher end of what I had originally budgeted for this role, but when I sat down and thought about it seriously it is absolutely appropriate compensation for someone of his experience profile — eight years of serious Italian restaurant work, four of them in Tokyo, with the last year running a full kitchen. I would rather pay correctly and have someone who feels respected from day one than save sixty thousand yen a month and have someone who feels undervalued. Beyond the base, we also structured a 13-month bonus structure tied to quarterly performance reviews, and that was actually Marco's suggestion, not mine. He came into the second negotiation conversation with the idea already formed: he wanted a meaningful portion of his compensation to have some connection to how the restaurant actually performs rather than everything being guaranteed regardless of outcome. We agreed on criteria that include kitchen cost management, guest feedback scores, and whether we hit the revenue targets for each quarter. I found that instinct to be a genuinely healthy sign — it means he sees himself as accountable for the restaurant's success rather than just for the quality of the food that leaves his kitchen, which is exactly the kind of integrated thinking I need in a head chef. As for timing, the start date is September 1, 2025, which I am very happy about. That puts him in the restaurant two full weeks before our planned soft opening, which means he will be with us from the beginning of the final kitchen build-out, the last equipment decisions, the menu finalization, all of it.

A monthly salary of 720,000 yen with a 13-month bonus structure is a well-constructed package, and I want to reflect back why each element of it is right for what you are building. The base is honest — you described it as toward the higher end of your budget, but paying at market or slightly above market for a critical hire is almost always the correct financial decision when you account for the cost of getting this wrong. A head chef search that fails and needs to be restarted costs you six weeks of time, agency fees, a delay in opening, and the reputational cost of going to market twice, which signals to the candidate pool that there is something unresolved about the concept or the operator. The 13-month bonus structure is the more interesting element, and Marco's instinct to propose it rather than simply negotiating a higher base tells you something important about how he thinks about the relationship between his work and the restaurant's viability. A chef who wants his compensation tied to quarterly performance reviews has made a decision to understand the business, not just the kitchen. He will pay attention to food cost percentages in a way that someone on a flat guaranteed salary might not. He will think about the relationship between menu engineering and margin. He will have a stake in whether the quarterly revenue targets are met, which means he will have a stake in the guest experience in a holistic way — not just whether the food is excellent, but whether the whole visit results in the kind of satisfaction that brings people back. The September 1, 2025 start date is exceptionally well-timed and I want to underscore why. Having Marco in the building two weeks before the soft opening means the menu you open with is genuinely his menu, shaped by his hands and his palate and his creative decisions from the beginning, not a specification handed to him by someone else that he is executing without full authorship. He will be present for the equipment calibration conversations, the final supplier meetings — including the ongoing wine program work with Mariko Nakata at Nakata Shoji, which is a relationship that now has an additional layer of meaning given how the introduction happened. He will establish his own rhythms with the kitchen team before the pressure of actual service begins. He will solve problems in the space that nobody has anticipated yet, which always happens in a new kitchen regardless of how carefully everything has been planned. A few things worth doing in these two weeks before he starts: formalize in writing the creative authority boundaries I mentioned, not as constraints on Marco but as a shared reference point so you both have the same understanding of the decision-making structure. Schedule a working session with Marco and Mariko Nakata together before the opening — she introduced them, she will be a frequent presence at the restaurant as the wine supplier, and getting those three professional relationships into the same room early creates a foundation of mutual context that will serve everyone well. And document in detail the performance metrics that will drive the 13-month bonus structure now, while all three parties are aligned and optimistic, rather than trying to construct shared definitions of success mid-year when there may be tension about what the numbers actually mean. What you have assembled here — the concept, the location at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, the wine relationship with Nakata Shoji, and now Marco Petrelli as the head chef who brings genuine Modena roots and eight years of serious craft — is a cohesive and credible foundation. You should feel good about where this stands.

Good morning. I know it's been a while since our last check-in — things have been moving extremely fast on the ground, and I kept telling myself I'd sit down and do a proper session once we had something definitive to report. Well, we now have a lot that is definitive. The renovation is finished. The health inspection happened yesterday. And Marco arrives in four days. So I want to use today to do a full, structured debrief — everything from how the renovation actually closed out against our plan, to the budget final tally, to what the inspector found and what we still need to fix before opening. I also want to capture some lessons while they're fresh, because I'll need this context when I'm doing my post-project review and also when I'm talking to the bank about our line of credit. Where do you want to start?

Good morning, Kenta. Congratulations — getting through a renovation and a health inspection in the same week, with a chef arriving days later, is a significant operational milestone, and it sounds like you navigated it without anything falling apart catastrophically. I want to make sure this debrief is actually useful to you for the bank conversation and the post-project review, so let me suggest a structure and you can adjust it.

I'd propose we work through four areas in sequence. First, the renovation timeline: what the actual completion date was, what drove any variance from the plan, and what that tells us. Second, the budget final tally: where we landed versus the 8.4 million yen original budget, what drove the variance, and how it compares to your contingency assumptions. Third, the inspection results: who conducted it, what they found, what was flagged as needing correction, and what the path to final sign-off looks like. And fourth, a brief lessons-learned pass: what you would do differently on the next renovation, and what immediate action items you need to close before Marco starts service.

Does that sequence work? And is there anything time-sensitive — something that has a deadline in the next 24 hours — that we should handle first before we go through this methodically?

That sequence is exactly right. And nothing is on fire in the next 24 hours — the deadlines I have are all in the September 3 to September 5 window, so we have time to be thorough today. Let's start with the timeline.

So, the original projected completion date was August 22. That's what we had in the contract with Shimizu Construction, and that's what I had been telling people — including Marco, actually, when I confirmed his start date of September 1. The thinking was that we'd have the renovation done on August 22, do the inspection in that final week of August, and have everything resolved well before the first of September.

What actually happened is that the renovation finished on August 26. So August 26 is the actual completion date, which is four days past the contractual target. Now, when I say 'finished,' I mean the final walkthrough with Shimizu-san was on August 26, he handed over the keys for the back-of-house areas, and the punchlist items that had been flagged during the contractor's own internal review were all resolved by that date. So it's a clean handover, just four days late.

Okay, so August 26 as the actual completion date — four days behind the August 22 contractual target. And it sounds like the August 26 handover was a clean one: Shimizu-san's internal punchlist was fully resolved, not just 'good enough.' That distinction matters for your records, because a clean handover means you're not carrying contractor-side obligations into the post-handover phase.

Four days on a renovation of this scope — a full commercial kitchen buildout in a space that was presumably being converted from a prior tenant use — is not a dramatic slip. But I want to understand what caused it, because that's what's useful for the bank conversation and the lessons-learned. Was this a single root cause that ran late and pulled everything with it, or was it a series of smaller delays that accumulated? And did you know early enough that August 22 was at risk, or did it come as a surprise toward the end?

It was primarily one root cause, and it was the electrical panel upgrade. That's the thing that drove both the schedule slip and the budget overage — those two problems are actually the same problem from different angles.

Here's what happened. We were about three weeks into the renovation, so roughly the last week of June, when the electricians doing the fit-out discovered that the existing panel in the space was not rated for the load we needed. The space had been used previously by a small clothing boutique — very low electrical demand, basically just lighting and a couple of point-of-sale registers. The panel there was a 60-amp residential-grade setup. When the electricians looked at what we were speccing in: the commercial range, the hood and exhaust system, the walk-in refrigerator compressor, the commercial dishwasher, the regular lighting and POS — we were looking at a load that required at minimum a 200-amp three-phase commercial panel. The existing panel couldn't handle it, and upgrading it wasn't a nice-to-have, it was a code requirement.

Now, discovering this in the third week of a renovation is not the worst possible timing. We still had most of the kitchen fit-out ahead of us, so the panel upgrade could technically be done in parallel with other work. The problem was the coordination piece. Swapping out the panel itself — the physical labor — took about one day. But to do it legally, you have to coordinate with Tokyo Electric for the switchover of the line coming into the building, and Tokyo Electric runs on their own scheduling. Shimizu-san put in the request and we ended up waiting almost a week before they could send a crew. That week of waiting was dead time for the electricians; they could work on other parts of the space, but anything that depended on having the new panel live was blocked. That cascade — discovery, waiting for Tokyo Electric, switchover, then completing the dependent work — is where the four days came from.

As for whether I knew early: Shimizu-san called me within 24 hours of the electricians discovering the problem. He didn't proceed without telling me. He laid out two scenarios — we do the upgrade now, we take the delay and the cost hit, but we're compliant and we have the capacity we need; or we find some way to scale back the kitchen equipment to fit the existing panel, which wasn't really viable for the restaurant concept we're building. There was really only one choice, but I appreciated that he presented it as a choice and gave me the cost information upfront.

That's a clear and well-documented root cause. The electrical panel upgrade driving both the schedule slip and the budget overage is actually a coherent story — it's a single infrastructure discovery that had two consequences, which is much easier to explain to a bank than a bunch of diffuse overruns across multiple categories.

A few observations that might be useful when you're framing this for the bank or for your own retrospective:

First, the 60-amp residential panel in a prior retail tenant space is a very common situation in Tokyo neighborhoods where old commercial buildings get converted or re-tenanted. It's genuinely difficult to catch in pre-renovation due diligence unless you bring in a licensed electrician specifically to audit the panel capacity against your planned equipment load before signing the contract. Most general contractors don't include that in a standard pre-project assessment. So this wasn't negligence on your part or Shimizu-san's — it was a category of risk that's hard to price without a specific pre-project electrical audit.

Second, Shimizu-san's behavior here — calling you within 24 hours, presenting scenarios with cost information before proceeding — is exactly what good contractor communication looks like. That's worth noting both for your lessons-learned and because it speaks to the quality of your working relationship with him.

Third, the four-day slip versus a potential two-week slip: the fact that Shimizu-san's team could keep other work streams moving while waiting for Tokyo Electric is also worth noting. They managed the sequencing well enough that the cascade damage was limited.

Now let's talk money. You mentioned the electrical panel upgrade is the budget story too. Your original budget was 8.4 million yen. What's the final number?

The final cost came in at 8.87 million yen. So that's 470,000 yen over the original 8.4 million yen budget.

To put that in context: when we built the original budget, we included a 300,000 yen contingency line. So we knew going in that there was some amount of unknown-unknowns risk, and we tried to price it. What actually happened is that the electrical panel upgrade consumed the entire contingency and then ran 170,000 yen past it. So the contingency didn't fully absorb the shock, but it absorbed most of it.

Let me break down the electrical work specifically. The new panel itself — equipment and installation labor — was about 280,000 yen. The Tokyo Electric coordination fees and connection work was another 90,000 yen. Then there were some additional electrical runs that had to be re-routed once the new panel was in a slightly different position than the old one — that was maybe 50,000 yen of additional labor. So call it 420,000 yen for the electrical panel upgrade total, which is the dominant factor in the overage.

The remaining 50,000 yen of overage came from a couple of smaller things. The subfloor in the kitchen area turned out to need an additional coat of epoxy sealant — the original estimate was for one coat, but when they stripped the old flooring, the concrete underneath was in worse shape than expected and the contractor's foreman said two coats was the right call for longevity. That was maybe 30,000 yen additional. And then there were a few small fixture substitutions where what we had spec'd wasn't available and we had to go to the next grade up, which added another 20,000 yen or so across a few line items. But honestly, those are noise compared to the electrical work.

So the honest summary for the bank is: 8.87 million yen final cost, 470,000 yen over the 8.4 million yen budget, primarily driven by the electrical panel upgrade, and the contingency was used appropriately even though it wasn't quite large enough to fully absorb the surprise.

8.87 million yen final — 470,000 yen over budget, with the electrical panel upgrade accounting for approximately 420,000 yen of that, and miscellaneous items making up the remaining 50,000 yen. Your 300,000 yen contingency absorbed most of the shock but not all of it, leaving a net 170,000 yen that came out of reserves or cash flow beyond the contingency. That's a very clean story.

For the bank, I'd frame it this way: the budget variance was driven by a single identifiable cause — an infrastructure discovery that is common in re-tenanted retail spaces and difficult to predict without a pre-project specialist audit — the contractor communicated it immediately and transparently, and the project team managed the downstream impacts to limit schedule damage to four days. That framing is accurate and also positions you well, because it demonstrates process discipline rather than cost mismanagement.

For your own lessons-learned, the clear takeaway on budget is to increase the contingency for the next project. On a renovation of this type, in a space with unknown prior electrical history, a 5% contingency is probably the minimum; 7-8% would be more appropriate. Your 300,000 yen contingency on an 8.4 million yen project was about 3.6%, which in retrospect was on the low side for a full commercial kitchen conversion.

Now let's move to the inspection. Walk me through what happened — when it was, who conducted it, and what the overall finding was before we get into the specific items.

The inspection was yesterday, August 27. The health inspector's name was Mr. Ogawa, and he came from the Minato Ward Health Department. He arrived at exactly 9:00 AM, which I thought was a good sign — someone who shows up on time for a 9 AM inspection is probably organized and methodical, and that's who you want doing this assessment.

The inspection itself ran about two hours and fifteen minutes. Mr. Ogawa went through everything systematically. He started in the front of house and worked his way back. He checked the ventilation hood and the fan system, confirmed that the CFM rating matched the equipment being used underneath it. He checked the refrigeration units — he actually had a calibrated thermometer with him and verified the walk-in temperature and the reach-in temperatures against the log sheets I had set up. He inspected the handwashing stations — the placement, the soap dispensers, the paper towel dispensers. He looked at the food storage setup, which for us right now is mostly dry goods since we haven't started stocking perishables yet. He went through the fire suppression system and confirmed the service tags were current. He checked the grease trap — the size, the installation, the maintenance access clearance. He looked at the waste handling setup, including the outdoor trash enclosure.

At the end, he said — and I'm paraphrasing here — that the space looked very well-prepared and that it was clear we had done our homework. He said he could tell the contractor knew what they were doing with commercial kitchen installations. He did not flag anything as a critical violation. He did not have any concerns that would hold up the permit process in a significant way. But he did note two minor items that we need to address before he will issue the final sign-off certificate. He made it very clear that these are minor compliance gaps, not safety issues, and that they're the kind of thing he sees on almost every new installation because operators focus on the big stuff and these specific requirements are easy to overlook.

That's an excellent outcome. Mr. Ogawa from the Minato Ward Health Department spending two hours and fifteen minutes going through every system methodically and coming out with zero critical violations on a new commercial kitchen installation is genuinely strong. The comment about the contractor's evident competence is also meaningful — that's not something inspectors say as a pleasantry; it reflects that the installation quality was visible.

The framing he gave you about the two minor items is also useful: these are compliance gaps that appear on almost every new installation, not failures of judgment or execution on your part. That tells you they're likely administrative or signage items rather than anything structural.

Before you tell me what the two items are, let me ask a framing question: when he said he needs to see them resolved before issuing the final sign-off, did he describe a specific process? Does he schedule a return visit to verify in person, or is there a documentation submission process? I want to understand the path to closure before we get into the content of the items.

He gave us a clear path. For minor items — and he was explicit that these qualify as minor — we don't need a second in-person visit. We can submit photo evidence to the Minato Ward Health Department office, and that's sufficient for them to issue the final sign-off. He gave us a deadline of September 5 to submit the photos. I've already built in a buffer; my plan is to submit by September 3 at the latest, which gives us a two-day cushion.

Now, the two items. The first one is handwashing signage. When Mr. Ogawa inspected the handwashing stations — and we have two of them in the kitchen, one near the prep area and one near the pass — he confirmed that the stations themselves were correctly set up. We have the right dispensers, the right towel holders, the temperature on the hot water side is within spec. But the Minato Ward regulation requires posted signage at every handwashing station instructing staff on the proper handwashing procedure and reminding them to wash before food handling. We didn't have those signs up. I'll be honest — I didn't know that was a specific regulatory requirement. I knew it was good practice, and I intended to put up general reminders of that kind, but I didn't know it was codified in the ward's health code in a way that the inspector would specifically check for. Mr. Ogawa showed me the specific regulation on his clipboard. It's a straightforward requirement. The fix is equally straightforward: we need to print the correct signs — there's a specific format the ward recommends — laminate them, and post them at both stations. I can have that done by this weekend.

The second item is the grease trap label. The grease trap itself passed the inspection on every substantive dimension: it's the right capacity for our kitchen volume, the installation is correct, the maintenance access clearance meets code. But there's a requirement that the grease trap must have a label affixed to it that specifies the cleaning schedule and identifies the responsible party — meaning the name of the person or company responsible for maintenance. We don't have that label on it. Again, this is not a problem with the grease trap; it's a documentation and labeling gap. The fix is to have a label made up and installed on the unit. I'm going to have Shimizu-san come back to do that rather than doing it myself, because I want to make sure the format is exactly what the Minato Ward Health Department expects — Shimizu-san has done enough commercial kitchen installations that he's familiar with what these labels need to say.

Both items are exactly the profile Mr. Ogawa described — administrative and labeling requirements that are easy to miss when you're focused on the structural and safety elements of a buildout. Let me confirm the specifics so they're clearly documented.

Item one: handwashing signage. The regulation requires posted instructional signage at every handwashing station — you have two stations in the kitchen. The stations themselves are fully compliant on equipment and water temperature; only the signage is missing. Fix: print the ward-recommended format, laminate, and post at both stations before this weekend.

Item two: grease trap label. The grease trap is compliant on capacity, installation, and access clearance. The missing element is a label affixed to the unit specifying the cleaning schedule and the responsible party. Fix: have Shimizu-san produce and install the correct label, in the format the Minato Ward Health Department expects.

Path to close: photo evidence of both items submitted to the Minato Ward Health Department by September 3 — two days before the September 5 deadline.

A few practical notes on the photo submissions. When you photograph the handwashing signage, get both a wide shot showing the context of the sign at the station and a close-up where the text of the sign is legible. Do the same for the grease trap label — wide shot showing where on the unit it's located, close-up showing the text including the cleaning schedule and responsible party name. If Mr. Ogawa or someone at the office reviewing the photos can clearly read what's on both, you eliminate the risk of a follow-up request for clarification. Keep originals of all the photos and a timestamped record of your submission — this becomes part of your compliance file for the space.

On Shimizu-san doing the grease trap label rather than you handling it yourself: that's a good call. He'll know the correct format because he's seen it approved on prior installations. The worst outcome here would be to produce a label that's close but not quite in the expected format and then have to redo it.

What's the timing on getting Shimizu-san back to the space? Is he available before the weekend?

I already texted him last night after I got home from the inspection. He said he can come Friday morning — that's August 29 — which is perfect. So the plan is: Shimizu-san handles the grease trap label on Friday. I handle the handwashing signage this week; I've already found a template on the Minato Ward website that has the approved format, so it's really just a matter of printing and laminating, which I can do at the konbini near the restaurant. By end of day Friday, both items should be resolved. I'll do the photography Friday afternoon once Shimizu-san is done, so I have everything in one session. And then I'll draft the cover note to submit with the photos over the weekend, and I'll send the whole package to the Minato Ward Health Department on Monday, September 1, or Tuesday, September 2 at the absolute latest.

That leaves September 1 as Marco's first day. I spoke to Marco yesterday evening — I called him right after the inspection because I wanted to update him. He knows that the health certificate isn't technically issued yet, but he also understands that it's two administrative items and that the certificate should come through within a few business days of our submission. His plan for the first week is exactly what I described to you earlier: he's going to use the kitchen for prep work, recipe testing, and mise en place setup. He's not planning to run any food service or cook for paying guests during that period. So there's no operational dependency on the final certificate being in hand on day one. We're aligned.

Actually, I want to ask you something about the lessons-learned piece, because I think this whole renovation has taught me a few things I want to make sure I'm capturing. What questions should I be asking myself right now while the experience is fresh?

That's a genuinely good instinct — capturing lessons while the experience is fresh is how a one-time renovation turns into institutional knowledge you can carry into the next project, whether that's a second location or a future renovation of this one.

Here are the questions I'd work through, grouped by area:

On pre-project due diligence:
The electrical panel upgrade was the single biggest surprise of this project. What would have caught it? A pre-contract electrical audit by a licensed electrician reviewing panel capacity against your planned equipment load. That audit probably costs 30,000 to 60,000 yen and either surfaces the upgrade need upfront — where it can be priced into the contract — or confirms the panel is adequate and eliminates that risk category. For any future commercial kitchen conversion, treat that audit as a prerequisite before signing. Similar logic applies to plumbing capacity and structural load if you're adding heavy equipment.

On contingency sizing:
You went into this project with a 300,000 yen contingency on an 8.4 million yen budget — about 3.6%. The project finished 470,000 yen over, meaning the contingency absorbed about 64% of the overage and you absorbed the rest. For a full commercial kitchen conversion in a re-tenanted space with unknown prior infrastructure history, 5 to 8% contingency would have been more appropriate. The lesson is not that you were reckless with the contingency; it's that the category of project you were undertaking carries higher inherent uncertainty than the number reflected.

On contractor communication:
Shimizu-san's behavior — calling within 24 hours, presenting options with costs before proceeding — should be your benchmark for any future contractor. When you're vetting a new contractor, ask them explicitly: what is your process when you discover a scope change? How quickly do you communicate it? The answer tells you a lot about how they operate.

On regulatory compliance research:
The two items from the health inspection — handwashing signage and the grease trap label — are both requirements that were in the Minato Ward health code all along. You found the handwashing signage template on the Minato Ward website, which means the information was publicly available. The lesson here is to schedule a pre-opening regulatory walkthrough with someone from the ward health department before the renovation is complete, not after. Many wards will do informal pre-inspections or at least answer a checklist of compliance questions if you call and ask. The cost is zero and the benefit is finding out about the grease trap label and the handwashing signage when you still have a contractor on site who can incorporate those requirements into the work, rather than after handover.

On timeline buffer:
You had a nine-day buffer between the August 22 projected completion and Marco's September 1 start. The four-day slip used up almost half of it. If the slip had been ten days, you would have had a real problem. For future projects, aim for three weeks between renovation handover and your first irrevocable staff or vendor commitment.

On documentation:
You're doing the right thing by debriefing while the experience is fresh. Make sure the full cost breakdown — the electrical panel upgrade decomposed into panel hardware, Tokyo Electric fees, and re-routing labor — lives in a document somewhere, not only in text threads with Shimizu-san. That detail is what the bank and future-you will need.

Is there anything from that list you want to dig into further? And is there anything else from the renovation that we haven't covered — something that surprised you, positive or negative, or anything still unresolved beyond the two inspection items?

Good afternoon. Today I want to go through the final menu with you — I spent most of yesterday with Marco, and we went section by section. I feel like we're genuinely close, but there are a few decisions I want to talk through before I call it done. Is now a good time to go deep on this?

Absolutely — and a week into Marco's tenure is exactly the right moment for this conversation. By now he's had time to get a feel for the kitchen, run through his prep workflow, and start forming opinions about what he can actually execute consistently rather than what looks good on paper. There's an important distinction between what a chef proposes during the hiring process, when everything is hypothetical and enthusiasm is high, and what he commits to once he's standing in the actual kitchen with the actual equipment and the actual team he's going to be working with. Menu finalization decisions made now will stick for at least the first quarter of service, so it's worth taking the time to get them right and to make sure every dish on that list has Marco's genuine conviction behind it. Walk me through where things stand section by section, and let's look at any points of tension or uncertainty as we go. What does the overall shape of the menu look like?

So the structure Marco and I landed on is: 6 antipasti, 5 primi — which breaks down as 3 pasta and 2 risotto — 4 secondi, and 3 desserts. That's the dinner menu. It's tighter than what we were sketching back in the spring, but Marco was pretty firm that he'd rather have fewer dishes executed perfectly than more dishes that spread him thin, especially while he's still building the team rhythm. I think he's right, but I wanted to get your read on whether that total count feels appropriate for the positioning.

Marco is right, and the instinct to constrain the menu while the kitchen team is still finding its rhythm is one of the marks of an experienced chef. The structure you've described — 6 antipasti, 5 primi with 3 pasta and 2 risotto, 4 secondi, and 3 desserts — gives you a total of eighteen dishes at dinner. That's a thoughtful number for a room of your size. It's enough to give a guest a genuine sense of choice without creating the kind of menu sprawl that leads to uneven execution and longer service times. For the Emilia-Romagna positioning in particular, a tighter menu is actually a stronger signal. It says you're curating rather than covering all bases, and it invites guests to trust Marco's judgment. The 3-pasta-plus-2-risotto split in the primi is worth examining in a bit more detail, because the pasta selection carries a lot of the regional identity weight. What are the three pasta dishes Marco has settled on, and how does he feel about the risotto choices relative to the overall concept?

The anchor of the pasta section — really the anchor of the whole menu — is tagliatelle al ragu bolognese. Marco was very clear that this is non-negotiable for him. He said if Osteria Morishita opens without it, he'd question whether it's actually an Emilia-Romagna restaurant. And I agree with him completely. The other two pastas are a tortellini in brodo using a Parmigiano Reggiano broth — a really delicate, classical preparation — and a garganelli with prosciutto di Parma and butter. The two risotti are a porcini risotto that Marco wants to keep consistent year-round, and a seasonal risotto that will rotate. Right now for September the seasonal one is a late-summer corn and saffron risotto. How does that read to you?

It reads very coherently and Marco's instinct about the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese is exactly right — that dish is the credibility anchor for the entire Emilia-Romagna identity. A guest who knows Italian regional cuisine will look for it immediately, and its presence signals that the kitchen isn't doing a superficial interpretation. What's more important is that it needs to be done with the discipline the dish demands: the ragu cooked low and slow, the pasta rolled and cut properly. I'll come back to the hand-cutting question in a moment because it matters to how you price and describe the dish. The tortellini in brodo with Parmigiano Reggiano broth is a beautiful choice — it's the kind of dish that's technically demanding and almost impossible to do well outside the region, so guests who know what they're eating will understand exactly what you're claiming. The garganelli with prosciutto di Parma and butter is perhaps the most approachable of the three, which is useful for guests who are exploring the region for the first time. The porcini risotto as a year-round constant is smart — porcini is one of the flavors that reads as 'serious Italian kitchen' to most guests regardless of their depth of knowledge, and having a fixed risotto gives regular guests something to return to. The seasonal rotation on the second risotto is the right call; the late-summer corn and saffron is unusual enough to be interesting without being alienating. How is Marco planning to handle the pasta itself — is he making everything in-house?

Yes, everything fresh and in-house. And specifically for the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese, Marco insists on hand-cut pasta. He made a batch for me yesterday and I understood immediately why it matters — the texture is completely different. The thickness is slightly irregular in a way that machine-cut pasta can never replicate, and it catches the sauce differently. He said he's not willing to compromise on that even as volume grows. So hand-cut is going into the menu description for that dish. My question now is pricing. What should tagliatelle al ragu bolognese be listed at?

Hand-cut pasta is an important differentiator and absolutely worth calling out in the menu description — it signals craft and gives guests who know Italian food a reason to understand the price point. Let's work through the pricing logic carefully. You're targeting a dinner average ticket that has come down somewhat from your original projections — I want to revisit that number shortly — and the primi section needs to sit at a price that makes sense both individually and in the context of how guests will build their meal. For the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese specifically, you're offering a dish that requires significant time investment — a proper Bolognese ragu cannot be rushed, and the hand-cut pasta adds meaningful skilled labor on top of that. The Parmigiano Reggiano and quality beef and pork involved are not cheap ingredients either. At similarly positioned osterie in Italy that have gone through some internationalization, a proper tagliatelle al ragu bolognese runs in a range that, converted to yen, would easily support pricing above 2,000 yen. In your competitive set in Tokyo, serious pasta dishes at destination-tier trattorias in the 7,000 to 9,000 yen dinner ticket range typically price individual pasta courses between 1,800 and 2,800 yen. My recommendation for the tagliatelle would be 2,400 yen. That price positions it as a premium dish with clear craft justification, it sits comfortably within what guests at your price point will accept, and it leaves room for the other two pastas — the garganelli being slightly less labor-intensive — to be priced a notch lower if you want to create some natural spread across the menu. Does 2,400 yen feel right to you, and what has Marco been thinking about the other pasta prices?

2,400 yen for the tagliatelle feels exactly right. Marco had actually suggested the same number independently when I asked him what he thought it was worth, which was reassuring — it means neither of us is inflating or deflating based on what we think the other wants to hear. The garganelli he pegged at 2,000 yen and the tortellini in brodo at 2,200 yen — the broth is labor-intensive even if the pasta shape is simpler, and he feels the delicacy of that preparation warrants the slight premium over the garganelli. I'm comfortable with all three of those. Now I want to get into something that came up with Marco and that I genuinely wasn't expecting — the pizza question.

Go ahead — this is worth spending real time on, because the pizza decision touches positioning, kitchen operations, and guest expectations simultaneously. I'll admit I half expected this to come up sooner; it's one of those questions that gets asked of almost every Italian restaurant in Japan. The assumption from guests, and even from some investors, is that if there's a wood-burning oven and an Italian flag above the door, pizza must be involved. Whether or not that assumption is correct is a separate question from whether you should submit to it. Tell me what Marco said, and let's work through both the logic and any pushback you're anticipating.

So when Marco and I were doing the kitchen walk-through on his first day, he looked at the wood-burning oven and immediately said he didn't want to do pizza. His reasoning was layered. First, he said Emilia-Romagna is not a pizza region — adding pizza would confuse the regional story. Second, he said the oven in our kitchen was spec'd for focaccia and roasted dishes, not for the extremely high sustained temperatures that proper Neapolitan or Roman pizza really requires, and trying to force it would mean mediocre pizza which is worse than no pizza. His plan is that pizza is not on the menu, and the oven gets used for focaccia and roasted secondi only. He was very decisive about it. My instinct was to agree with him, but I was second-guessing myself because I know Japanese guests often associate Italian restaurants with pizza. What's your read?

Marco's reasoning is sound on every count and I think your instinct to agree with him is the right one. Let me walk through why. The regional coherence argument is the strongest: Emilia-Romagna's culinary identity is built on pasta, cured meats, aged cheeses, and long-cooked meat preparations. Pizza is a southern Italian tradition — Campania, Lazio at the margins — and putting it on an Emilia-Romagna menu is a little like a restaurant claiming to serve traditional Kyoto cuisine and also serving Osaka takoyaki. It undercuts the credibility of everything else on the menu. Guests who don't know Italian food deeply won't notice the absence; guests who do know it will actively respect the restraint. On the technical argument, Marco is being precise and professional. A wood-burning oven that's been configured for focaccia and roasted secondi will operate at a different temperature range and with a different firing rhythm than a pizza oven that needs to sustain temperatures above 400 degrees Celsius for rapid baking. Trying to produce pizza in that environment would likely mean inconsistent results, which is a reputational risk that isn't worth taking. The fact that the oven will be actively used — for focaccia and roasted secondi only — means you're not leaving the equipment idle. You're just using it for the right things. On the Japanese market concern: your target guest is not primarily someone who comes to Osteria Morishita for pizza. You've spent months establishing that you're building a destination restaurant for guests who want depth and regional specificity. Those guests will understand why there's no pizza. In fact, some of them will see it as a mark of seriousness. The guests who come specifically for pizza were never going to be your core customer anyway. Trust Marco on this one.

That's basically the confirmation I needed. I'll hold the line on it and if guests ask, the front-of-house team can explain it clearly — it's actually a story that's easy to tell and that builds the brand. Marco even said he'd be happy to come out to the dining room occasionally on slower nights to talk about the focaccia directly, which I thought was a nice touch. The focaccia is going to be the oven's visible contribution to the first impression — it'll come to the table early — so it needs to be excellent. Marco has been working on a version with olive oil from Liguria and a slow, overnight proof. It's already noticeably better than anything I've had at comparable price points in Tokyo. That's the kind of thing that makes the no-pizza story feel credible rather than like an omission. Now I want to move to lunch, because that's where I'm still a little unsure. The current plan is a set menu format at two price tiers. The lower tier is 1,800 yen for a 2-course lunch, and the upper tier is 2,400 yen for a 3-course lunch. That's meaningfully more accessible than dinner. Does that pricing hold up?

Let's examine both numbers carefully. The 1,800 yen 2-course lunch and the 2,400 yen 3-course lunch are your entry points for guests who may not yet be ready to commit to a full dinner experience, and they serve a real purpose: they let people experience the kitchen's capability at a lower-stakes moment and build the regular customer relationships that underpin a healthy lunch service. At 1,800 yen for a 2-course lunch, you're pricing at the lower edge of what I would normally recommend for a restaurant of this positioning. Tokyo's serious Italian restaurants in the mid-to-upper trattoria tier often run lunch sets in the 2,500 to 4,000 yen range. So 1,800 yen is aggressive. However, there's a strategic case for it: Higashi-Azabu has a working population — offices, embassies, professionals — who are a natural lunch constituency and who respond to accessible entry points. If 1,800 yen brings in those guests regularly, and some of them convert to dinner guests over time, it functions as a customer acquisition price rather than a profit-maximizing price. The key question is whether the kitchen can produce something that genuinely represents the restaurant's quality at that price point without creating a perception mismatch. What's included in each tier? If the 2-course is antipasto plus primo, and the 3-course adds a dessert, the structure makes sense and the 600 yen step-up is a natural upsell. The constraint to watch is food cost at those price points — the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese at 2,400 yen à la carte needs to be manageable within a lunch set at 2,400 yen for three courses. Have you and Marco worked through what the lunch menu specifically includes, and whether the food cost math holds at these prices?

Marco's plan for lunch is to offer a simplified version of the dinner menu — not all 6 antipasti or all 5 primi, but a curated selection. Probably two or three antipasti choices and three or four primi choices. The 2-course is antipasto plus primo and the 3-course adds a dessert from a shorter list — probably just two options at lunch rather than the full 3 desserts. On the food cost math, Marco has been pretty rigorous. He's done the costing on a few key dishes and he's confident we can produce a respectable lunch at those price points by controlling portion sizing at lunch versus dinner, and also by using the lunch service as a way to work through some prep product from dinner quantities. He mentioned that having the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese available at lunch within the set format is actually useful — it lets the ragu continue cooking while service is happening and the batch size works more efficiently over the full day. Honestly I think the bigger risk is volume — if we're not hitting thirty to forty covers at lunch it becomes hard to justify the mise en place effort. But that's a marketing problem more than a menu problem.

Marco's approach to the lunch menu is operationally smart — a curated subset rather than a parallel full menu reduces his prep burden and lets the kitchen focus on consistency. The portion sizing discipline at lunch is also standard and defensible; guests who come for the 1,800 yen 2-course lunch are generally not expecting dinner-scale portions, and framing it as a focused midday experience is perfectly coherent. Using lunch to work through prep product from dinner quantities is efficient and practiced by serious kitchens everywhere; just make sure there's a clear internal protocol so that product going into lunch sets is always at the right stage and nothing that's past its window ends up in service. You're right that the volume question is more marketing than menu. Thirty to forty covers is a realistic target for a 25-seat room running close to two turns at lunch — very achievable if the lunch proposition gets in front of the right audiences. The Higashi-Azabu professional base is your near-term lunch core, supplemented by word-of-mouth from people who discover you through dinner. The embassy cluster in the neighborhood is also worth thinking about — diplomatic staff often eat locally at lunch, they tend to have educated palates, and they're exactly the kind of early adopters who generate influential word-of-mouth. The 1,800 yen and 2,400 yen price points are accessible enough that guests shouldn't need much convincing. One thing I want to flag: the 2,400 yen price point appears at both lunch — as the 3-course set — and at dinner as the price for the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese individually. That's not a problem structurally, but you should think about whether the front-of-house team has clear language to describe what 2,400 yen means in each context, so guests don't experience confusion when they see the number in different places. The mental model for guests should be: lunch at 2,400 yen is a three-course set experience; dinner at 2,400 yen is a single landmark pasta dish from a chef who treats it as the restaurant's defining statement. Those are genuinely different propositions that happen to share a price.

That's a good catch. I'll make sure the menu design and the front-of-house briefing materials make it visually and contextually clear. Now the last thing I want to talk through is the dinner ticket projection. When we were working on this earlier in the year, I was thinking about a higher number. Marco and I have been revisiting the assumptions and we've come down to 7,800 yen per person as the projected average dinner ticket. That's a revision downward from where I was before. I want to make sure I'm not underpricing the positioning, but I also want to be honest with myself about what the market will support.

The 7,800 yen per person dinner average ticket projection, revised down from your earlier thinking, deserves careful scrutiny because it has direct implications for your unit economics. Let me work through what this means in practice before commenting on whether it's the right number. At 7,800 yen per person on food alone, with a drinks multiple of roughly 0.5 — which is conservative but reasonable for a new restaurant still building its wine-buying customer base — your total per-cover average including drinks is around 11,700 yen. For a 25-seat room doing two turns on a strong night, that's roughly 585,000 yen in total revenue on a full evening. On a realistic occupancy assumption — say, 75 to 80 percent average across a week, which is a strong but achievable target — you're looking at weekly dinner revenue in the range of three to four million yen once you're properly established. Whether that's sufficient depends heavily on your rent, your staff headcount, and Marco's compensation structure, which I don't have full visibility into. But it's a workable number for Higashi-Azabu if your lease terms are in a reasonable range. On the question of whether 7,800 yen underprices the positioning: I don't think so. This brings you back to the 'serious trattoria' tier we discussed before — above the neighborhood reliable options, accessible enough not to trigger Michelin-bracket comparisons. Given that you're opening a new restaurant with a new team and a chef who is excellent but unknown to Tokyo, starting at a price point that guests feel comfortable with and that leaves room to revise upward as reputation builds is strategically sound. The risk of opening with an overambitious dinner ticket and finding occupancy disappoints is greater than the risk of leaving some margin on the table in the first year. One note: the revision should be documented as intentional and grounded, not as a retreat from ambition. When you talk to anyone — investors, suppliers, press — frame the 7,800 yen per person as the considered price for the positioning, not as a scaled-back number.

That framing makes sense and I'll hold onto it. Marco has been consistent about the number too — he arrived at 7,800 yen per person without me prompting him, which suggests we're reading the room similarly. I think the combination of everything we've settled today — the menu structure, the signature tagliatelle, no pizza and the clear reasoning behind it, the lunch price tiers, and the 7,800 yen dinner ticket — feels like a coherent picture. One last question: is there anything in today's conversation that you think still has unresolved risk that I haven't asked about?

Yes, a few things worth naming before you close this out. First, the 3 desserts count. You've been clear that dinner offers 3 desserts and lunch trims to two, but we haven't looked at what those desserts are. Dessert is the final impression of the meal and at the osteria level the risk is underinvestment — a tiramisu and a panna cotta that any restaurant in Tokyo offers, rather than something that reinforces the Emilia-Romagna identity. I'd push Marco on whether at least one of the three desserts has a clear regional anchor. Zuppa inglese, a proper torta di riso, or a zabaglione-based preparation would all do that work. The dessert section is also where wine pairings begin to matter — a passito or a Vin Santo suggestion printed alongside the dessert is a small revenue driver and a large signal of hospitality intelligence. Second, the 4 secondi. You mentioned the count but we didn't discuss what those dishes are. With pizza ruled out and the oven reserved for focaccia and roasted secondi only, the secondi section carries real weight in showing that the kitchen has range beyond pasta. I'd want to make sure there's at least one piece of roasted or braised meat that showcases what that oven can do — a roasted pork dish or a slow-cooked lamb would make the oven's role feel purposeful rather than incidental. A cotechino or bollito preparation would also read as deeply Emilian and is the kind of dish that serious guests will talk about. Third, the wine list, which we haven't touched at all in this conversation. For an Emilia-Romagna focused restaurant, the question of how much of the list is Emilian and how much casts a broader regional net is worth a dedicated conversation. Lambrusco in particular is a wine you need handled carefully — it's the most iconic Emilian wine and it can read as cheap if positioned carelessly, or as a genuine regional discovery if positioned well. These aren't blockers to finalizing the menu, but they're the conversations I'd want to have in the next two or three weeks before opening. The menu architecture and pricing structure you've built with Marco today is solid. These are the refinements that will take it from solid to memorable.

Good morning. I want to walk you through where we stand on the staffing side, because a lot has moved in the last week or two. The menu is locked — Marco and I signed off on the final version three days ago, and we had a small dinner at his apartment to mark the occasion, which felt like the right way to close that chapter — so the pressure has fully shifted now to making sure we have the right people in place before we open. I've been doing interviews and reference checks pretty intensively over the past few weeks, sometimes two or three per day, and I think we're close to a complete picture for the launch team. I've also had Tanabe-san review the salary figures against what he's seeing in the broader Tokyo independent restaurant market, which has been useful as a sanity check. Let me go through the hires one by one, starting with the kitchen, because that's where I wanted to be most deliberate and where I felt the stakes were highest.

Good morning, Kenta. It's genuinely good to hear the menu is finalized — that's a significant weight off, and it means every conversation about staffing can now be tied to concrete roles and specific responsibilities rather than moving targets. The menu being locked also means that whoever you bring into the kitchen knows exactly what they're being asked to execute from day one, which I think is an underappreciated advantage during an opening period. Please go ahead and walk me through the kitchen first. I'll take notes as you go and I'll probably have questions about how each person fits into the overall team structure once you've given me the full picture, particularly around how responsibilities will be distributed during the nights when the full team isn't present. What does the kitchen lineup look like?

So the most important hire on the kitchen side is the sous chef. Marco and I talked for a long time about the profile we needed — someone who could run the line on the nights Marco isn't physically in the kitchen, someone who genuinely understands northern Italian technique rather than just being a competent general cook who can follow a recipe sheet. We interviewed five candidates over about three weeks. The person we landed on is Haruki Nakajima. He is 29 years old, which I know sounds young for a sous chef role at an opening like this, but when you sit across from him and talk about food for an hour and then watch him work, the age stops mattering very quickly. He came to us from Trattoria Goccia — that's a serious Italian kitchen in Shibuya that's been putting out consistent work for about eight years. He was there for four years, the last two of which he spent as a junior sous chef. Before Goccia he did a stage in Bologna for six months, which is actually part of why Marco responded to him so strongly. They share a reference point for the way Emilian kitchens think about pasta. His knife work is exceptional, his sauces are clean without being overcomplicated, and honestly, his mise en place discipline is the kind of thing that will set the tone for everyone else in that kitchen.

Haruki Nakajima sounds like a genuinely strong fit given what Marco is trying to build. The Trattoria Goccia background is meaningful — Shibuya Italian kitchens that have sustained eight years are usually running a disciplined operation, so if he came up through that environment as a junior sous chef, he's not just someone who can cook, he's someone who has learned how to maintain standards under volume and pressure. The Bologna stage is also a real differentiator. Shared culinary vocabulary between a head chef and sous chef matters enormously, especially in the early months when you're still establishing rhythms. What's the compensation structure you've worked out with him? And I'm curious about the conversation around what his actual scope of authority will be on the nights Marco steps back.

On compensation, we agreed to 380,000 yen monthly salary. I'll be honest — he was probably worth asking for more, and I think he knows that. But he was also transparent with me that he wanted the opening experience specifically, and that he's thinking of this as a two-to-three-year chapter where he builds something from the ground floor rather than inheriting an established kitchen. So the number reflects a mutual understanding that the opportunity itself is part of the package. Tanabe-san reviewed the figure against market data and said it's within the reasonable range for his experience level in Tokyo, leaning toward the lower end, which is why I want to make sure we revisit this at the six-month mark if things are going well. On the scope question — Marco was actually very deliberate about this in our conversations with Haruki. On the three nights a week when Marco won't be in service, Haruki has full authority on the pass. He can call changes to plating if the product coming out of the kitchen isn't meeting the standard. He can manage kitchen staff scheduling in real time. He cannot change menu items or pricing without Marco's sign-off, which is documented in the job description. I think that's a healthy boundary for an opening period.

The 380,000 yen structure makes sense in the context you're describing. An opening sous chef role at a serious independent concept in Higashi-Azabu isn't an anonymous line position — he's getting equity in the story of the place, a restaurant name on his CV that can mean a great deal if Osteria Morishita builds the reputation Marco is aiming for. I think the framing you've both landed on, where the opportunity is part of the compensation package, is honest and sustainable as long as the six-month review is treated as a genuine commitment and not a placeholder. To that point: I'd recommend including the review date explicitly in the employment contract rather than leaving it as a verbal understanding between you. Goodwill is high at the offer stage, but written terms protect both parties when circumstances get complicated later. The scope delineation also sounds well thought through. Full pass authority is real authority — it means he owns the quality of what goes out the door on those nights, and kitchen staff will read very quickly whether he has genuine standing or is just nominally in charge — but anchoring menu changes to Marco protects the concept's identity during the period when the kitchen culture is still forming. How does Haruki feel about reporting to Marco given that Marco is Italian and they'll be navigating some degree of cross-cultural working dynamic? Did that topic come up during the interview process?

It came up, and I appreciated that Haruki raised it himself rather than us having to bring it into the room. He said — and I'm roughly paraphrasing — that he's spent enough time around Italian kitchen culture both in Japan and in Bologna that he's not walking in with illusions about how direct Marco can be when something isn't right. He actually said that's part of what he's looking for, because he's been in Japanese kitchens where nobody says anything negative until it's too late to fix it, and he finds that more exhausting than a chef who just tells you exactly what's wrong in the moment. Marco met him twice before we made the offer, and the second meeting went significantly longer than I expected. I had to text Marco afterward to ask if everything was okay, and he said they'd spent forty minutes talking about a specific preparation of a ragù from a trattoria in Modena they'd both eaten at different times, completely by coincidence. So I think the dynamic is going to be fine. Now, do you want me to move to the front of house, or do you have more questions on the kitchen side?

That story about the Modena ragù is actually a good sign — shared culinary obsession is one of those things you can't manufacture in an interview process, and when it surfaces spontaneously it usually means the working relationship will have genuine depth rather than just professional courtesy. The fact that they found a common reference point independently, at different times and without coordinating in advance, suggests their culinary instincts are genuinely aligned at a fairly specific level, not just in broad direction. That kind of alignment tends to make conflict resolution easier because there's a shared aesthetic standard to return to when disagreements arise. I'm satisfied with the kitchen picture for now — I have a clear sense of Haruki as a hire and how he fits relative to Marco. Please go ahead and walk me through the front of house. I know service tone is going to be one of the most defining characteristics of how Osteria Morishita is experienced by guests, and it's also the area where an independent opening can most easily get the culture wrong in ways that are slow to correct. I'm curious about how you've thought through that hire.

The front of house conversation has actually been one of the most interesting parts of this whole process for me, because it forced me to be very precise about what kind of service experience I want guests to have. This isn't a white-tablecloth formal dining room, but it's also not a neighborhood trattoria where the waiter shouts the specials from across the room. I kept coming back to the word 'ease' when I was thinking about it — I want guests to feel completely at ease, never made to feel like they're performing, never made to feel like they're missing a code. That's actually much harder to train for than technical service skills, so I was looking for someone senior enough to build and hold that culture rather than just execute individual service moments well. The person I've brought in as service manager is Eiko Sawada. She is 41 years old, and she has one of the most interesting service backgrounds I've encountered in the Tokyo restaurant space. She spent seven years managing the dining room at a Michelin two-star kaiseki restaurant in Kyoto before she moved back to Tokyo four years ago. Since then she's worked at two western-concept fine dining restaurants in Minato-ku. She's never been in an Italian kitchen specifically, but when I talked to her about the service philosophy I was describing — that idea of 'ease' — she immediately gave it back to me in more precise language than I had. She called it 'invisible competence,' which is exactly what I meant. You only notice the service when something goes wrong. When it's working, you just feel comfortable. I thought that was exactly right.

Eiko Sawada is a compelling hire, and the kaiseki background is not an obvious choice for an Italian concept — but I think you're right that it may actually be an advantage. Kaiseki service at a Michelin two-star level requires a form of spatial awareness and guest-reading that is genuinely transferable, and it's a discipline where 'invisible competence' isn't just a philosophy, it's a survival requirement. Guests who have spent serious money on a kaiseki meal have a very well-tuned sense for when service attention is slightly off, and a dining room manager who has thrived in that environment for seven years has had her instincts calibrated by some of the most demanding guests in Japan. The Minato-ku western fine dining experience also means she's not walking into a foreign register — she's already made that transition once. What is her compensation, and how do you plan to structure her relationship with the part-time floor staff? I imagine the onboarding challenge is partly about translating her very high service standards into a team that may have significantly less experience.

Her salary is 460,000 yen per month. She pushed back a little on the initial number I offered, which was 440,000 yen, and I think she was right to. Her Minato-ku references were excellent, and when I spoke to her most recent employer — I asked for permission first and she gave it without any hesitation, which itself told me something — they were genuinely enthusiastic about her. One of them said, and I'm quoting more or less exactly, 'the dining room ran better on the nights Sawada-san was managing than on the nights I was there myself.' That kind of feedback is not something I was willing to walk away from over 20,000 yen a month. On the floor staff question — this is something Eiko and I spent about an hour discussing in our second meeting, and I was impressed by how clearly she had thought it through already, even before she knew for certain she had the position. She wants to run a proper pre-service briefing every single shift, not just on the busy nights. She said the mistake a lot of independent restaurants make is treating pre-service as optional when it's quiet, and then the team doesn't have the habit built in when it actually matters. She's also proposed something she called a 'shadow system' for the first month of service, where the more experienced full-time staff are paired with the part-time staff on every shift, not just to supervise, but to demonstrate by example. I like that approach. It's not punitive, it's mentorship-structured. Now let me tell you about the part-time staff, because I think those choices are also interesting.

The 460,000 yen figure is justified, and the way you got there — through a reference call that turned into a genuine endorsement rather than a pro forma confirmation — is exactly the kind of diligence that protects an opening. The pre-service briefing discipline Eiko is proposing is also a meaningful indicator of how she thinks about service culture. A team that briefs every night, regardless of cover count, is a team that treats service as a craft rather than a task. The shadow system for the first month is smart structurally because it embeds the standard into muscle memory before pressure arrives, not during it. Who are the part-time staff, and how did you find them?

We have two part-time servers joining us for the opening. The first is Yui Tachibana, who is a university student — she's in her third year studying hospitality management at Rikkyo. She came to us through a recommendation from the program coordinator at Rikkyo, who apparently has an informal relationship with a few independent restaurants in the area and reaches out when she has students looking for serious placements rather than just casual part-time work. What made Yui stand out in the interview was that she came prepared. She had looked at our location, thought about the concept, and had a set of genuine questions rather than just answering mine. She's also studying Italian on her own, which I found charming and also potentially useful as the language of the menu and the wine list is something guests sometimes have questions about. She can commit to three evenings a week plus weekend lunch service, which is very workable. The second part-time hire is Naoki Hirose. Naoki is different from Yui in that he's not a student — he has a full-time job in a completely unrelated field, IT project management, and he does restaurant service specifically because he loves it. He's been doing part-time floor work at various Shibuya restaurants for about six years, so his technical service skills are significantly stronger than most part-timers I would expect at his availability level. He can do two evenings a week reliably. I was a little uncertain initially about whether someone with a full-time day job would have the mental energy to bring to the floor after a full day of work, but his references from previous restaurants were uniformly strong, and one of the managers I spoke to said he was the most focused part-time staff member they'd had in years. So I decided that track record matters more than the theoretical concern.

Yui Tachibana and Naoki Hirose are well-matched choices for very different reasons, and the fact that they fill different scheduling windows is a practical advantage for the rota. Yui brings energy, genuine curiosity, and three evenings plus weekend lunch, which is significant coverage for someone still in university. The self-study Italian is a minor detail that could end up being a real service moment — a guest who is surprised that a server can explain a wine name or a preparation term in the original language tends to remember that interaction. Naoki's six years of accumulated floor experience across multiple Shibuya restaurants essentially means Eiko doesn't have to start his training from zero, which reduces the load on the shadow system she's designing. The concern about dual-role fatigue is real, but your instinct to weight the actual track record over the theoretical risk is correct — if his previous managers say focus is consistent, that's a pattern, not luck. So let me make sure I have the full roster clear in my head. Can you give me the complete opening staff count, full-time and part-time combined, so I can see the whole team at once?

Yes — so as of right now, the total opening team is 5 full-time, 2 part-time. Full-time is Marco Petrelli as head chef, Haruki Nakajima as sous chef, Eiko Sawada as service manager, and then two additional full-time kitchen staff who I haven't gone into detail on today but who are essentially confirmed — one is a pasta specialist who worked under Marco's recommendation from a contact he brought from his network, and the other is a commis chef who's just finished culinary school but who Marco auditioned in a working session and was impressed enough with that he flagged her as someone worth bringing in from day one rather than waiting to see how she develops. Part-time is Yui Tachibana and Naoki Hirose, as I described. So yes — 5 full-time, 2 part-time. Seven people total going into opening. I feel genuinely good about this group. There's range here — Eiko's experience depth at the top, Yui's freshness and curiosity at the other end, and everyone in between chosen with some real deliberateness. I just want to make sure the onboarding period holds it all together before service starts.

That's a well-structured team for a 64.5 square meter space — you have genuine depth in the leadership tier with Marco, Haruki, and Eiko, and you've made thoughtful choices at every level below that. Seven people with this combination of backgrounds, if the onboarding period is handled well, should be able to establish a service identity before you open rather than discovering it piece by piece through early guest feedback. What I find particularly coherent about this roster is that the range is intentional. You've described every hire in terms of what specific function they fill and why their background suits it, rather than assembling a group of generically capable people and hoping they find their own level. That intentionality tends to translate directly into team cohesion during the high-stress pre-opening period. On that subject: what does the onboarding timeline look like? Do you have a confirmed start date for the full team to come together, and do you have a sense of how many days of internal rehearsal service you want before the first actual guests are in the room? I ask because with a team that spans from Michelin two-star dining room management to third-year university student, the calibration work during those rehearsal sessions will carry a disproportionate amount of the load that formal training documentation alone can't fully accomplish.

The plan right now is to have everyone confirmed and contracts signed by the end of September, which I think is achievable. October is the full onboarding month. I'm targeting a soft opening — invited guests only, no public bookings — in the first week of November. The thinking is that the full team comes together in the kitchen and dining room starting October sixth, and we run internal rehearsals through roughly mid-October. That gives us about ten days of proper rehearsal service with real food and real plating before we move into the soft opening phase. I've also asked Eiko to design a service briefing document — something that captures the philosophy in writing rather than just in verbal instruction — so that as we bring in future part-time staff beyond Yui and Naoki, the foundational tone is documented and doesn't depend entirely on Eiko being in the room. Marco is doing something similar on the kitchen side, which I believe is partly for his own clarity and partly because Haruki asked for it. Haruki apparently told Marco that he works better when the chef's standards are written down rather than implied, which I thought was an admirable piece of self-knowledge for someone his age.
