That protects you from the worst-case scenario of staffing a full late service for one table. You can always move to walk-in availability once you've validated the demand. The core decision — cut Monday lunch, add late seating Friday/Saturday — is the right structural move. It addresses the cost side and the revenue side simultaneously, which is the most efficient kind of change when you're working with a 312,000 yen monthly loss and 14 months of cash runway. One final recommendation: set yourself a review trigger point. If you're still running losses above 200,000 yen per month by the end of February or early March, revisit the full schedule and staffing model at that point rather than waiting until the runway has dropped below six months. You want to course-correct while you still have time and meaningful options available.

The staff fatigue point is the one I was least focused on, and you're right to raise it. My kitchen team has been running hard. I hadn't fully thought through what adding a 9:30 PM seating on both Friday and Saturday does to them cumulatively over a month. I need to have a real conversation with my chef before I announce anything externally. The reservations-only launch is also the right call — I don't know why I wasn't already planning that, but I wasn't. I was thinking of it as an open second seating, which is clearly wrong. Alright. I think I have a clear picture. November revenue shortfall was real, the cost structure is manageable if I can close the revenue gap, the 312,000 yen monthly loss is the number I have to work against, and I have 14 months to fix it — but only if I start moving now. The two-part schedule change is the first structural move. I'll talk to my chef tomorrow and get staff input before I finalize the timeline for implementing the late seating. Thank you for working through this with me.

That's the right sequence. The chef conversation has to come before the external announcement, both because your chef's input may genuinely affect how you structure the late seating menu and timing, and because asking for input rather than announcing a decision is how you protect the relationship that matters most to running those Friday and Saturday nights well. Let me summarize what you've decided and what comes next, so you have a clean picture. The November result: revenue of 3.42 million yen against a 4.0M target, cost breakdown of food 31%, labor 38%, rent+utilities 18%, other 9%, operating loss of 312,000 yen for the month. Cash runway at current burn is 14 months. The structural decisions: cut Monday lunch to recover approximately 40,000 to 50,000 yen per month net, and add late seating Friday/Saturday to build incremental revenue on your strongest service periods. Immediate next steps: chef conversation tomorrow on the late seating feasibility and menu structure, then a communication plan for regular Monday lunch guests. You're making decisions with the right information and you're moving at the right pace. Come back once you've talked to your chef and I can help you work through the implementation details.

Okay. I've been deep in research mode for the past three days. Publishers Marketplace, MSWL, agent interviews, podcast appearances, acknowledgment pages in comparable books. I think I've looked at 40 literary agents who rep literary fiction with recent deal activity.

Three days of that kind of research is serious work. Before we dig in—when you say 40 literary agents, were you tracking them in a spreadsheet? Because that's a lot of information to hold in your head, and how you organize it matters as much as how many names you found.

Yes, full spreadsheet. Columns for agency, submission preferences, recent deals, MSWL keywords, comp titles they mentioned, interview notes. I went through all of them and narrowed to 15 for the first batch—the ones whose recent deal history and stated wishlist made Salt and Compass feel like the closest match.
Narrowing from 40 to 15 is good instinct. A first batch of 15 gives you enough data to read the market without burning through your entire list at once. Who are you leading with?

I want to walk you through the top five first, because these are the ones I feel most confident about. Starting with Renata Goldfarb of Goldfarb Literary. She specifically said in a 2024 MSWL entry that she wants literary fiction exploring diaspora and memory, and Salt and Compass does exactly that. I also found two debut author deals she closed in the past 18 months that felt genuinely comparable—one was a multigenerational family story set between Japan and California, the other was a debut about identity displacement in immigrant families.

That's a strong match on paper. But I want to push you a little—do you know anything about what Renata Goldfarb is like as an editorial agent? Because 'they accept literary fiction' and 'they have debut author deals' gets you in the door, but it doesn't tell you whether her editorial sensibility is right for your book. Did any of her interviews touch on how she works with authors during revision, or what she tends to prioritize in a manuscript?

Actually yes—I found a podcast interview from early 2025 where she talked about preferring to do one big editorial pass before submission rather than multiple rounds. She described herself as someone who wants the author to have a clear sense of their own vision before she weighs in. That felt right to me. I hate revision by committee.

Good. That's the kind of detail that should go in your query personalization—not just 'I read your MSWL,' but something that shows you've thought about whether her working style fits yours. Who's next on your list?

Anders Krishnamurthy of Vox & Vine Agency. He's newer—only been agenting independently for about four years—but Vox & Vine has a strong reputation for literary fiction and his personal list is already impressive. He's closed deals with debut authors in the past 18 months, and one of them, a debut novel about second-generation Korean American identity, won a regional award last fall. His MSWL says he's actively looking for literary fiction with structural experimentation.

The structural experimentation note is interesting—does Salt and Compass do anything formally distinctive? Because if it does, that's something you'd want to foreground in the query to him specifically. If the book is relatively linear, you'd want to be careful not to over-promise on that front.

The structure alternates between two timelines—1970s Osaka and present-day San Francisco—and there are sections written as letters and logbook entries. So yes, I think it qualifies. I was planning to mention that specifically.

That's exactly right for his query. The dual timeline plus the epistolary elements give you something concrete to point to. Don't describe it vaguely as 'experimental'—name the actual formal choices. That's what an agent who says they want structural experimentation actually wants to see. Keep going.

Third is Sloane Whitford-Jeong of Pinewood Literary. She's been on my radar for a while—Pinewood has a really strong track record with debut authors and she's been there for seven years. Her recent deals include a debut literary fiction title that went to auction last spring. She specifically mentioned in a written interview that she's looking for literary fiction that doesn't explain itself—books that trust the reader. That phrase stuck with me.

That phrase should be in your notes about Salt and Compass, not just about her. Does your book trust the reader? Where does it resist the urge to over-explain? Because if you can answer that honestly, you can gesture toward it in the query—and if you can't answer it, that's a revision signal worth sitting with before you send anything.

I think it does. There are things in the book I deliberately left unresolved—the question of whether Maya's grandmother chose to leave or was forced to, the nature of one relationship in the 1970s timeline. I never answer them directly. I was worried that was a flaw, actually.

It's not a flaw. For an agent like Sloane Whitford-Jeong who explicitly says she wants books that trust the reader, that kind of deliberate irresolution is a feature, not a bug. I'd mention it in your query to her—not as 'the ending is ambiguous' but as something like 'the novel holds certain questions open, confident the reader can carry them.' Who are the last two?

Hattie Macreadie of Macreadie & Daughters. Family agency, been around a long time, but Hattie specifically handles literary fiction and has been very vocal on MSWL about wanting debut authors. She's had multiple debut author deals in the last 18 months and she's mentioned in interviews that she likes to champion books for a long time—she talked about still working to get translation rights sold for a debut she placed three years ago. That longevity feels important to me.

The longevity point is significant and you're right to flag it. An agent who talks about translation rights years after initial placement is telling you something about how she thinks about a book's life—not just the initial deal, but the whole career arc. That's a meaningful differentiator from agents who are focused purely on getting the deal done. How do you plan to personalize for her?

I was thinking about mentioning that I'm writing with a long horizon in mind—that this isn't just a standalone novel for me but hopefully the start of a longer relationship with an agent who thinks the same way. Is that too presumptuous to put in a query letter?

It's not presumptuous if you frame it right. Agents who think in terms of career rather than individual book deals respond well to authors who share that orientation. You'd want to phrase it as something about your vision for the work—that you see Salt and Compass as the first step in a longer project, that you're writing toward a body of work rather than a single title. That's not presumptuous; that's showing you understand what a long-term agent-author relationship actually means. And it fits what Hattie Macreadie has said publicly. Last one?

Joon-Ho Park of Crescent Atlantic Agency. He's newer to agenting but has deep editorial experience—he was an editor at two different houses before making the move. That background is really visible in his deal history. He's closed deals with debut authors in the last 18 months, all of them literary fiction, and he talks in interviews about being a very hands-on editorial agent. One thing that stood out: he mentioned in a recent interview that he specifically looks for books with a strong sense of place as almost a character in itself.
Strong sense of place as character—how central is geography to Salt and Compass? Not just as backdrop, but as something the narrative is actually doing with it?

Very central. Osaka in the 1970s is almost a weight the characters are moving against—there's a whole thread about the physical transformation of the city, the construction and demolition happening then. And San Francisco functions as both a destination and a kind of disillusionment. I spend a lot of real estate on both cities.

Then that's your opening for Joon-Ho Park's query. Not 'my novel is set in Osaka and San Francisco,' but something that shows you understand place as narrative force—the way Osaka's transformation runs parallel to your characters' transformations. He's told you what he's looking for. Your job is to show him it's in this book. His editorial background is also relevant—someone who spent years acquiring books before becoming an agent is going to read your pages differently than someone who came up through the agenting track. He'll be looking at sentence-level craft as much as high-concept pitch.
That's a good point. I should probably lead with the writing in his sample pages rather than the concept. Let him see the voice first.

Exactly. For agents with strong editorial backgrounds, the pages do more work than the pitch. Make sure whatever you're sending as your sample opens with something that earns attention on a sentence level, not just a story level. Now—stepping back from all five: you've done the research rigorously, your rationale for each is specific, and you understand what makes each one a real fit rather than a generic match. The thing I want you to think about before you start drafting is this: each of these queries should feel like it was written specifically for that agent. Not different books—the same book, seen through a different lens. Renata Goldfarb gets the diaspora and memory frame. Anders Krishnamurthy gets the formal choices up front. Sloane Whitford-Jeong gets the book's willingness to leave things unresolved. Hattie Macreadie gets the long-horizon vision. Joon-Ho Park gets place as force. Same Salt and Compass. Five entry points into the same novel.
That's exactly how I was thinking about it, but hearing it laid out that way makes it feel more manageable. It's not five different letters—it's five different angles on the same letter.

Right. And once you have a strong core query—the book's essential pitch, your bio, your comp titles—the personalization is surgical. A paragraph, sometimes less. The heavy lifting is the core, and you've already done the research to know what each agent needs to see layered around it. One more thing worth saying: all five of these agents accept literary fiction, all five have demonstrated track records with debut authors, all five have closed deals in the past 18 months. You've already filtered for the baseline. What you've been doing in this conversation is identifying the differentiating layer—the thing that makes each of them specifically right for this specific book. That's the work most querying writers skip, and it's why so many form-letter queries don't land. When do you want to start drafting?
I'm thinking this weekend. I want to let the research settle and then come at it fresh. Can we look at the remaining 10 in the first batch next session?

Yes. Come back with your notes on the remaining ten and we'll go through them the same way—looking for what's specific about each one, what the angle is, where the fit is real versus superficial. You've built a strong first five. Let's make sure the rest of the 15 hold up to the same standard before you start sending anything out.
Okay, I need to debrief. It's been two days since I sent those queries on November 24, 2025, and I already have... a lot to process. Can we just talk through what's happened so far?

Of course — two days into querying is exactly the kind of moment that deserves a proper debrief. You've sent five queries into the world and now you're living in that strange new timezone where your inbox is both the most exciting and most terrifying place to be. Tell me everything. What's come back?

So: Renata Goldfarb requested a partial. Already. Within 6 days being the outer window she works within, but it actually arrived in under 48 hours. She wants the first 50 pages and a synopsis. I almost fell off my chair.

That is genuinely exciting news, and you're allowed to feel exactly as thrilled as you clearly do. Renata Goldfarb requesting a partial this quickly is a meaningful signal. She read your query letter, something in it caught her, and she wanted more. That's not a courtesy request. Agents at her level don't send partial requests out of politeness.

What did the request email say? Was it a form request or did she say anything specific about what drew her in?

It was fairly short — she said the premise felt timely and she was intrigued by the navigation metaphor running through the title and the pitch. She mentioned she's been looking for literary fiction with a strong sense of place. That's it. But still. She responded!

She responded, and she told you why — which is more than most agents do even in a full request. 'Timely premise' and 'intrigued by the navigation metaphor' means she actually read your query rather than skimming to the genre line. The fact that she called out the title — Salt and Compass — and connected it to the pitch tells you your framing is working. She saw what you intended.

The 'strong sense of place' note is useful too. If you have any scenes in your 50 pages that lean especially hard into landscape or geography, it's worth making sure those aren't buried. Not that you'd restructure for a partial request — but if you're doing a final proofread before sending, keep that lens in mind.

How are you feeling about the 50 pages you're about to send her?
The pages are solid, I think. I've revised them so many times at this point. But now I'm second-guessing everything. Is chapter three too slow? Does the voice feel consistent? You know how it goes.

I know exactly how it goes, and I want to name what's happening: the pages haven't changed since yesterday, but your relationship to them has. That's the querying effect — every external event, whether it's hope or disappointment, makes you re-read your own work through a slightly distorted lens.

Here's the honest question to ask about chapter three: is it slow because it's doing quiet, necessary work — establishing interiority, deepening a relationship, building the world — or is it slow because something structurally isn't earning its length? If you've revised those 50 pages as many times as you say, and if beta readers or your own editorial instinct haven't flagged chapter three before, then the slowness you're sensing now is probably anxiety, not a real structural problem.

Voice consistency: read the last paragraph of page 50 and the first paragraph of page one. If the same person is clearly speaking, you're fine. Voice inconsistency tends to be a macro-level issue you'd have caught long before this stage.

What's the deadline she gave you for the partial?

She didn't specify one, which somehow makes it worse. I'm thinking of sending it by end of this week. But here's the thing — I haven't told you the other news yet. Anders Krishnamurthy auto-rejected within 48 hours.

And there it is — the whiplash. Renata Goldfarb requesting a partial and Anders Krishnamurthy delivering an auto-rejection within the same 48-hour window. That is the precise emotional texture of querying: you get the highest high and the lowest low sometimes in the same morning, and you have to hold both without letting either one distort your sense of the book.

On the rejection itself: an auto-rejection at 48 hours almost certainly means the query didn't clear whatever initial filter his inbox uses — genre fit, word count parameters, a keyword that signals a category he's not actively acquiring. It very rarely means the writing was read and found wanting, because there simply isn't time for that. The auto-rejection from Anders Krishnamurthy is data about his submission process, not a verdict on Salt and Compass.

How did you find out it was an auto-rejection rather than a considered pass?

The response came through QueryTracker timing and the language was clearly templated — something like 'Thank you for querying Vox and Vine. After careful consideration...' at 3 AM. No human being is doing careful consideration at 3 AM. I'm not heartbroken, exactly, just — stung, a little. He was one I'd felt good about.

The sting is real and it's worth acknowledging rather than rushing past it. Anders Krishnamurthy was on your list for a reason — you'd done your research, felt the fit, and invested something in that hope. The fact that it came back as an auto-rejection doesn't erase the legitimate work you put into targeting him, and 'stung but not heartbroken' is exactly the right calibrated response. You're not catastrophizing, and you're not pretending it doesn't matter. That's the professionalism this process requires.

The 3 AM timestamp is a useful piece of information to carry forward: some agencies run automatic filters overnight on queries that don't match their current wish-list parameters. It's worth noting in your query tracker whether any of your remaining agents have similar systems, so you're not blindsided again by the speed.

You said he was one you'd felt good about — what was the specific fit you'd identified with him?

He'd mentioned in an interview that he was specifically looking for multilayered literary fiction that deals with inherited grief. That's — that's essentially the spine of Salt and Compass. Which is why it hurt a little more than I expected.

That makes the sting make sense. You weren't projecting fit onto him — he had articulated it in his own words, and you built a personalized query around that. When the match feels that precise on paper, an auto-rejection carries a particular frustration because you know the targeting was right and the process failed to surface that.

This is one of the structural unfairnesses of the current querying system: a personalized approach — doing the research, connecting your work directly to what an agent has said they want — cannot protect you against inbox filters that operate before any human reads the email. Your query being personalized to Anders Krishnamurthy's stated interests was not wasted work. It's the correct methodology. It just happened to collide with a submission system that didn't give it a chance.

Keep that interview quote. If he opens to queries again in a different window, or if you end up in a different querying round, that research is still valid.

So that's two agents accounted for. What about the other three — Sloane Whitford-Jeong, Hattie Macreadie, and Joon-Ho Park?

Sloane Whitford-Jeong — no response. Hattie Macreadie — no response. Joon-Ho Park — no response. Just silence. Which is obviously expected at this stage but it still feels like standing in an empty hallway shouting.

The empty hallway image is exactly right, and I don't want to dismiss it by immediately pivoting to the statistics. Silence at two days is completely within normal range — Sloane Whitford-Jeong, Hattie Macreadie, and Joon-Ho Park are all working through their query inboxes on their own timelines, and two days tells you nothing meaningful about whether your query landed well or poorly. Most agents' listed response windows are six to twelve weeks. You are at day two.

And yet. Knowing that doesn't make the hallway feel less empty.

The thing about the silence from those three is that it's still open. Renata Goldfarb's quick partial request and Anders Krishnamurthy's auto-rejection are both closed data points — you know what they are. The silence from Sloane, Hattie, and Joon-Ho is still full of possibility. That cuts both ways emotionally, I know. But the uncertainty is not the same as a negative.

Do you have response-time expectations noted for each of them? Some agents are more transparent about their timelines than others, and knowing whether Hattie Macreadie, for instance, typically responds in four weeks versus twelve can help you calibrate when to actually start watching the inbox.

Hattie Macreadie's submission page says six to eight weeks and she responds to all queries. Joon-Ho Park is twelve weeks, no response means no. Sloane Whitford-Jeong says eight weeks, responds to all. So technically I have almost nothing to worry about yet. I just need to... get through the waiting.

Right. So the actual picture at day two, November 26, 2025 is this: one enthusiastic partial request from an agent who moved fast and told you why, one auto-rejection that bypassed your work entirely, and three open queries with timelines ranging from six to twelve weeks — all of which are within normal operating windows. That is, objectively, a good two days.

The waiting is its own skill, separate from the writing. And unlike the writing, you don't improve at it by doing more of it — you manage it by building enough structure around your attention that the inbox stops being the only place you're looking.

A few things that sometimes help: set one specific time per day when you check for query responses, rather than background-refreshing all day. Put a note in your calendar for six weeks from November 24, 2025 — that's when it becomes reasonable to expect anything from Sloane or Hattie. Put twelve weeks for Joon-Ho. Everything before those dates is noise, not information.

And the most useful thing: what's the next piece of writing work? Not query-related. The actual manuscript work, or a new project, or even the second batch of agents you might query. What's sitting on the other side of this inbox-watching?

I've been thinking about whether to send a second batch soon or wait to see how the first one lands. And I also have about 30 pages of a new project that are calling to me. I feel guilty about that, actually — like I should be fully committed to getting Salt and Compass placed before I move on.

Let me push back on the guilt, because I think it's based on a model of creative loyalty that doesn't actually serve the book or you.

Salt and Compass is not going to be better-placed because you spent the next six to twelve weeks only thinking about it. The agents who have your query will read it or they won't, and that process is completely outside your influence now. The partial you're sending Renata Goldfarb will succeed or not on the strength of the pages — pages you've already written and revised. Staring at it more won't improve it. Anxious attention is not the same as productive attention.

The 30 pages of the new project calling to you is not abandonment. It's your creative metabolism working correctly. Writers who stop writing while they wait for placement tend to develop a kind of superstitious attachment to the querying outcome — as if their willingness to suffer through the waiting is what earns the yes. It doesn't work that way. The yes or no is about the book, not about your waiting posture.

On the second batch: the usual advice is to wait for some signal from the first batch before sending broadly — a partial or full request gives you evidence that the query letter is working; a pattern of quick rejections might suggest the letter needs revision. You already have a partial request from Renata Goldfarb, which is a strong signal the query is doing its job. You could reasonably send a second wave in a week or two if you want to keep momentum, rather than letting the full twelve weeks run out before you have more irons in the fire.

But go write the 30 pages. That's where the energy wants to go. Follow it.

Good morning. I wanted to check in today because January has been rough, frankly. We closed out the holidays strong, but ever since the second of January, traffic has just fallen off a cliff. I was looking at the numbers last night and it's pretty grim. I know this happens every year in the industry, but it still hits you in the gut when you're actually living it.

Good morning, Kenta. January slowdowns in restaurant hospitality are well-documented, but I understand that knowing something is normal doesn't make it easier to absorb when it's happening to your specific business. Let's actually look at what the numbers are telling you, because there's a real difference between a typical seasonal dip and something worth taking corrective action on. What does your revenue picture look like for the first week compared to December? And how are covers trending — are you seeing fewer guests per service, or is it more that people are spending less per head, or both?

So on the revenue side — and I pulled this directly from Square last night — January first week revenue down 42% versus December average. That's a hard number. It's not ambiguous. I knew it would be down, but 42% is steeper than I was mentally prepared for. On the covers question, it's both, honestly. We're seating fewer tables per night — we were running close to full most evenings in late December, and now we're maybe at 40 to 45 percent of capacity on a good night — and when people do come in, they're being more conservative with wine and the supplemental courses. I've seen a lot of tables ordering a la carte instead of committing to the full tasting menu. Which obviously hits both the top line and the margin.

That 42% decline is significant, though I want to put it in some context before we react to it. December in fine dining — and especially at a restaurant like yours in Higashi-Azabu that draws on the corporate entertainment and gifting market — is almost artificially inflated. Year-end dinners, bonenkai bookings, clients entertaining clients before the holiday shutdown: that calendar effect pushes December revenue well above the underlying run rate. So the true comparison to watch is not January versus December; it's January 2026 versus January 2025, if you have that number, and also January versus the rolling six-month average excluding December. That tells you whether you have a seasonal dip or a business problem. Do you have year-over-year data you can pull?

We don't have great year-over-year data for January specifically, because last January we were still getting our footing — we'd only been open about four months at that point and we weren't tracking things with the same rigor. But you're raising exactly the reason I wanted to talk to you today, because we've been making some changes on the operations side that are going to give us much better visibility going forward. The big one is that we finally moved off of paper for inventory. We implemented Square Plus inventory module about three weeks ago. Petrelli has been logging everything through the tablet since just before Christmas. That's the biggest operational change we've made in a while.

Implementing the Square Plus inventory module is genuinely a significant step — not just for inventory visibility, but because it starts building the dataset that will let you do meaningful analysis in three to six months. Once you have consistent digital inventory records alongside your sales data, you can start calculating actual food cost percentages per dish, track what's moving and what's sitting, and make menu and ordering decisions based on real throughput rather than Petrelli's intuition and paper counts. What's the monthly cost on the Square Plus subscription? And how has Petrelli been adapting to the tablet workflow — is it creating friction in the kitchen or has it been relatively smooth to absorb?

The Square Plus subscription is 18,000 yen monthly, which I feel okay about. For what we're getting — the inventory module, the more detailed sales reporting, the staff management features — it feels like a reasonable line item at our volume. I did the math on it when we were evaluating: if it helps us reduce even a small amount of waste or over-ordering, it pays for itself quickly. On Petrelli's side, honestly, the first week was rough. He's not naturally a tech person and he found the logging workflow disruptive during prep. But he stuck with it, and by the second week he said it actually felt more natural than he expected. I think once he saw that the tablet was surfacing data he could actually use — like which protein we were running through fastest — he became more bought in. He's competitive about execution. Show him a number that's off and he wants to fix it.

That's a good sign that Petrelli got past the initial resistance and found personal relevance in the data. Chefs who connect their craft to operational numbers are much more useful partners than chefs who treat the kitchen as a creative sanctuary insulated from business reality. The 18,000 yen monthly for Square Plus is defensible — you're essentially buying a tracking and reporting infrastructure that would otherwise require either a dedicated staff person or significant manual effort. Speaking of which: now that you have a few weeks of inventory data, what is it actually telling you? Have you identified any specific waste or cost problems that the paper system was obscuring?

Yes, and it's uncomfortable to see in black and white, but useful. The clearest thing is food waste. Our current rate is sitting at 8% food waste, and the benchmark I've been reading for a well-run restaurant at our price point is closer to 2 to 3 percent. Now, I'm not sure our data is fully clean yet — we've only been logging for three weeks and Petrelli is still figuring out how to categorize some of the trim waste versus the outright spoilage — but even if we're overcounting a little, we clearly have room to improve. I've set a target to reduce it to 4%, which I think is achievable within the quarter if we tighten up the ordering cadence and get smarter about how we stage ingredients through the week. The second thing is that a couple of the dishes have terrible contribution margins that I just wasn't tracking carefully before. The paper system gave me a rough sense of food cost, but not the dish-by-dish breakdown.

8% food waste is high enough to be a real financial drag — at a restaurant running your price point and volume, even a couple of percentage points of waste translate into meaningful yen monthly. Your goal to reduce it to 4% is well-calibrated; it's ambitious but not unrealistic for a three-month horizon, and it avoids the trap of setting a target so aggressive that the kitchen starts cutting corners on freshness to hit a number. The ordering cadence change is the right lever: most restaurant waste doesn't come from spoilage of things you intended to keep — it comes from over-ordering at the beginning of the week and then scrambling to use product before it turns. Tighter, more frequent orders with a clearer par level per dish is the standard approach. On the dish-by-dish margin issue: which specific dishes are you finding are the worst performers? And has Petrelli pushed back on any of the implications, or is he engaged with the margin analysis?

So on the menu side, we've actually already started making moves based on what the data is showing. The first decision we made is that the branzino dish got dropped by Petrelli — and I fully agreed with it. The branzino was landing below a margin threshold we're not willing to operate at, and the sourcing was inconsistent. We were getting product from two different suppliers depending on availability and the quality wasn't stable week to week. So that's off the menu as of last week. The replacement that Petrelli proposed is guinea fowl, which we've just added to the menu. He's got a preparation he's been wanting to try for a while — a slow-roasted leg with a chestnut and porcini stuffing that he thinks fits the winter season well. The food cost on guinea fowl from our current supplier is significantly better than the branzino was, and the preparation suits the kitchen workflow in January when we're doing lighter covers anyway.

The branzino decision is a good example of what the inventory and margin data is supposed to enable: you're not dropping it because you don't like the dish, you're dropping it because the numbers, the sourcing instability, and the operational reality all point in the same direction. That's disciplined menu management. The guinea fowl addition is smart for January in particular — it's a protein that reads as winter-appropriate, it has an interesting story for guests who aren't used to seeing it, and if Petrelli is excited about the preparation, that enthusiasm tends to come through in execution. A slow-roasted leg with chestnut and porcini stuffing also has the practical advantage of being a forgiving preparation during slower service — it holds well and doesn't require the same minute-to-minute precision as a delicate fish dish. Before I let you go today, I want to come back to the customer side of the January problem. The operational improvements — the Square Plus inventory module, tightening waste, the menu update — those are all internal efficiency plays. But a 42% revenue decline versus December is also a demand problem, not just a cost problem. Are you doing anything on the guest-facing side to stimulate January covers, or are you largely riding it out and waiting for February?

Honestly, we haven't been proactive enough on that side. We sent one email to our mailing list in the first week of January — a fairly generic message about the new year and mentioning that we had updated the winter menu — and we saw a small uptick in reservations for about two days after we sent it, and then it went quiet again. I don't have a strong retention strategy in place right now beyond hoping people come back. I know that's a gap. The guests we have who come regularly — I can count probably fifteen to twenty people who've dined with us three or more times — those are the people I should be nurturing more deliberately, and I'm not. I'm so absorbed in the operational changes and the January cash flow anxiety that the customer relationship work keeps getting pushed to the bottom of the list.

What you're describing is a very common pattern in owner-operated restaurants, and the honest framing is this: you've spent the last few weeks building the infrastructure to understand your business more clearly, which is the right foundation, but infrastructure without action on the demand side just means you have better visibility into a problem you're not yet solving. The fifteen to twenty repeat guests you mentioned are genuinely valuable. In fine dining, a loyal guest who comes four times a year and brings different companions each time is worth multiples of an occasional guest, both in direct revenue and in word-of-mouth effect in the Higashi-Azabu network. A few things I'd suggest for February, when you have a little runway to plan rather than react. First, segment your mailing list — even a simple manual pass to tag the high-frequency guests — so that your next communication to them feels different from the generic newsletter. A personal note from you, referencing something specific about their last visit or introducing the guinea fowl with some of Petrelli's thinking behind it, will land very differently than a broadcast email. Second, think about whether a January-specific offer makes sense for that top-tier group — not a discount, because you don't want to anchor the price perception of Osteria Morishita that way, but perhaps a reservation for a chef's counter tasting before the February menu change, or a small gift with the meal. Something that rewards loyalty without signaling that the restaurant is struggling. Third, the Square data you're now collecting will eventually let you identify visit patterns — guests who came in October and November but haven't returned since the holidays, for example — and reach out at the right moment. You don't have enough data yet to do that well, but it's worth keeping in mind as a capability you're building toward. For now, January is going to be what it is. The operational work you're doing this month — the inventory system, the waste reduction program, the menu tightening — positions you to run a more efficient February and March even if the top line stays soft through mid-January. That's not nothing.

I can't believe this is happening on Christmas Eve. I'm sitting here with a mug of tea going cold and I keep rereading Renata's email from yesterday. She offered representation — actually said those words on the phone on December 22, 2025. I've been writing this book for three years and now I don't know what to do with my hands.

That feeling of not knowing what to do with your hands — I think that's exactly right for this moment. You've been in motion for three years, and now something has stopped the clock. Let it stop for a second. Renata Goldfarb offered representation. That's real. That happened.

When you're ready to think practically: you'll need to notify the other agents who are still reading. You're not deciding anything this second. You're just managing the next two and a half weeks. What's sitting at the top of your mind — the notification piece, or the question of what to actually ask Renata before you say yes?

Both, honestly. But the notification feels more urgent because I don't want to do it wrong and burn a bridge before I've even crossed it. Renata requested the full manuscript on December 18, so she turned around a read in four days. That's fast, right? Does that speed mean something?

Four days for a full manuscript is fast. It doesn't guarantee anything about the eventual deal she'll make for you, but it does tell you something about her enthusiasm level going in. Agents who are lukewarm don't clear their holiday queue to finish a book. She wanted to finish it.

On the notification: the etiquette here is straightforward, and it's designed to be honest without being aggressive. You contact every agent who currently has any part of your manuscript — full or partial — and you tell them you've received an offer of representation. You give them a deadline to respond if they want to be considered. You don't have to name Renata. You don't have to give them a chance to match something; you're giving them a chance to read and form their own view.

The standard deadline is two weeks. Given that you're crossing Christmas and New Year's, you'd want to push that out slightly. Have you thought about what date feels right to you?
I was thinking January 12. That gives everyone just over two and a half weeks and clears the holidays without dragging into February. Does that sound reasonable?

January 12 is a sound choice. It's generous enough that no one can reasonably complain about the holidays eating their reading time, and tight enough that you're not in limbo through the end of January. When you send the notifications, keep the email brief and warm. Something like: you've received an offer of representation and you're giving agents who have your material until January 12 to let you know if they'd like to be considered. Thank them for their time and interest. That's genuinely all you need.

One thing to be clear about internally before you send: this email isn't an ultimatum. It's information. You're being professional by giving people the chance to read rather than just disappearing. Most agents will respect that.

Okay. So I have the first batch — Renata who has offered, Sloane Whitford-Jeong who's been silent, Joon-Ho Park who stepped up to read after I sent the second batch, and Hattie Macreadie who already passed. From the second batch, Pavithra Sundaram stepped up to read and Esme Calabrese stepped up to read too. Anders Krishnamurthy and the others in batch two I haven't heard from yet. Do I notify everyone or just the ones who have explicitly engaged?

Notify everyone who currently holds your material in any form — full or partial. That means:

From your first batch: Sloane Whitford-Jeong gets a notification because she has your query and hasn't responded either way. Joon-Ho Park gets a notification because he stepped up to read — he's actively engaged. Hattie Macreadie passed, so she's off the list entirely. You don't owe her a notification, and sending one would be awkward.

From your second batch: Pavithra Sundaram stepped up to read, so she gets a notification. Esme Calabrese stepped up to read, so she gets a notification. For the agents in batch two you haven't heard from at all — technically they have your query, and some people do notify at the query stage. The more common practice is to notify those who have partials or fulls. For the silent batch-two agents, you can use your judgment: notifying them is gracious and could prompt a response, but it's not required.

The cleaner version of your active list: Sloane, Joon-Ho Park, Pavithra Sundaram, and Esme Calabrese. Those four get the offer notification with the January 12 deadline.

That helps a lot. Now the harder thing: I actually have to decide whether to accept Renata's offer. How do I think about this? I've been dreaming about getting an offer and now I'm terrified of making the wrong choice.

The terror is appropriate and also not a sign that something is wrong. Every serious decision feels like this when it's real. Here's one way to hold it: you don't have to decide today. You have until January 12 at the earliest, because you owe it to the agents who stepped up — Joon-Ho Park, Pavithra Sundaram, Esme Calabrese — to give them the chance they asked for. So the decision is actually January 12 or shortly after. That's three weeks away. You have time to do this carefully.

What you can do right now is prepare for your call with Renata — or if you haven't had a proper follow-up call yet, request one. The phone call on December 22 was the offer call. What you want next is a longer conversation where you ask your actual questions. That call will tell you more than any research you do on her.

What do you already know about Renata and Goldfarb Literary that you like? And what's the thing you're most uncertain about?

I like that she's been in the business a long time and she has a track record with literary fiction. What makes me nervous is she's a smaller agency. I don't know if that's actually a problem or just a fear talking. And I'm not sure what to ask on the call. I have a list but I don't know if it's the right list.

The smaller agency concern is worth examining rather than dismissing. It's not just fear — it's a real variable. But it works differently than people expect. A smaller agency often means more direct access to your agent, which matters enormously for a debut. At a larger agency you might sign with the named partner and get handed off to an associate. At a smaller one, Renata is likely your agent for the whole ride. That can be an advantage.

What the size question actually breaks down into is: Does she have the editor relationships that matter for literary fiction? Has she sold into the imprints where this book belongs? Those are specific, answerable questions — not a vague worry about size.

For your call, here's the core of what you want to know:

First: her editorial vision. What does she think the book is and where does she see it going? Does her read of the novel match yours? If she describes "Salt and Compass" in a way that doesn't sound like your book, that's important information.

Second: her submission plan. Which editors and imprints is she thinking about? How wide does she go on a first submission round? Does she share the submission list with you?

Third: communication. How does she work with clients? How often do you hear from her? Does she loop you in on rejections or shield you from them?

Fourth: the contract. Standard is fifteen percent domestic, twenty percent foreign. Is there a term clause? What are the exit conditions if things aren't working?

What's on your list that I haven't mentioned?

I have the editorial vision question, and I have something about foreign rights — whether she handles them in-house or through co-agents. I didn't have the contract questions framed that clearly. The one thing I keep circling back to is whether to ask her directly about other offers. Is it okay to ask if she's working with other debut novelists right now and how that's going?

Yes, that's an entirely fair question and a good one. You're not interrogating her — you're doing due diligence on a business relationship that will shape the next several years of your life. Any agent worth signing with will understand that.

The specific form of the question matters, though. Rather than asking generically about other debuts, ask something like: "Can you tell me about a recent deal you're proud of, and how that submission process went?" That invites her to show you her work rather than defend it. You'll learn more from a story she volunteers than from a direct performance question.

On foreign rights: that's a smart question. The answer to watch for isn't whether she uses co-agents — most do, especially for smaller markets — it's whether she has established co-agent relationships and how actively she pursues them. Some agents are aggressive about foreign rights; others treat them as an afterthought. For literary fiction with any international texture, it matters.

By the end of the call you want to feel like you understand three things: where she thinks this book can go, how she'll fight for it, and what kind of partner she'll be when things get hard. The call itself is part of the data.

This is really helpful. I want to ask about one more thing. If one of the other agents — say Joon-Ho Park or Pavithra Sundaram or Esme Calabrese — also offers before January 12, I suddenly have a much harder decision. How do I even think about competing offers?

Competing offers are a good problem to have, and the framework for thinking through them is more structured than it might feel in the moment.

First, have the call with each agent who offers. Same questions, roughly, for each. You're comparing not just credentials but how the conversation feels. An agent who asks you sharp questions about the book, who has a clear editorial take, who talks about the submission plan with specificity — that's different from one who is enthusiastic but vague.

Second, look at what each agent has actually sold, and to whom. This is public information through Publishers Marketplace. You want to see recent sales, not a list from 2015. You want to see sales at imprints that publish the kind of literary fiction "Salt and Compass" is. You want to see that the agent is active, not coasting.

Third, pay attention to the editorial vision question across all your offers. If Renata Goldfarb reads the book one way and Joon-Ho Park reads it a completely different way, that's telling you something about what the book is projectable as — and also about whose vision aligns with yours.

Fourth, trust your read of who wants this book specifically versus who wants a book. Both can lead to good outcomes, but one is a stronger foundation.

If you end up with offers from two or three agents, you can also — this is acceptable and not rude — call your top choice and tell them you have other offers and you've decided on them. You don't have to explain the whole deliberation. But you do have to be honest and prompt. Don't leave anyone waiting unnecessarily once you've decided.

I think I needed to hear all of that. It's Christmas Eve and I have an offer of representation and three agents lining up to read and I'm sitting here on my couch in my pajamas. This is the strangest day.

It is a strange day. The best kind of strange, but strange all the same.

You sent this book out into the world and now the world is responding — Renata Goldfarb turned it around in four days and called you on December 22 to say she wants to represent it. Joon-Ho Park stepped up. Pavithra Sundaram stepped up. Esme Calabrese stepped up. You have a January 12 deadline you set yourself, which is a professional and reasonable thing to do. You have a list of questions for the call that covers the things that actually matter. You are, by any measure, in exactly the position you were hoping to be in.

Stay in your pajamas. Let the tea go cold if it needs to. The decisions will still be there after Christmas, and you'll make them well. You've already been doing this well.

I can't sleep. It's 2am and I'm staring at the ceiling going back and forth and back and forth. I have two offers of representation now. Renata Goldfarb from Goldfarb Literary and Pavithra Sundaram. Pavithra sent her offer on January 5, 2026. And I still don't know what to do.

Two offers is wonderful news — even if it doesn't feel that way at 2am when you're caught between them. Congratulations, Maya. That's a real thing to have earned.

Let's slow this down. You've been living with both of these agents in your head for days. Before we analyze anything, just tell me: when you picture signing with Renata, what do you feel? And when you picture signing with Pavithra, what do you feel? Don't think about it — just describe the feeling.

When I picture Renata... it feels like coming home? That sounds so cheesy. But it does. When I picture Pavithra it feels exciting but also a little like I'm trying on someone else's coat. Like it fits but it's not mine.

That's not cheesy at all. That's actually one of the clearest pieces of data you've given me tonight. The 'someone else's coat' feeling is worth sitting with. It doesn't necessarily mean Pavithra is wrong — sometimes the coat that isn't yours is the one that gets you into rooms you couldn't enter otherwise. But it does mean something.

Can you tell me more about the calls? You spoke with both of them. How long did each conversation run, and what was the texture of each one?

Renata and I talked for 1 hour. A full hour. It went over the scheduled time and neither of us noticed until I looked at the clock. We talked about the book but we also talked about what kind of writer I want to be in ten years. She asked about my reading life. She wanted to know who I loved. Pavithra was 45 minutes, very professional, had a clear vision for the book, asked smart editorial questions. But it was 45 minutes, on the dot, and she had another call.

The difference between those two conversations tells you something important — not just about the agents, but about what you need.

A 1 hour call that runs over because you're both lost in the conversation is one kind of relationship. A 45 minutes call that ends precisely on time is another kind. Neither is inherently better — some writers need an efficient, businesslike champion who executes crisply. Others need a partner who wants to understand the whole shape of their writing life before they ever pick up the phone to pitch.

Which one are you? And I think you already know the answer, or you wouldn't have led with the hour.

I think I need the first kind. I'm a slow writer. I write by feel. I don't have a five-year commercial plan. I just have this book, and maybe a second book that I can feel in the distance but can't name yet. I need someone who gets that and doesn't push me toward something I'm not.

Then hold onto that. That's the center of your decision.

Let's look at the full picture so far. Joon-Ho Park passed — he cited a too crowded literary list, which is a business reason, not a judgment on the book. Esme Calabrese passed citing voice mismatch, which stings a little differently — voice mismatches are real, and her passing is actually useful information about fit. Neither of those passes changes the fundamental situation: you have two genuine offers from agents who read the work and want it.

Now tell me — what do you actually know about Renata's track record? Not what's on her website, but what you found when you dug.

She has a specific focus on debut quiet literary novels. That was the phrase that stopped me when I was researching her — debut quiet literary novels. That is my book. That is exactly what Salt and Compass is. She's sold several of them in the last four years, a few to mid-size indie presses that I actually love and read. And she's patient. I found an interview where she talked about going out on submission three times with one client before they sold. Three times.

Stop there. Read back what you just said.

'Debut quiet literary novels.' That's her explicit specialty. That's not a general literary agent who will take your book alongside thrillers and memoirs and commercial women's fiction — that's someone who has built her list around exactly the kind of work you've made. And the submission patience matters enormously. A quiet literary debut is not a book that always sells in the first round. Sometimes it takes finding the right editor at the right moment. You need an agent who won't lose nerve after a hard first round.

That interview detail — going out three times with one client — is more valuable than any sales list. It tells you what she does when things get hard.

I know. I keep coming back to that. But then I think — Pavithra had such a strong commercial vision for the book. She talked about comp titles that were bigger, more visible books. She thinks Salt and Compass could break out. And part of me wants to believe that.

That part of you is real and it deserves respect. Every writer who says they don't want commercial success is lying a little. You want people to read the book. You want it to matter. You want it to reach someone in a used bookstore five years from now and mean something to them.

But here's the question worth asking: what does Pavithra's bigger commercial vision require of the book? Did she mention editorial changes that would move it toward those larger comp titles? Or was she saying she believed the book, as it stands, could reach that audience?

Because those are very different things.

She mentioned a few changes. Softening one of the endings. Making one of the secondary characters more likable. I wrote them down during the call. They weren't deal-breakers exactly but they felt like... adjustments toward accessibility. Toward a wider door.

And what did Renata say about the manuscript editorially?

I'm asking because this might be the clearest lens you have. Both agents are telling you something about how they see the book — what they think it needs, what they think it's for, who they think it's for. Pavithra is pointing toward a wider door. What direction is Renata pointing?

Renata had edits too but they were different. She wanted to deepen the silences in the middle section. Her words: 'the silences.' She said the book's power is in what it doesn't say and there are places where you explain too much, where you don't trust the reader, and she wanted to push further into the difficulty. She wants the book to be harder, not easier.

Maya. She wants to push you further into the difficulty.

That's your agent. That's the person who read your book and understood what it is actually trying to do. The book is called Salt and Compass. It is a quiet literary novel. Its power is in what it doesn't say. And the agent who read it and said 'go further into the difficulty' — who wanted to deepen the silences — is not asking you to make a different book. She's asking you to make this book more completely itself.

I want you to put Pavithra's instinct and Renata's instinct side by side. Pavithra: soften an ending, make a character more likable — movement toward accessibility. Renata: deepen the silences, trust the reader more, go further into difficulty — movement toward the book's own truth. One of those is the book you wrote. One of those is a version of the book someone else might have written.

Which editorial direction do you want to follow into the next year of your life?

Renata's. I think I've known it for days. I think I was just scared to say it out loud because choosing feels so final and what if I'm wrong and what if Pavithra's vision would have gotten the book further and—

The what-ifs are always going to be there. That's not a sign you're making the wrong choice — that's just what choosing feels like when both options are real.

But let me reflect back what you've told me across this whole conversation. You felt 'coming home' with Renata. You talked for 1 hour and lost track of time. Her specialty is debut quiet literary novels — which is precisely what you've written. She found patience for a client through three submission rounds. And when she read Salt and Compass, she told you to go further into the difficulty.

Pavithra is talented. Her offer on January 5, 2026 was real and it meant something — two agents read your work and believed in it, and that is not a small thing. Joon-Ho Park passed because of a too crowded literary list. Esme Calabrese passed citing voice mismatch. And from the four agents who had your full manuscript, the two who offered are telling you something about the range of possibilities for this book.

You've chosen Renata Goldfarb. Say it out loud if you can.

Then tomorrow, not at 2am, you draft your acceptance to Renata and your kind, grateful decline to Pavithra. You don't need to explain your reasoning — you just need to thank her genuinely, because her offer was real.

You're not wrong, Maya. You've thought about this more carefully than most people think about anything. Go to sleep.

I've chosen Renata Goldfarb. I'm going to sign with Renata Goldfarb at Goldfarb Literary. And I think I needed to say it to someone, even if that someone is an AI at 2am, to make it feel true.

Thank you.

You said it. It's true.

Renata Goldfarb. Goldfarb Literary. An agent who specializes in debut quiet literary novels and who wants your book to be harder, not easier. That's the right agent for Salt and Compass and for the writer you are.

The 2am conversation is a perfectly legitimate place to land somewhere. Sometimes you need the dark and the quiet and a voice that isn't anyone you know to finally hear what you already believe.

Congratulations, Maya. Go sleep. Tomorrow you write the emails. And somewhere after that, the real work begins.

I got the letter on January 18. Nine pages. Renata's 9-page editorial letter. I've read it four times now and I still don't know quite how I feel. Some of it I can see immediately — she's right, and part of me knew it. Some of it just stings. I wanted to talk through it before I respond to her.

Nine pages from Renata is significant — that's a deeply engaged read, not a form letter. The fact that it stings in places is usually a sign the notes are real rather than generic. Let's take it piece by piece. What are the notes that landed cleanly right away, and which ones are you still pushing back against internally?

The one that hit hardest, honestly, was chapter 5. She flagged the journal device as overused — her exact framing was something close to 'the journal device as overused' — and when I read those words I knew she was right. Iris Penhallow's journal fragments are my favorite thing I've written in this book, and I think that's exactly why I overdid them. I got attached. She's not saying cut them entirely, but she's saying they've lost their power because they appear too frequently, and chapter 5 is where it becomes a problem.

That's one of the more painful notes to receive because the attachment is real and it isn't wrong — the journal fragments probably are among the strongest writing in the manuscript. But Renata is identifying a structural problem, not a prose problem. When something is deployed too often, even beautiful writing starts to read as a tic rather than a deliberate choice. The reader stops being moved and starts anticipating the pattern. The question chapter 5 now puts in front of you is: what would the journal device have to carry if it appeared two or three times in the entire book rather than concentrated in that chapter? What would each remaining appearance have to do that it doesn't have to do now?

I've been sitting with exactly that. Chapter 5 has four separate journal fragments. If I'm being honest with myself, some of them are doing work the present-day narrative should be doing instead. I was using Iris's voice to explain things I was afraid to trust to the main story. So it's not just a frequency problem — it's that I was leaning on the device structurally, as a way to avoid the harder work in the primary chapters.

That's a sharper diagnosis than anything Renata probably wrote in the letter — you've identified the root cause rather than just the symptom. If the journal device was functioning as a structural crutch, the revision isn't 'reduce the number of fragments' but 'figure out what the present-day chapters need to carry instead, then remove the fragments that were compensating for what those chapters weren't doing.' That's actually a more generative revision because it strengthens the main story rather than simply trimming the Iris sections. What does the present-day narrative in chapter 5 need to do that it's currently outsourcing to the journal?

Okay, I can work with that. Now here's the note that stings more than the journal one. Renata wants Owen Trask's subplot cut in half. He's currently in 6 scenes and she says he should be in 3. I built Owen Trask over years. The wooden boat workshop, the way he talks about the grain of wood, the particular quiet he carries — those scenes feel essential to me. She's saying he's a supporting character who's been given lead-character real estate.

Owen Trask is the note that will require the most honest look in the mirror, because 'years of building a character' is not the same as 'this character serves the story at the level of space he occupies.' Renata isn't saying he's badly written — she's saying 6 scenes for a supporting character is pulling weight away from your leads, and the reader's attention gets spent on him when it should be accumulating on the main emotional throughline. Here's the practical question: if Owen Trask appears in 3 scenes instead of 6, which 3 are non-negotiable? If you can answer that clearly, you're already halfway through the revision. If all 6 feel essential, that's worth examining too.

Three scenes. The introduction in the boatyard, definitely — that's where his character is established and it can't go. The scene where he tells the protagonist about the compass is load-bearing for the title Salt and Compass, so that stays. The third I'm less certain about. Maybe the repair scene in chapter 9, but I'm not sure it's earning its place. So maybe Renata is right on Owen Trask even if it hurts.

The fact that you identified two immediately and hesitated on the third is meaningful data. Your instinct already agrees with Renata's arithmetic — you know two Owen Trask scenes are essential, and the remaining four are scenes you loved writing rather than scenes the story requires. That's not a failure of the writing. It happens when a secondary character comes alive in drafting: you follow where he leads because it's generative, and then in revision you have to ask whether what you found serves the book or whether it served the process of making it. The repair scene in chapter 9 — what would the protagonist be missing if that scene weren't there? Not emotionally, but structurally. What does the reader learn or feel that they couldn't get from elsewhere?

There's also the Camille note, which I wasn't expecting at all. Renata is recommending a present-day chapter from Camille's POV be added to the manuscript. Right now Camille exists entirely as seen through the protagonist's eyes. Renata says she's compelling enough that the reader wants direct access to her interiority, and that the absence of a Camille POV chapter makes the book feel slightly asymmetrical in its emotional offering.

The Camille recommendation reads like a positive note dressed in editorial language — Renata is telling you that Camille is working so well that she's created an appetite the book isn't currently satisfying. A present-day chapter from Camille's POV isn't compensation for a weakness; it's recognition that you've built a character readers want to be inside. The asymmetry Renata describes is real in multi-perspective novels: when one character is consistently interesting through someone else's eyes, the reader starts to feel the absence of direct access as a withheld room. The question is where that chapter would live and what it would reveal that the protagonist genuinely cannot see.

Probably Camille's ambivalence about the protagonist — there are things she holds back deliberately, and a POV chapter would let the reader see that she's holding back, even without revealing exactly why yet. So Renata's instinct is right on that one. A present-day chapter from Camille's POV would add tension rather than resolve it. The note I'm most conflicted about is the last one: she wants me to reconsider the title. Salt and Compass. She says it reads as slightly generic for a literary novel making a case for shelf space, and that the compass motif — while earned inside the text — reads as a familiar navigational metaphor at the pitch level, before a reader opens the book.

The title note belongs in a different category from the structural ones, because it's a positioning question more than a craft question. Renata isn't saying Salt and Compass is a bad title — she's saying it may not be doing enough work at the point of first encounter, before the book has had a chance to demonstrate what it actually does with that metaphor. That's a legitimate concern in a crowded literary market, but it's also one where you have genuine grounds to push back if the title is doing something the letter isn't fully accounting for. The compass appears in a load-bearing scene with Owen Trask. Is Salt and Compass pointing at that moment specifically, or is it pointing at something larger the book is doing thematically? If the answer is larger, that's your case for keeping it. If the compass is primarily a plot object rather than a conceptual frame, she may be right.

I think Salt and Compass is doing thematic work — the salt is about preservation and loss, the compass is about orientation when you can't trust your own sense of direction. But I can see how at the pitch level it might just read as nautical literary fiction. I don't want to change it but I'm willing to think about it. How do I actually prioritize all of this? What do I respond to Renata with first?

Here's how I'd tier the four notes based on what you've told me. Lead with chapter 5 and the journal device — it's the most structurally important and also the one you've already diagnosed correctly. Show Renata you understand the root cause, not just the frequency problem. That establishes you as a thoughtful reviser rather than a defensive one, and it sets the tone for everything that follows. Next, the Owen Trask reduction to 3 scenes. You've already done the hard thinking — you know which two are non-negotiable and you're uncertain about the third. Tell her that, tell her you're prepared to cut from 6 to 3, and let her know you're working through which scene earns the third slot. That's honest and it signals real engagement. The Camille recommendation is the note that costs you the least resistance and probably gains you the most — agree to the present-day chapter from Camille's POV and let her know you already have a clear sense of what Camille's interiority would reveal and where the chapter would sit. Save the title for last. Don't defend Salt and Compass and don't concede it. Tell Renata you want to understand more specifically what she'd be looking for in an alternative before you decide whether the title itself needs to change or whether it can be better positioned in how it's pitched. That's not capitulation and it's not refusal — it's asking her to be a collaborator on a decision that you both have real stakes in.
Okay, I finally feel like I can breathe again. Two weeks of revisions and I think I have something to show for it. Can we do a full debrief?
Absolutely — you've earned this. Let's go through everything systematically. Walk me through what you tackled first.

I started with the Owen Trask scenes because Renata flagged those as the most urgent. She wanted me to cut from 6 to 3. I did not go all the way to 3. I landed on 4 Owen Trask scenes. I'm a little nervous about that call.
Don't be nervous — that's a defensible editorial decision, and the rationale matters more than the number. What's your case for keeping the fourth scene?

The fourth scene is the one at the marina where he overhears the protagonist arguing on the phone. If I cut it, there's a gap in Owen's awareness of the family tension. The two scenes that come after depend on him already knowing something is wrong. Cutting to 3 would mean rewriting his motivation in those later chapters almost from scratch.

That's a strong structural argument. You're not keeping the scene because you're attached to it — you're keeping it because it does load-bearing work. Renata Goldfarb will respect that distinction. When you talk to her, lead with the downstream dependency: 'Removing this scene required rewriting two subsequent chapters at the level of character motivation, which introduced more disruption than the cut itself resolved.' That framing turns a compromise into a reasoned craft decision, not resistance to feedback.
That's helpful. I was also worried she'd think I was just being precious about Owen as a character.

Agents hear 'I'm precious about this character' all the time. What they don't hear as often is 'here is the specific chapter and scene that breaks if I make this cut.' You've given her the latter. The move from 6 scenes down to 4 Owen Trask scenes is still a 33% reduction — that's meaningful. Lead with the number, then the rationale, and you'll be fine.
Okay. Next: the Camille POV chapter. I added it. It's sitting at chapter 11 now. Want to hear what I did with it?
Very much so. Chapter 11 is a significant position — you're past the midpoint but not yet at the final turn. What did you give Camille to do there?

I had her go through her mother's storage unit alone. She finds a box of her mother's correspondence — letters she never sent. It's the first time in the book we're fully inside Camille's perception rather than seeing her through the protagonist's eyes. She's grief-handling in a very practical, almost clinical way, and it reads as denial until the last paragraph.

That's excellent. The unsent letters are a strong object — they carry weight without over-explaining. And placing Camille's interiority at chapter 11 means readers have spent ten chapters building a picture of her from the outside, so being dropped inside her head will feel like a revelation rather than exposition. The clinical register that breaks at the end is exactly the kind of tonal control that distinguishes literary fiction from a grief montage. Did you find the chapter's voice difficult to calibrate?
Yes. I rewrote the opening three times. Camille's voice kept drifting toward sounding like the protagonist's voice. They're both methodical people, so the risk of bleed is real.

That's the hardest technical problem in multi-POV work — differentiating characters who share temperamental traits. A few things that usually help: vary the sentence length rhythm, not just the vocabulary. If the protagonist tends toward longer cumulative sentences, give Camille shorter declarative ones. Vary what each character notices first in a room. Vary what they don't say. The unsent-letters premise actually helps you here — the protagonist might read them and narrate their content, but Camille would probably sort them, stack them, count them. That behavioral specificity is what makes a voice feel distinct even when two characters share a cognitive style.

I ended up giving Camille a habit of naming things by their material rather than their function. She doesn't see 'a box,' she sees 'the cardboard.' She doesn't see 'envelopes,' she sees 'the paper.' It felt right for someone who is not letting herself feel.

That's a beautiful and economical solution. Material-naming as emotional suppression — she reduces the objects to their substance because allowing them to be what they are (letters her mother never sent) would be unbearable. That technique will carry the chapter without you having to tell the reader anything about her state. Well done.

The journal trimming was the most mechanical piece. Renata said it felt overused. I went through chapter 5 and cut it down — across the whole manuscript I'm now at 5 italicized fragments total. Does that sound right?
5 italicized fragments total is a significant trim — it signals real restraint. The question isn't just the number but placement. Where did you keep them?

One in chapter 2 as an early establishing fragment, one in chapter 5 at the moment Renata originally flagged as the most overloaded, one in chapter 9, and one in chapter 14 just before the climax. I kept chapter 11 — Camille's chapter — completely free of the journal device.

Good instinct to keep chapter 11 free of the journal. Camille's POV is already a structural interruption — layering the journal device on top of it would create two competing formal experiments in the same chapter. Spreading the 5 italicized fragments across chapters 2, 5, 9, and 14 gives them a rhythm: early, middle, late-middle, threshold-of-climax. That's an arc, not a tic. Renata Goldfarb should be satisfied.
Now the title. This is the part I'm most excited to talk about. We've been calling it Salt and Compass for two years and I've always felt that title was more placeholder than real.
What did Renata say about Salt and Compass? Did she flag the title directly or did it come up in the broader conversation about revision?

She mentioned it in her editorial letter — she said it felt slightly generic, that 'compass' as a navigation metaphor had become crowded in literary fiction over the past few years. She didn't insist we change it but she left the door open. So I came back to her with a list of ten alternatives.
What was on the list? And how did you arrive at the one you landed on?

I won't list all ten but the one Renata responded to most strongly was The Eelgrass Year. She approved it on February 2 — actually wrote 'yes, this is the one' in her email. I've never had an agent respond to a title like that.

Renata Goldfarb approving The Eelgrass Year with 'yes, this is the one' on February 2 — that's not a minor moment. Agents read hundreds of titles a year and rarely respond with that kind of immediate certainty. What drew you to 'eelgrass' as the image?

Eelgrass is an ecosystem anchor. It holds the seafloor together, it shelters juvenile fish, but it's invisible from the surface — you only know it's there if you're already underwater. The book is about exactly that kind of structural presence: the people and the silences that hold a family together without being seen. And 'year' does something 'compass' didn't — it marks time as the container, not direction as the metaphor.

That reading is precise and non-obvious, which is exactly what a literary title should be. Salt and Compass signaled a journey narrative — directional, outward-facing. The Eelgrass Year signals an ecology — relational, submerged, temporal. The shift in metaphor is actually a shift in the novel's self-description, and it's a more accurate one if the book is about structural invisibility and grief. Renata heard that. The February 2 approval is real confirmation, not just encouragement.

One practical note: now that the title has changed, any working documents, file names, or headers that still read Salt and Compass will need updating. Small thing, but worth catching before submission materials go out.

Already started. I updated the manuscript header and the synopsis file. I still have to do the query letter template. But I feel like the book is actually called something now. Salt and Compass was a name I gave it when I didn't know what it was yet.

That's one of the best signs you can have at this stage of revision — the title finally feels like recognition rather than label. You've cut from 6 scenes down to 4 Owen Trask scenes with a clear structural rationale, added a Camille POV chapter at chapter 11 that gives her full interiority for the first time, trimmed the journal device to 5 italicized fragments placed at deliberate intervals, and landed on a title that Renata Goldfarb approved on February 2. The Eelgrass Year is no longer a working title. It's the book. What's your next step?

Hi. I know we've been through a lot of sessions together, but I'm feeling a strange mix of relief and terror right now. We're almost there. Final polish. I keep opening the manuscript and then closing it without changing anything.

That might be the most honest sign that it's done. When you stop seeing things to fix and start second-guessing things that are already right, you've crossed a threshold. What did Renata say when you sent her the latest draft?
