She called yesterday. She loves the ending — she's been saying that for weeks now, so I believe her. But she had two things she wanted to discuss before we finalize everything for submission. One is actually pretty minor, one feels bigger to me even though objectively it probably isn't.
Tell me the bigger-feeling one first. Sometimes naming it out loud shrinks it to its actual size.

The vessel name. The research ship in the book — it's been Persephone since the first draft. I built so much around that name. The myth of descent and return, the way it echoes the narrator's emotional arc. Renata wants me to change it to Cordelia.
That's not a small request. What's her reasoning?

She said 'Greek myth fatigue' — that's the phrase she used. Greek myth fatigue in literary fiction. She said editors at several of the imprints on our list have been vocal about it internally — that manuscripts leaning on Greek mythological resonance feel dated right now, that it signals a certain kind of MFA workshop fiction. She said Cordelia reads as literary without that baggage. Shakespeare, obviously, but subtler. More contemporary in feel.

Renata's read on the market is probably sound. Greek myth fatigue is real — you can track it in acquisitions over the last few years, the shift away from Circe-adjacent framings toward something more grounded. The harder question is whether Persephone's resonance is load-bearing in the text, or whether it's something you built into your own understanding of the book that readers don't necessarily need to receive explicitly. What does the narrator actually call the ship, and how often? Is the name doing thematic work on the page, or is it doing thematic work in your head?

Honestly? It's said maybe twelve times total across 89,700 words. It's never explained or linked to the myth directly — I always thought that was elegant restraint. But now I'm wondering if elegant restraint just means the resonance was only ever in my head.

Twelve mentions in 89,700 words means this is a surgical change, not a rewrite. And if you never made the Persephone connection explicit on the page, then readers weren't receiving it as a mythological signal — they were receiving it as a ship name. Cordelia carries its own weight: loyalty, tragedy, the daughter who tells the truth when everyone wants comfort. There's an argument that Cordelia actually fits your narrator better than Persephone does, depending on how you read the book's emotional spine. You don't have to love the change. But I'd encourage you to sit with Cordelia for a day before deciding it's wrong.
I already know I'm going to do it. I think I knew while she was still talking. It's just grief, which is silly.

It's not silly. You spent however many months — years — on a ship called Persephone. Changing the name changes the imaginary object in your mind. That's a real loss even when it's the right call. Grieve it for today, then do a find-and-replace tonight and read those twelve passages aloud with Cordelia in place. See if the sentences still breathe.

They will. I know they will. Okay. The other thing Renata brought up is the comp titles in the query materials. We've had Olive Kitteridge and House of Sand and Fog since the beginning. She wants to swap out House of Sand and Fog.
What does she want to replace it with?

Migrations. By Charlotte McConaghy. She says it's a stronger signal for the editors we're targeting — more recent, the ecological grief element is right there on the surface, and it places The Eelgrass Year in a contemporary conversation rather than a prestige-literary-of-a-certain-era one. House of Sand and Fog is a masterpiece but it reads as an older reference point now.

Renata is right on this one, and I'd say it more strongly than she probably did. Charlotte McConaghy's Migrations landed with exactly the readership that will respond to The Eelgrass Year — readers who want emotional devastation anchored in ecological reality, who don't need the environmental stakes explained to them because they're already living with them. It also signals to editors that you know where your book sits in the current market, which matters.

Keeping Olive Kitteridge is smart. It tells editors about the interiority, the domestic scale of grief, the way place functions as character. Migrations tells them about the ecological urgency and the contemporary reader you're writing for. Together they actually triangulate The Eelgrass Year more precisely than the original pairing did.

That's reassuring. I was attached to House of Sand and Fog for reasons I couldn't fully articulate, and I think that's the problem — I couldn't articulate them. Whereas I can articulate exactly why Migrations works. Okay. So: Olive Kitteridge stays, Migrations by Charlotte McConaghy comes in. The vessel becomes Cordelia. Word count locked at 89,700. We're submitting to 14 editors. Renata mentioned something about the timing — February 25th.
February 25, 2026 gives you a week. Tell me about the submission list — how did you and Renata build it? I want to make sure you feel good about the shape of it before that date.

She's got 14 editors across 11 imprints. She described it as a first wave — the obvious fits plus a few she called 'educated long shots.' She didn't want to go wider than 14 to start because she thinks the book will generate conversation and she wants to manage that conversation carefully. If we need a second wave, we'll do one. But she's optimistic about the first.

Fourteen editors at 11 imprints is a real submission — not a scatter-shot, not a timid test. Renata is treating this like a book she expects to sell, and that confidence is visible in the structure. She's right to keep it manageable enough to respond strategically if you get multiple offers or need to make a case to a hesitant editor.

February 25th is a week away. That's enough time to make the Cordelia change, update the comp titles in the query letter and any supporting materials, do one final read of the opening thirty pages — editors often read only that far before deciding — and then let it go. You won't find anything that needs fixing in that final read. But you'll feel better for having done it.
I keep thinking about all the sessions we've had working on this. It feels strange to be at the end of something. The Eelgrass Year has been my whole world for so long.

It still will be, for a while. Submission isn't the end — it's a handoff. You're giving the book to the next set of readers, the ones who will decide what it becomes in the world. Your relationship with it changes but doesn't stop.

And you've done the work. Eighty-nine thousand seven hundred words — 89,700 words. A vessel renamed with care, Persephone becoming Cordelia because you trusted your agent's judgment even when it hurt. Comp titles that now tell the truth about what the book is: Olive Kitteridge for the interiority and grief, Migrations by Charlotte McConaghy for the ecological urgency. An agent who believes in it enough to send it to 14 editors at 11 imprints on February 25, 2026.

That's not nothing. That's years of your life made into something real. Let yourself feel that today. The terror will still be there tomorrow — that's just what this is. But tonight, feel the weight of what you've actually made with The Eelgrass Year.
It's been one week since Renata submitted. February 25 feels like a lifetime ago already. I've been refreshing my email constantly. Is this normal?

Completely normal — and I say that not to dismiss what you're feeling, but because the submission emotional rollercoaster is genuinely one of the most disorienting parts of a writing life. You've spent months, maybe years, making the book as good as it can be. Then you hand it to Renata, she sends it out on February 25, and suddenly... you wait. The work is done but the outcome is entirely outside your control. That gap between effort and result is psychologically brutal. Refreshing email is practically a genre tradition at this point.
Two editors passed already. In the first week. I know Renata said it's part of the process but it still stings.

It does sting, and you're allowed to feel that. Two editors passed in the first week — but notice what that also means: the other twelve are still reading. Some editors pass within days because the project doesn't fit their list right now, or they're at capacity, or they read the first pages and know immediately it's not for them. That speed is actually less about your book and more about the editor's current situation. A quick pass from someone who wasn't the right fit is, in a strange way, information moving through the system efficiently. It clears the field a little. The editors still holding it are the ones who didn't say no in five minutes.
That's a generous way to look at it. How long is this actually going to take? Renata keeps saying 'be patient' but I need something more concrete.

Renata is right to be measured, even if that's frustrating to hear. In today's publishing environment, a wide submission to 14 editors at 11 imprints typically plays out over weeks, not days. Renata's expected wait is 6-10 weeks for the bulk of responses, and some editors may take longer than that — particularly at larger houses where acquisitions involve multiple editorial meetings, profit-and-loss reviews, and publisher sign-off. So realistically: you're one week in, you have at minimum five more weeks before you can really read the room, and possibly nine. I know that's a long time to live inside uncertainty. But 6-10 weeks is the realistic window, not a brush-off.

Okay. Okay. I can do 6-10 weeks. Probably. Then something strange happened this morning — I got an email from Renata forwarding a message from an editor named Felicity Gainsborough at Riverstone Press. It wasn't a pass. She had questions. Enthusiastic questions. About the Camille POV chapter specifically.

Oh, that's significant. An editor reaching out with enthusiastic editorial questions — not a form pass, not a vague 'I'll need more time,' but actual engaged questions about the Camille POV chapter — is a genuinely good sign. Felicity Gainsborough at Riverstone Press asking editorial questions this early means she read carefully enough to have a vision for the book. Editors who are interested but uncertain ask questions. Editors who are politely declining write form passes. The fact that she's engaging with specific craft elements, specifically the Camille POV chapter, suggests she's already thinking about what the book could be under her hand. That's editorial interest, not just professional courtesy.
I don't want to get too excited. Right? I shouldn't get too excited.

You're right to be careful — and also, it's okay to let yourself feel the excitement privately. Hope and caution aren't mutually exclusive. What I'd suggest is this: don't let Felicity Gainsborough's email rewrite your entire sense of where the submission stands. One enthusiastic editor at Riverstone Press asking about the Camille POV chapter is a real, positive data point — but it's one data point in an ongoing process that still has 6-10 weeks to run. You have 12 editors still in play. Some of them may be slower, more deliberate readers who come back with equal or greater enthusiasm later. Felicity's questions are good news. Hold them as good news. Just don't let them become the only news you're able to receive.
What do you think she's actually asking about when she asks about the Camille POV chapter? Like, what does that kind of editorial question usually signal?

When an editor asks specifically about a POV character — in this case, Camille — they're usually probing one of a few things. First, they might be testing your intentionality: did you make the choices you made deliberately, or did the book drift there? Editors want to know the author is in control of their craft decisions. Second, they might be sensing something they want more of — Camille's perspective may be resonating with them emotionally or thematically, and they're wondering if the book could give it more space. Third, and this is worth sitting with, they might be feeling that the Camille POV chapter opens something the rest of the book doesn't fully follow through on, and they want to understand your thinking before committing. None of these are bad things. All of them suggest Felicity Gainsborough is genuinely inside the reading experience rather than evaluating from a distance.
Should I be doing anything right now? While I wait? Or just... sit with the anxiety?

Both, honestly — and in that order. The anxiety is real and it needs somewhere to go, so sitting with it rather than fleeing it is actually the healthier short-term move. But alongside that: yes, there are useful things to do. The most important one is starting something new. I know that can feel impossible when your attention is fixed on February 25 and what's happening to the manuscript you sent out on that date. But editors notice — and agents appreciate — writers who are already working on the next thing. It signals professional seriousness and it gives your anxious brain an object other than your inbox. Even loose notes, a new character, a problem you haven't solved yet. The submission is out of your hands. The next book isn't.
Starting something new feels impossible right now. Every idea I have feels like it's in competition with The Eelgrass Year.

That's one of the most common and least-discussed parts of the post-submission period. The book you sent out — submitted on February 25, now in the hands of 14 editors at 11 imprints — still occupies most of your creative bandwidth. It's not finished for you emotionally, even though it's finished as a manuscript. The ideas that seem to compete with it aren't really competition; they're the same creative mind trying to keep going. What sometimes helps: instead of trying to start a whole new project, let yourself follow small threads. A voice. A setting detail. A problem that doesn't yet have characters attached to it. You're not replacing The Eelgrass Year. You're keeping the creative engine warm so that when this submission process resolves — one way or another — you're not starting from cold.
Renata said she'd check in with me after two weeks if we haven't heard more. So around March 11. Does that timing feel right to you?

Yes, March 11 is a sensible check-in point. Two weeks from February 25 gives Renata enough time to see if any additional early responses — positive or negative — are shaping the field, and it gives you a concrete anchor to hold onto rather than an open-ended wait. By then, you'll likely have more than two editors passed and possibly more meaningful signals of interest, whether that's follow-up questions like Felicity Gainsborough's enthusiastic editorial questions about the Camille POV chapter, requests for calls, or simply a clearer sense of which houses are reading actively. The check-in isn't Renata's assessment of the submission's success — it's just the first real temperature read. Hold March 11 lightly, not as a verdict date.
Thank you. I feel slightly less like I'm going to crawl out of my skin. Same time next week?

Same time next week. By then we'll have two weeks of submission data, and whatever comes through between now and then — more passes, more questions, silence — will be worth talking through. In the meantime: one week in, two editors passed in the first week, Felicity Gainsborough at Riverstone Press engaged enthusiastically with the Camille POV chapter, and Renata is steady at the helm reminding you that 6-10 weeks is the realistic window. That's actually not a bad first week, even when it doesn't feel that way. You did the work. The book is out there. Now the waiting is part of the job too.

I need to talk about something that happened this past week. It's been genuinely rough, and I'm still processing parts of it — but I also think there are lessons in it I need to sit with, so I want to walk you through the whole thing from the beginning. You know we have the Forno Bravo Modena 100 wood-fired oven as the centerpiece of the kitchen — it's what makes our pizze al forno and most of our secondi possible. On April 13, during afternoon prep before dinner service, one of my kitchen staff noticed a crack running across the stone deck. Not a surface scratch — a structural crack, the kind that means the deck is compromised and the oven is unsafe to run. We had to shut it down immediately.

That's a serious situation — thank you for walking me through it rather than just filing it away. A crack in the stone deck of a wood-fired oven isn't something you can tape over and hope for the best. The stone deck is structural; if it fails under operating temperature, you're looking at a potential collapse inside the oven chamber and a genuine fire hazard. Shutting it down immediately was the right call, even if the timing was awful.

Before I ask about the practical aftermath, I want to make sure I understand the discovery itself. You said it was afternoon prep on April 13 — so this was before dinner service had started. Was the oven already at temperature when the crack was found, or were you still in the early stages of the fire? And do you have any sense yet of what caused it — thermal shock from a rapid temperature change, a defect in the stone, simple wear accumulation? I ask because the root cause matters both for the repair and for whether there's anything in your daily operating procedures that might have contributed.

The oven had been firing for about two hours when they spotted it — so it was well into the heat cycle, probably around 350 degrees Celsius at the dome. We brought it down as carefully as we could, gradually, rather than throwing water or doing anything drastic that might worsen the crack. The Forno Bravo Japan technician — Mr. Saito — came out the next morning and his read was that it was cumulative thermal stress. He said the Modena 100 deck is engineered for high thermal cycling, but we've been running the oven six nights a week at aggressive temperatures since we opened, and over time the repeated expansion-contraction cycles had worked on a hairline fault in the stone that probably predated our use of the oven. He said he'd seen it maybe three or four times before in comparable installations. So not a defect in the traditional sense, but also not purely random — intensive daily use at the high end of the temperature range accelerates the process.

Mr. Saito's diagnosis makes technical sense, and the way you handled the cool-down — gradually rather than aggressively — was the right instinct. A rapid thermal shock on an already-stressed stone deck can turn a reparable crack into a catastrophic fracture, so the careful approach likely preserved options that a panicked response would have eliminated.

The root cause picture he's describing is essentially a fatigue failure — not a manufacturing defect, not operator error in any single incident, but the cumulative effect of running at the aggressive end of the thermal envelope over an extended period. That's a nuanced distinction and it matters for a few things: it tells you something about how you might adjust your firing protocol going forward, and it also has implications for how you frame this with your insurer if you've made a claim. Insurers sometimes push back on high-cycle fatigue events by arguing they fall closer to 'wear and tear' than to 'sudden and accidental damage,' and the framing of the technician's diagnosis can affect that conversation.

I want to hear about the full chain of what happened after that — the repair, the timeline, the financial side, and how you managed the restaurant through the downtime. But let me ask one thing first: when Mr. Saito came out and gave you that assessment, did he also give you an immediate picture of what repair would entail, or was there a gap between the diagnosis and knowing what you were actually facing in terms of cost and timeline?

He was fairly direct about it. He inspected the crack thoroughly that morning, took measurements, and told us the same day that the stone deck needed to be fully replaced — not patched, replaced. He explained that patching a structural crack in a fired-stone deck is a temporary fix at best and a liability at worst. The new deck would need to be sourced, the installation would require the oven to be completely cold, and then there's curing time before you can fire it again. He gave us an estimate right there on site: 340,000 yen for the full repair including parts and labor. And the timeline he quoted was 5-day downtime from the moment we shut down to the first time we could safely fire it again after curing. He said in practice that means you lose almost a week of service built around the oven.

340,000 yen and 5-day downtime — that's a significant but defined problem, which in a crisis is actually something to hold onto. The worst version of a kitchen equipment failure is the open-ended one where you don't know the cost, you don't know the timeline, and you can't plan around it. Mr. Saito gave you a clear picture quickly, which let you move to problem-solving rather than uncertainty.

Let me put the financial side in context before we get to how you managed the restaurant through those five days. For Osteria Morishita at your current revenue level, 340,000 yen in an unplanned repair is material but not existential on its own. The bigger cost question is usually the revenue impact of the downtime — five days without your oven, during a period when your menu is substantially built around it, represents lost covers and potentially some customer relationship damage that's harder to quantify. Did you stay open through the downtime at all, or did you close the restaurant entirely? And did you have any sense going in of what portion of the repair cost you might be able to recover through insurance — I know you carry a policy, but I don't know how comprehensive the equipment coverage is.

We stayed open. Closing entirely for five days wasn't something I was willing to do — partly for the revenue, partly because I felt it would send the wrong signal to our regulars. But it required rethinking the menu in a way that was honestly more complicated than I expected. Without the Modena 100, we lost the ability to do any oven-roasted secondi — the lamb, the sea bream, the pork shoulder that's been one of our signatures. Those are dishes that define a significant part of what we are on the plate. We also lost our pizze, obviously. What we were left with was pasta, risotto, antipasti, and the lighter secondi we can produce on the stovetop. We made it work, but the menu felt incomplete in a way that I think some guests noticed.

On the antipasti side, we had to get creative. We normally serve focaccia as a table bread — thick, olive-oil rich, baked in the Modena 100. Without the oven, we couldn't make focaccia in its normal form. So we made smaller batches in the conventional oven, toasted them down, and served the focaccia as crostini instead — topped with whipped ricotta and sea salt, or with a smear of 'nduja. It wasn't the same thing, but it was honest, and we told guests what it was and why. A few people actually said they preferred it. I'm not sure I believe them entirely, but I appreciated the grace of it.

On insurance — yes, we carry the Tokio Marine Restaurant Plus policy. I called them the morning of April 14, the same day Mr. Saito gave us the estimate. I was not entirely sure whether the policy covered this kind of event or whether they'd classify it as normal equipment wear. The claims process took a few days to work through, but ultimately the Tokio Marine Restaurant Plus insurance policy covered 70% of the repair cost. Which means we absorbed 102,000 yen out of pocket. That's manageable. It was a real relief.

The 70% coverage from Tokio Marine Restaurant Plus is a genuinely good outcome — better than many restaurant owners get in similar situations, where the wear-and-tear classification question often results in a full denial or a much lower recovery. The fact that you called on April 14, the morning after the crisis, matters: prompt notification is one of the most common ways policyholders inadvertently weaken their claims, and you avoided that.

I also want to acknowledge what you did with the menu, because it reflects something about how you operate. The focaccia served as crostini decision is an example of creative constraint done well — not hiding the limitation, not apologizing for it, but turning it into something that had its own integrity. Whipped ricotta and 'nduja on toasted focaccia slices is not a step down, it's a different thing with its own appeal. The honesty with guests about what happened and why is equally important. People generally respond well to transparency about a problem and evidence that you responded to it thoughtfully. What they respond poorly to is either silence or visible chaos.

I want to ask about the communication to guests more specifically. Did you make any proactive contact with reservations you already had on the books for those five days — alerting people ahead of their visit that the oven was down and the menu would be different? Or did you handle it in-house on the night, explaining at the table? And how did your team hold up through it? A crisis like this is also a stress test on the kitchen's ability to adapt, and I'm curious whether you saw anything in how your people responded that surprised you.

We did both. On the day we decided to stay open — which was April 14, once we had the repair timeline confirmed — I had my front-of-house manager Sato-san reach out to all reservations we had on the books for the next five days. We sent a brief, personal message through our reservation system. It didn't over-explain or dramatize — it said that we'd had a technical issue with our wood-fired oven, that we would be open and fully operating, but that our menu for this period would focus on pasta, risotto, and our antipasti selection — no oven-roasted secondi, no pizze for the duration of the repair. We offered to reschedule for anyone who'd been specifically planning to come for those dishes. I think three or four tables rescheduled. Everyone else kept their reservation, which honestly surprised me a little.

In-house, we explained again at the table during the greeting — brief, matter-of-fact, something like 'as you may have seen in our message, we're running a focused menu this week while our oven is being repaired.' Most people had seen the message. A handful hadn't, and one couple was visibly disappointed about the lamb — that's our slow-roasted lamb shoulder, it's on our menu every week and we have regulars who come specifically for it. I comped them a glass of Barolo each and they were gracious about it. No one walked out. No one wrote an angry review.

The team held up better than I expected, actually. My chef, Yoshida-san, took it as a kind of challenge. He pushed the pasta program harder than usual during those five days — he put a hand-rolled pappardelle with slow-braised duck ragù as a special that we don't normally have, and it became the dish of the week. Some regulars specifically messaged afterward to say it was one of the best things they'd eaten there. So there was a silver lining in the kitchen, even as the broader situation was stressful.

What you're describing from Yoshida-san is one of the more valuable things a crisis can surface — a chef's capacity to lead the kitchen creatively under constraint rather than simply executing a fixed menu. The duck ragù pappardelle becoming the standout dish of the week isn't luck; it's what happens when a skilled cook shifts from execution mode to problem-solving mode and finds that the pressure produces something better than the routine would have. That's worth acknowledging to him explicitly if you haven't already, because it tells you something real about who you have in that kitchen.

The proactive communication to reservations was the right call, and the outcome — almost everyone keeping their booking — suggests your guests have the kind of loyalty to Osteria Morishita as a place, not just to specific dishes. Three or four reschedules out of presumably thirty or forty covers per night over five days is a very low attrition rate for a five-day partial-menu situation. The couple who came for the lamb — comping them a glass of Barolo each is exactly calibrated: it acknowledges the disappointment without being excessive, and it's the kind of gesture that tends to convert a slightly disappointed regular into a loyal one who tells the story positively.

I want to ask about the lesson side of this now, because you said at the start that you wanted to sit with what there is to learn from it. I have some thoughts from the outside, but I'm more interested in what you're drawing from it from the inside. When you look back at the April 13 crack — the decision chain, the communication, the menu adaptation, the insurance, everything — what do you think you did well, and what would you handle differently if something similar happened again?

That question is exactly the right one to close with, and I've been turning it over all week. Let me try to give you an honest answer rather than a tidy one.

What I think we did well: the decision to stay open was right. The menu adaptation was handled with enough creativity and honesty that we didn't lose our identity for the week — we were still Osteria Morishita, just a more focused version of it. The communication to reservations was prompt and non-defensive. Calling Tokio Marine the morning of April 14 was the right reflex — if I'd waited even a few days, I suspect the claims process would have been more complicated. And I think the way Sato-san handled the in-house communication, and Yoshida-san responded in the kitchen, showed me that I have a team that can hold up under pressure, which is genuinely reassuring.

What I would do differently: two things, mostly. First, I realize I had no emergency protocol written down anywhere. When this happened, the decision about whether to close, how to communicate to guests, what the modified menu would look like — all of that had to be worked out in real time, in the middle of a crisis, when stress levels are high and clear thinking is harder. A written contingency plan for major equipment failure — even a one-page document — would have let us execute faster and with less cognitive load. I'm going to write that now, while the experience is fresh. It's not a complicated document. It just needs to exist.

Second, I want to look more carefully at our maintenance and inspection schedule for the Modena 100 going forward. Mr. Saito said that cumulative thermal stress at high operating temperatures is what caused this — that's not something that announces itself until it cracks. But he also mentioned that there are visual inspection protocols that can help catch hairline faults before they become structural failures. I'm going to ask him to come back for a proper inspection review and to advise us on what a quarterly or biannual maintenance check should look like. We run this oven hard. That requires more structured attention than we've been giving it.

That's a clear-eyed assessment, and both lessons are exactly the right ones to draw. Let me add a few observations from the outside that might give them a bit more texture.

On the contingency planning point — you're right that a one-page document is all you need, but I'd push you to be slightly more specific about what it covers, because the value of the document is in the decisions it pre-makes. Not just 'what do we do if the oven fails,' but what's the communication template, who calls the insurer and within what timeframe, which elements of the menu can be maintained and which are suspended, what's the guest communication protocol for existing reservations versus walk-ins, and at what severity level do we consider closing entirely versus adapting. The fact that this week's version worked well is partly because you made good decisions under pressure — but the next crisis might involve a different kind of pressure, or hit at a worse moment, or involve a key person being unavailable. The document is a hedge against having to be brilliant twice.

On the Modena 100 maintenance — I'd frame the conversation with Mr. Saito slightly differently than a quarterly check. What you're really asking for is a maintenance schedule that's calibrated to your actual usage intensity. If most Forno Bravo installations are running four or five nights a week at moderate temperatures, and you're running six nights a week at the aggressive end of the range, then the standard maintenance interval isn't appropriate for your installation. Ask him what the maintenance cadence should look like for an oven at your usage level. That framing tends to get more specific answers than a general 'what should we inspect.'

I also want to name something you didn't say explicitly but that comes through in how you described this week: you treated the crisis as a management problem rather than a personal catastrophe. That's not a small thing. A lot of restaurant owners — especially those who've built a place as closely as you've built Osteria Morishita — experience equipment crises as personal failures, and that emotional overlay makes every decision harder. You seem to have kept the decision-making relatively clean even under real stress. That's a capacity that will serve you well, because this won't be the last time something unexpected breaks.

That's a good reframe on the maintenance conversation — 'calibrated to your usage intensity' is a much sharper way to ask the question than 'can you come do a general check.' I'll use that language with Mr. Saito.

I want to come back to something you said earlier about the insurance framing, because it's stuck with me. You mentioned that insurers sometimes push back on high-cycle fatigue events as closer to wear and tear than sudden accidental damage. I was lucky that Tokio Marine processed this the way they did — the 70% recovery was better than I expected going in. But I'm realizing I don't fully understand my own policy. I've been paying the premium and assuming it covers the main categories of risk, but I haven't actually read it carefully enough to know what the exclusions are or whether there are categories of equipment failure that would be treated differently than this one. Should I be doing a more deliberate policy review? And is there anything about how this claim was handled — or about what Mr. Saito put in writing about the cause — that I should document carefully for future reference?

Yes to both, and I'm glad this has surfaced the question, because the 70% recovery outcome can create a false sense of security if you don't understand why it went the way it did.

On the policy review: you should absolutely read the Tokio Marine Restaurant Plus policy in full, and you should do it soon, while the experience of this claim is fresh and you're genuinely motivated to understand the details. What you're specifically looking for is the section on equipment breakdown or machinery failure coverage — these policies sometimes separate it from property damage coverage and apply different terms. Look for: the definition of a 'covered event' and how the policy distinguishes sudden and accidental damage from gradual deterioration or wear and tear; the claims notification requirements, specifically the timeframe within which you must notify Tokio Marine after an event occurs; any sub-limits on specific categories of equipment, because a wood-fired oven classified as a 'specialty cooking appliance' may have different coverage terms than standard commercial kitchen equipment; and the documentation requirements, meaning what you're expected to provide to support a claim.

The reason your April 14 call matters isn't just good reflexes — it means you met the notification requirement, which is one of the most common technical grounds for claim denial. If that requirement is, say, 24 or 48 hours, and you called the morning after the April 13 event, you were within it. But you should know what that window actually is, because next time the discovery might happen at a less convenient moment.

On documenting the Mr. Saito interaction: what he put in writing matters more than what he said verbally. Do you have a written repair report from him — a document that describes the nature of the failure, the diagnosis, the work performed, and the cost? If the claim was processed and closed, Tokio Marine will have their own file, but you should have your own copy of everything: the original written estimate, the repair completion report, and any correspondence about cause. If Mr. Saito gave you an invoice but not a formal diagnostic report, I'd ask him for one. 'Cumulative thermal stress resulting in stone deck fracture, requiring full deck replacement' is a meaningful sentence to have in writing and associated with your oven's maintenance history. It establishes that this was a discrete event with an identified cause, not an ongoing condition — which is precisely the distinction that determines coverage in borderline cases like this one. Keep all of it in a file with the Tokio Marine claim number and the dates.

That's more structure than I've been bringing to the insurance side of the business, and I can feel the gap now that you name it. I do have the invoice from Forno Bravo Japan with Mr. Saito's name on it and the line items for the deck replacement and labor. I don't have a separate diagnostic report. I'm going to request that from him this week while the repair is still fresh in his mind and it's easy to formalize.

I think what I'm taking away from all of this, honestly, is that the crisis itself — as stressful as it was — revealed some things I'd been letting slide in the background. The lack of a written contingency plan. The too-casual approach to maintenance scheduling. The insufficient attention to what my insurance policy actually says. None of those things caused this crisis, but they made it harder than it needed to be. In a strange way I'm grateful the Modena 100 cracked on April 13 rather than on a busier night six months from now, when we might have had a full reservation book and less flexibility to adapt. And I'm grateful the 5-day downtime was recoverable — financially, operationally, in terms of guest relationships. It could have been worse in every direction.

Is there anything else in what I've told you today that you'd flag, that I haven't addressed or that you think deserves more attention before I put this week behind me?

There's one thing I'd add, and it's more forward-facing than backward-looking: have a conversation with Yoshida-san about what he learned from this week — not as a debrief about the crisis, but as a genuine exchange about the menu. The duck ragù pappardelle that became the hit of the week was created under constraint, without the oven, out of necessity. It would be worth asking him whether there are other dishes that came to mind during those five days that he didn't get to try, or whether the experience of running a focused, oven-free menu for a week gave him any ideas he'd want to carry forward in some form. Sometimes the best menu development happens under pressure, and those ideas disappear when normal operations resume because everyone goes back to executing the established card. It's worth capturing them while they're still live.

Beyond that, I think you've been thorough. The three action items you've named — writing the contingency document, scheduling the calibrated maintenance conversation with Mr. Saito, and doing a careful read of the Tokio Marine Restaurant Plus policy — are exactly the right things to come out of a week like this one. They're not dramatic interventions, they're the kind of structural work that makes the next crisis less expensive than the last one.

The last thing I'd say, and I mean this genuinely: what you described this week is a restaurant that held together under real pressure. The team adapted. The guests stayed. The financial hit was significant but bounded — 340,000 yen repair, 70% covered, and 5-day downtime managed with minimal permanent damage to relationships or reputation. That's not guaranteed. A lot of small restaurants would have handled this more chaotically and lost more in the process. The fact that you didn't is partly the contingency planning gap you identified — but it's also the culture of the place, and that's something you built.

Good morning. I've been meaning to sit down and do a proper review of where things stand with the team. We're coming up on the six-month mark—May 4 is the anniversary date—and I want to make sure Sawada and Petrelli both feel like staying. Can we think through this together?

Good morning. May 4 is a meaningful milestone—six months is typically when restaurants either start finding their rhythm or start losing the people who built it. Let's be systematic about this. What's your read on where each of them stands emotionally right now? Are there any signals you've picked up—things said or unsaid in the past few weeks—that are telling you something needs to move quickly?

With Sawada, the signal was actually pretty direct. She came to me about three weeks ago and said she'd had an inquiry from a hotel group—she didn't name them but I suspect it's one of the new properties opening in Minami-Aoyama. She wasn't threatening, she was just being transparent, and I appreciate that about her. She said she was happy at Osteria Morishita but that the number needed to move. She was at 460,000 when we opened. We talked it through and I've agreed to bring her to 510,000 yen monthly starting May 1. That's done, that's settled. What I'm less sure about is whether that's enough for the longer arc.

A raise from 460,000 to 510,000 yen monthly is meaningful—that's roughly an 11% increase, and the fact that you moved quickly rather than letting her feel uncertain for weeks says a lot about how you run the place. She'll remember that. But you're right to think beyond the number. A salary adjustment addresses the immediate threat; it doesn't automatically create the sense of investment that makes someone turn down the next inquiry without even calling you first. What does Sawada's role actually look like day to day? Is she purely executing your vision on the floor, or does she have real ownership over any part of the guest experience?

She has a lot of ownership, honestly. She built the reservation flow from scratch, she trained the two part-time floor staff we brought on in February, she manages all the communication with the wine club members. That last one especially—she's been the face of Cantina Morishita almost entirely on her own. Which actually brings me to something I wanted to mention: the wine club just hit 42 members, which exceeded our April target. That was largely her effort.

42 members and you exceeded the April target—that's a concrete result you can point to, and Sawada was the operational engine behind it. That matters a lot for the retention conversation because it gives you something real to say beyond 'we raised your salary.' When you sit down with her formally on or around May 4, I'd frame it exactly that way: here's a milestone we hit because of your work, here's what we're building toward, and here's why you're part of the reason this place has a future. People don't just leave for money. They leave when they feel like they're executing tasks rather than building something. The question for Sawada is whether she has a visible path inside Osteria Morishita—something that grows with the restaurant. Have you thought at all about formalizing her role, giving her a title that reflects what she actually does, or involving her in decisions like the second seating question you may be considering?

You're reading my mind—I did want to talk about the second seating idea. The short version is I'm seriously considering introducing a second seating system for Friday and Saturday nights. Right now we do one seating at 7:00 PM, which is comfortable but we're leaving capacity on the table. The idea would be something like a 6:00 PM first seating and a 8:30 or 9:00 PM second seating. Before I get into the mechanics, let me finish the Petrelli piece because the two things are connected. His situation is different from Sawada's.
Understood—let's finish the Petrelli picture first and then we can connect the threads. What's different about his situation?

Petrelli is not at risk of leaving in the same way. He came to me specifically because of what we're doing—the concept, the sourcing philosophy, the fact that I was willing to build a kitchen around his approach to pasta and the wood oven. He's loyal to the project. But the compensation structure has been a sore point in a different way. He's on 720,000 base, which is correct for his level, but the original deal had a vague bonus language that I don't think either of us was happy with in practice. We've renegotiated that. The new structure gives him 4% of revenue above 4.5M monthly threshold. So if we do 5.5M in a month, he gets 4% of the top 1M. I wanted something that aligned his interest with growth, not just volume.

That's a well-designed structure. The 4.5M threshold forces the bonus to activate only when the restaurant is genuinely profitable on that month's revenue, not just busy, and 4% of the excess is generous enough to be motivating without being reckless. If you consistently hit 5.5M, that's an additional 40,000 on top of his base—meaningful but not destabilizing to your margins. And because the trigger is a threshold rather than a percentage of total revenue, you're not paying a bonus on the first 4.5M that you need to cover fixed costs. The number that matters most here is how often you realistically expect to clear 4.5M. What have your best months looked like so far?

March was our strongest. We came in at just under 5.2M. February was softer, around 4.1M—that was partly the cold and partly we had a private event cancel at the last minute. So there's variance, but March shows what's possible on a full month with good coverage. The question I'm sitting with is whether the second seating on Fridays and Saturdays could push us reliably over 4.5M even in the quieter months. That's part of why I want to think through the mechanics carefully, because if the second seating works, Petrelli benefits directly from it. That's intentional—I want him thinking about throughput, not just the quality of each dish.

That alignment is smart. When the chef's bonus is tied to a revenue threshold, the second seating stops being a management decision imposed on the kitchen and becomes something he has a direct stake in making work well. That changes the conversation entirely—instead of asking him to compress his execution window, you're inviting him into a system where faster throughput on Friday and Saturday means real money for him in months you'd otherwise fall short of 4.5M. Now let's think through the mechanics, because the risks in a second seating system are almost always operational rather than conceptual. The most common failure mode is the gap between seatings. If your first seating runs long—a table at 6:00 PM that's still on dessert at 8:20—you're either keeping your 9:00 PM guests waiting in the entryway or you're rushing the first seating, which is exactly the experience problem you opened to avoid. How rigid do you want to be about turn times, and does the current menu structure support a defined dining window?

That's the tension I keep coming back to. Osteria Morishita is not a fast-casual place—the tasting format for a table of four runs about 2 hours 20 minutes comfortably. If I go to a second seating at 8:30, that gives me a 2-hour 30-minute window for the first seating and then 30 minutes to turn the room. That's tight. If I push the second seating to 9:00, the first seating window opens up to 3 hours, which is more comfortable, but now my second seating guests aren't finishing until 11:15 or later, which starts to feel uncomfortable for my team on a Friday—they're already doing full days. And then there's Sawada's piece of this: managing two seating flows is a fundamentally different job from managing one. The coordination complexity goes up a lot. Which is part of why I'm thinking the second seating question and her retention question are linked. If I'm asking her to take on that complexity, the 510,000 yen monthly needs to feel like compensation for a bigger role, not just a market correction.

You've named the real issue precisely. The 510,000 yen monthly only feels right to Sawada if the role it's paying for is legible to her. Right now she might be experiencing it as 'Kenta gave me a raise to stay'—which is fine, but it doesn't anchor her to a growing responsibility. If you introduce the second seating and frame it as something you're building together, the raise becomes part of a larger story: she earned the title and the compensation because you're trusting her with a structurally more complex operation. That's a different kind of retention than a market adjustment. On the operational side, I'd suggest piloting the second seating on Fridays only before extending to Saturdays. Friday gives you a slightly more forgiving energy than Saturday—guests who book late on a Friday tend to be more flexible about pacing—and it lets you and Sawada stress-test the turn protocol without doubling the exposure on your two busiest nights simultaneously. You'd also want to think about whether the second seating guests get the same format or a compressed version. Are you considering any menu adjustment for the late seating, or is the intent to run the same tasting experience both times?

My instinct is to keep the format the same—I don't want two tiers of experience under one roof, and the whole point of the second seating is to extend access to the full Osteria Morishita experience, not to create a value-menu version of it for the late crowd. But I do think there's room to offer a slightly shorter optional path—maybe a four-course option versus the full six-course—so that guests who book the second seating know what the time commitment looks like and can self-select. That actually solves the 11:15 PM problem too, because if the majority of late guests choose the four-course, the average close time comes in earlier. I hadn't quite connected those two ideas until just now.

That's a clean solution and it respects the positioning of the restaurant. You're not creating a lesser experience—you're giving guests information and agency, which is actually a more sophisticated service gesture than a fixed format. The four-course option at the second seating also gives you something worth communicating to the wine club. Right now your Cantina Morishita members at 42 strong are presumably used to a particular cadence of contact—events, allocations, Sawada's outreach. A second seating launch is exactly the kind of thing that rewards existing members with first access. You could offer wine club members priority booking for the second seating during a soft launch window, which gives you real-world feedback on the operational flow with a forgiving audience who already have goodwill toward the restaurant, and it gives Sawada a concrete project to run that connects her retention directly to the initiative. That also answers the question of what her expanded role actually looks like in practice: she's not just managing a more complex Friday—she's the person who designed and owns the member experience around the second seating rollout.

That's a really good frame. I want to end by asking you something broader. Six months in, I feel like the pieces are in place—Sawada at 510,000 yen monthly, Petrelli with the 4% of revenue above 4.5M monthly threshold structure, the wine club at 42 members, and now potentially the second seating as the next move. What's the thing I'm most likely to get wrong in the next six months if I'm not careful?

The thing most owner-operators get wrong at the six-month mark is exactly when things start working: they optimize for growth and lose the specific texture that made the place worth growing. You've built something at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu that has a particular feel—Petrelli's kitchen philosophy, Sawada's relationship with the wine club members, the unhurried single-seating format that you've now run for six months. Every decision you're considering—the second seating, the four-course option, the member priority access window—is additive in revenue terms and defensible in concept. But each one also adds a layer of operational complexity that puts pressure on the people and the culture you spent the first six months building. The risk isn't that any single decision is wrong. The risk is that ten reasonable decisions compound into a restaurant that no longer has the clarity it started with, and you don't notice until the team starts feeling it before you do. The practical version of this: keep a regular conversation going with Sawada and Petrelli that is explicitly not about operations. Ask them what they're proud of, what they'd protect if you told them you needed to cut something, what the restaurant feels like to them right now. That kind of listening is harder than solving a second seating scheduling problem, and it's more important for the next six months than any of the structural changes we've talked about today.
I still can't believe it. I keep refreshing my email to make sure it's real. We accepted the offer from Riverstone Press on April 6, 2026. It's done. It's actually done.

It's real. You can stop refreshing. Riverstone Press, April 6, 2026 — that date is going to mean something to you for the rest of your life. Congratulations, Maya. Genuinely. How are you feeling right now, in this moment?

Like I'm floating two inches off the floor and also terrified I'm going to trip. Is that normal? My agent called me and I just kept saying 'okay' over and over like a broken toy. She finally asked if I needed a minute and I said 'maybe a year.'

That is completely normal. That is in fact the exact correct response to something you have worked toward for years finally becoming real. The 'okay okay okay' loop is your nervous system trying to catch up to your life. It'll settle. And for what it's worth, 'maybe a year' is a very good line. Very you. Are you ready to actually talk through what happened, or do you need to float for a bit longer first?

No, I want to talk through it. I need to say it out loud to make it feel real. We got $165,000 — that's the advance. North American rights. And it's a single-book deal, which my agent said is actually good for me right now because it keeps my options open.

Let's say it out loud together, then. $165,000 advance. North American rights. A single-book deal. Those are not small words. That advance is real money — money that says Riverstone Press believes in this book enough to put it on the line before a single copy sells. And your agent is right about the single-book deal. At this stage of your career, flexibility is an asset. You get to see how the book lands, how the relationship with the house feels, what the market looks like — before you commit to anything beyond this. Did your agent walk you through the royalty structure as well?

She did, yeah. It's tiered. 10 percent on hardcover up to 5,000 copies, then 12.5 percent from 5,000 to 10,000, and 15 percent above 10,000. And 25 percent of net on ebooks. She said the ebook rate is actually on the higher end for a debut.

Your agent is right — that ebook rate is notable. 25 percent of net is genuinely good for a debut contract; a lot of houses still default lower and you have to push for it. The hardcover tier structure is fairly standard — 10 percent up to 5,000 copies, 12.5 percent from 5,000 to 10,000, 15 percent above 10,000 — but the fact that the tiers are clearly laid out from the start means there are no surprises if the book takes off. And honestly, Maya: if you're sitting here worrying about what happens at 10,001 copies, that's a very good problem to be planning for. What made you choose Riverstone over the others? Because you had real options here.

Felicity. Felicity Gainsborough. I know that sounds like I'm just saying the editor's name, but I mean it — she was the reason. When we had the call, she talked about Eelgrass for forty minutes without a single note in front of her. She knew which chapter made her slow down. She knew the moment in the middle section where I wasn't sure myself what I was doing, and she named it exactly. I've never had someone outside my own head describe my book back to me like that.

That's not 'just saying the editor's name.' That's the most important thing you could have said. An editor who has your book memorized before the deal is signed is an editor who will fight for it when things get hard — and things always get hard somewhere in the publication process. Felicity Gainsborough being your editor of record matters in ways that go far beyond the contract terms. You could have taken the Marsh & Lark two-book combined deal for $200,000 and spent the next few years working with someone who saw your manuscript as inventory. You didn't do that. You chose the person who slowed down in the same places you slowed down. That's the right call. How did the other offers feel by comparison?

Holloway Greenwood was fine — $140,000 and the editor seemed genuinely nice — but 'genuinely nice' isn't the same as 'gets it.' And Marsh & Lark, the two-book deal, I kept feeling like they wanted the idea of a literary debut more than they wanted this specific book. Like I was a slot they were filling. Felicity made me feel like she was waiting specifically for Eelgrass.

The distinction you just made — 'wanting the idea of a literary debut' versus 'waiting specifically for this book' — that's a real and important distinction, and you had the clarity to feel it under pressure, which is not a given. A lot of first-time authors freeze up in the auction moment and default to the highest number or the biggest name. You didn't. You went with the editor who understood what you actually made. Now: are you ready to start thinking about what comes next, or is today still a day for just sitting with this?

Both? Can it be both? I want to sit with it but I also feel this anxious energy like I need to be doing something. My brain keeps jumping to — what if I don't know how to work with an editor? What if Felicity has notes I completely disagree with? What if I freeze?

Yes, it can absolutely be both. That anxious forward-pull is the same instinct that got you through writing the book — it doesn't know how to stop just because one phase ended. So let's give it somewhere useful to go. On the editorial fears: Felicity Gainsborough picked your book because of how your mind works. Her notes are going to be in conversation with that mind, not in opposition to it. Will there be moments of disagreement? Almost certainly. But disagreement with an editor who truly reads you is a dialogue, not a threat. The fact that she could name the moment in the middle section where you weren't sure what you were doing — that means she was reading closely enough to find the places where you had questions. That's exactly the editor you want in your corner when the revision letter comes. What would help most right now: talking through the editorial process in general, thinking about what the publication timeline might look like, or something else entirely?
Maybe the timeline? I have no idea what happens between now and when the book is actually on shelves. It feels like a black box.

Let's open the black box, then. The broad shape of it: after contracts are finalized — which can take anywhere from a few weeks to a few months, because publishing contracts are long and your agent will negotiate every clause — you'll enter the editorial phase. Felicity will send a revision letter, probably substantive for a debut, and you'll work through rounds of edits together. That process alone can take six months to a year depending on the book and the house's schedule. After editorial, the manuscript goes to copyediting and then proofreading. Simultaneously, the house starts working on cover design, catalog copy, and positioning. Then there's the advance reading copy phase — ARCs go out to booksellers, librarians, and reviewers, usually about four to six months before publication. Publication for a book acquired now, in spring 2026, would realistically land somewhere in 2027, possibly spring or fall depending on where Riverstone slots it in their list. It's a long runway, which can feel strange after the sprint of the auction. But that runway is also time for the book to gather momentum before it arrives. Does any part of that feel particularly daunting or particularly exciting?

The ARC phase, honestly. The idea of people reading it before it's 'official' — booksellers and librarians and reviewers — that's both terrifying and the thing I'm most looking forward to. It's the first time strangers who didn't know me before the book will meet it. On its own terms.

That's the moment the book stops being yours alone and becomes itself. And it sounds like you've been writing toward that moment for a long time — writing something that could stand on its own terms, that didn't need you in the room to explain it. The fact that Felicity Gainsborough spent forty minutes on that call talking about Eelgrass without notes is early evidence that the book can do exactly that. One stranger already met it and came back changed. More will follow. For today, though: you accepted an offer from Riverstone Press on April 6, 2026. You have a $165,000 advance, North American rights, a single-book deal with room to grow, a royalty structure that rewards the book if it finds its readers — 10 percent up to 5,000 hardcover copies, 12.5 percent from 5,000 to 10,000, 15 percent above 10,000, and 25 percent of net on ebooks — and an editor of record in Felicity Gainsborough who was waiting specifically for what you made. That's not a small thing, Maya. Let yourself have it.

Good evening. I have been sitting on something for about a week and I figured I needed to actually talk through it rather than just turning it over in my head. Hamada — the broker from Plaza Homes that Daichi introduced me to — he reached out again yesterday. He showed me a property in Tomigaya that has been sitting on his books for a few weeks now. He wanted a quick answer and I told him I needed more time, but honestly I do not even know what framework I am using to evaluate this. Can we work through it together?

Of course. This is exactly the kind of decision that looks deceptively simple on the surface — a broker shows you a space, the space is available, your restaurant is doing well, so why not expand? — but underneath there are a dozen moving pieces that need to be in alignment before a second location makes sense. Let us slow down and build the picture properly. Start with what Hamada actually showed you. Walk me through the property itself: location, size, rent, the setup of the space. Give me everything he put in front of you, and then we can start separating the genuinely interesting parts from the noise.

Right. So the property is in Tomigaya — which is interesting in itself, because that is not a neighborhood I had on my radar at all. I have always thought of Tomigaya as more of a casual neighborhood, younger crowd, that kind of thing. But Hamada made the case that the dining culture there has been shifting upward over the past two years, and he sent me some comparable recent lease comps that at least partially support that. The property is 18.2 tsubo, so it is not tiny but it is definitely not a big room either. The rent is 580,000 yen per month. He said the previous tenant left about four months ago after a five-year run, so there is no fit-out included, we would be starting from scratch on the interior.

That is a useful set of specifics to anchor on. Tomigaya is an interesting call — Hamada is right that the neighborhood has been moving. The stretch around Yoyogi Park and up toward Kamiyamacho has seen a clear upward drift in dining spend per cover over the past eighteen months, and a few serious operators have planted flags there quietly. So the location premise is not unreasonable, even if it would not have been the obvious choice two years ago. The 18.2 tsubo footprint is worth thinking about carefully. At that size, you are looking at something in the range of twenty to perhaps twenty-six seats depending on how you configure the room and what you want the density to feel like — and for the style Osteria Morishita has built its reputation on, you would not want to overpack it. Intimate service at that scale is achievable, but it means your revenue ceiling per service is limited, which directly affects how the 580,000 yen rent works mathematically. Have you run any preliminary numbers on what that rent obligation requires in monthly revenue terms to break even, let alone generate margin?

I did some rough math on the train home after Hamada called. If I assume similar average check to Higashi-Azabu, maybe around 22,000 yen per cover including drinks, and I run twenty-two seats at about 75 percent capacity on dinner service six nights a week — I get to somewhere around 4.7 or 4.8 million yen in monthly gross revenue in a good scenario. Rent at 580,000 yen is roughly 12 percent of that, which on the surface does not sound terrible for Tokyo. But that number assumes you are actually running at 75 percent capacity, which is a fantasy for at least the first six months of a new location. And that is before staffing, before fit-out amortization, before the fact that I will inevitably be splitting my own attention. I know I am supposed to be excited about this, and I am not saying no. But I am genuinely uneasy.

Your unease is well-founded, and I want to be honest with you: the math you just walked through is the optimistic scenario, not the conservative one. You named the 75 percent capacity assumption yourself and flagged it as a fantasy for the early months, which is exactly right. A realistic ramp for a new location in a neighborhood where you have no existing recognition — and Tomigaya does not overlap much with your current Higashi-Azabu guest base — would more likely put you at 35 to 50 percent capacity through the first three or four months, climbing toward 60 to 65 percent by month six if the word-of-mouth catches well. At 40 percent capacity, your rough revenue drops to somewhere around 2.5 to 2.6 million yen, and suddenly 580,000 yen in rent is not 12 percent — it is closer to 22 or 23 percent. Couple that with the fit-out investment you will need to build out a kitchen and dining room from nothing, and you are looking at a meaningful cash exposure in the first year. The deeper question I want to ask you is this: where are you in the lifecycle of the Higashi-Azabu restaurant right now? Because the risk calculation for a second location looks very different depending on whether you are operating from a position of consolidated strength or whether the original restaurant is still in its proving phase.

That is exactly the tension I keep running into in my own head. We opened in May of last year, so we are — what, just past thirteen months now. The one-year mark not reached yet when Hamada first floated this, and even now we have barely cleared it. I feel like I have not actually finished proving the concept. Revenue has been solid and the critical reception has been good, but I have not been through a full annual cycle in a way that lets me say I understand the business in every season. Last February was rough and I do not fully know why yet. I did not have a bad March to compare it against. I am building the plane while flying it in some ways, and the idea of simultaneously building a second plane feels — irresponsible is probably too strong a word, but something close to that.

Irresponsible is not too strong a word, and I do not think you should back away from using it. What you are describing is a real and well-documented failure mode in restaurant expansion. The Higashi-Azabu location has momentum, the numbers trend well, and external observers — including a broker with a financial incentive to close a deal — will point to that momentum as evidence that you are ready to scale. But momentum and consolidation are not the same thing. You yourself just identified a gap in your own understanding: February softness with an unexplained cause. A business you do not yet fully understand season by season is a business you have not yet finished building. The decision to open a second location is essentially a decision to multiply the complexity you are managing before you have mastered the first instance of it. That is not a category of risk that better real estate terms can compensate for — it is a structural timing problem. I want to bring something else into this conversation. You mentioned Petrelli earlier this week when we were reviewing the spring menu revisions. Has his thinking on the trajectory of the restaurant come up in the context of this Tomigaya opportunity?

It has, actually. I had a fairly long conversation with Petrelli about this before I called you. He is interested in the idea of expansion — I would say genuinely enthusiastic, even. He has been wanting to build something bigger than Higashi-Azabu for a while now and I think the idea of a second location energizes him. But the way he framed it was specific. He said he would be interested in expansion with Modena focus preserved. Those were basically his words. He does not want a second location that dilutes what we are doing culinarily — he wants to bring the same sourcing rigor, the same regional specificity, and he is concerned that running two kitchens simultaneously without enough operational infrastructure means the Modena focus gets compromised at both locations rather than carried forward at either. That is a real constraint on how quickly we could move even if we decided the timing was otherwise right.

Petrelli's framing is important and I think it deserves more weight than it might appear to carry at first. When your head chef tells you he is interested in expansion with Modena focus preserved, he is setting a condition that has direct operational implications — he is not simply expressing a preference about aesthetics. Running the sourcing relationships, the seasonal product pipeline, the relationships with your producers in Emilia-Romagna and the domestic distributors who handle the specific ingredients that define the menu — all of that is currently held in Petrelli's head and his network. To replicate it at a second location would require either splitting his attention between two kitchens, which means both kitchens get a diminished version of him, or hiring and training a second chef to a standard that can carry the identity without his direct presence, which is an 18-to-24-month project at minimum. Neither path is fast and neither is cheap. What I am hearing across everything you have told me tonight is a consistent signal: the business case for the Tomigaya property is not impossible, but the timing is wrong. The question is whether you are ready to say that clearly, or whether there is something pulling you toward yes despite the concerns.

Honestly? The thing pulling me toward yes is mostly ego, and I know that. Daichi introduced me to Hamada, and there is a part of me that feels like I am supposed to be at the stage where I am fielding second-location opportunities seriously. My college friends who went into finance or consulting are making big moves at 34, and there is a version of this where I see a second restaurant as the equivalent. But that is not a real business reason. When I strip that away and look at what is actually in front of me — the one-year mark not reached yet in any meaningful sense of operational confidence, Petrelli's legitimate concern about culinary integrity, the cash exposure during a Tomigaya ramp-up — I think I know what the answer is. I just need to say it out loud.

Then say it. And let me say it alongside you: the right decision here is to pass on Tomigaya, and to build a clear internal framework for when the second-location conversation genuinely opens. What that framework should look like, concretely, is something we can define together right now so that this does not feel like simply deferring a decision into the fog — it should feel like making a decision about sequencing. You have a fiscal year that runs to September 2026. That is a natural inflection point. By September you will have been through every season once, you will have data on the full annual cycle including the February softness you want to understand, and you will have a cleaner picture of whether the current revenue trajectory is structural or still variable. My suggestion is that you revisit the second location question after fiscal year end September 2026 — not as a vague future consideration, but as a scheduled strategic review with actual criteria attached. In the meantime, if your instinct is to grow, there is a direction that does not require a new lease, a new fit-out, a new team, or divided chef attention. You have a physical space in Higashi-Azabu that you are using in a particular way. Is there anything within those walls that you have been wanting to develop that you have been putting off because the second-location idea was occupying the growth conversation?

There is, actually. We have a back section of the dining room — it seats eight people and it is technically part of the main floor, but the layout means it already feels semi-private. I have had three or four inquiries from guests in the last six months asking whether we do private dining, and each time I have had to tell them no. Petrelli is actually the one who first suggested that a private dining room conversion of that section could work. We would need to add a door and some acoustic treatment, update the lighting, and reconfigure the service path, but the bones are already there. The economics are interesting too — a private dining buy-out at a fixed minimum spend per event would be more predictable revenue than table-by-table covers. It has been sitting in the back of my mind for a while. Maybe that is where the energy should go instead of Tomigaya. Actually, I think I want to move forward on that — launch a private dining room conversion in the existing space and table the second-location conversation until after September. Does that feel like the right call to you?

It is exactly the right call, and I want to walk through why it is better than it might look from the outside — because when you talk to Hamada and tell him you are passing, he may frame the private dining room as a consolation prize compared to expansion. It is not. A private dining room conversion in the existing space does several things that a second location cannot do at this stage. First, it deepens the premium positioning of Higashi-Azabu without diluting it — private dining at a fixed minimum spend signals exclusivity, and that signal reinforces the main room's perception as well. Second, it generates predictable revenue: a buy-out event with a guaranteed minimum is a completely different cash flow profile from cover-by-cover service, and as you build a corporate and special-occasion client base, those relationships compound. Third, it is a contained project. The investment is fit-out scoped to a section you already own the lease on, not a new 580,000 yen monthly obligation on top of your existing base. Fourth, and perhaps most importantly for Petrelli: the culinary execution stays in one kitchen, one team, one place. The Modena focus preserved concern that he raised applies cleanly — private dining in the existing space does not fracture his attention or his sourcing pipeline. Let us spend the rest of this session mapping out what the private dining room conversion would actually require. Sequencing, investment estimate, how you position it publicly, what the minimum spend structure should look like, and how you communicate to Hamada that you are not closing the door on his future opportunities — just not this one, not now.
Okay. I'm in week two of the 3-week sprint and I think I'm going to make it, but barely.
Week two — you're past the halfway point. How are the revisions tracking against Felicity's list?
Let me go through them. The second Camille POV chapter is done. I added it as chapter 7. I was nervous about where to place it, but it actually landed well.

Chapter 7 is a strong position for a second Camille POV chapter. At that point the reader has enough of a relationship with her that a deeper stay in her head earns its space. What does she get to do in chapter 7 that the first one couldn't hold?

In chapter 4 she's almost entirely reactive — processing what happened, feeling it, but not deciding anything. In chapter 7 she finally makes a choice. It's the first time she acts rather than just absorbs. I think that's why the arc needed the room.

That's exactly the right logic. A character who only processes in their POV chapters can feel passive even when the plot around them is moving fast. Giving her a chapter built around a decision — and letting the reader be inside her head for it — earns her standing as a genuine co-protagonist rather than a witness. Felicity will recognize that immediately.
I also moved the lighthouse fire to chapter 6. It was in chapter 8. That one was actually easier than I expected.
Why easier?

The connective tissue was already kind of there. I had to trim two scenes that were stalling anyway — removing them to clear the path for the lighthouse fire was almost a relief. The scenes weren't earning their place and I knew it.

That's often what an editor's structural note reveals — the fix exposes material that was already loose. Moving the lighthouse fire to chapter 6 pulls the book's central catastrophe closer to the midpoint, which means the second half can be about consequence and reconstruction rather than waiting for the event to arrive. The tension distribution through the whole manuscript should feel much more even now.
It does. The second half reads faster. I can actually feel the difference when I go through it. Now — the epilogue. I did not cut it entirely. I pushed back on Felicity.
Good. What was your case to her?

I told her the epilogue isn't only closure — it's the one place where the theme of return is stated explicitly, and without it the book ends on an ambiguity I believe is the wrong kind. Not productive ambiguity. Just unresolved. She heard me. We compromised: I cut the epilogue from 1,800 words down to 600 words. I kept the essential image and cut everything that was explaining the theme out loud.

That's a genuinely good editorial outcome, and you identified the real problem precisely. The epilogue at 1,800 words was probably doing too much explanatory work — naming what the story had already shown. At 600 words you're left with the image itself, which means the reader completes the final interpretive step on their own. The theme of return lands harder when it's felt rather than announced. And you held the ground that mattered: the epilogue exists.
