I ran a word count this morning. 91,800 words total. It was around 93,200 before, so I've cut roughly 1,400 net even with the new chapter 7 material added.

91,800 words is a clean literary fiction length — substantial but not unwieldy. And a net reduction of about 1,400 words while adding a full new chapter means you cut more than the chapter weighs, which is exactly what a developmental revision should accomplish: build where the book needs depth, remove where it was coasting. That's difficult to do cleanly in two weeks. You should be proud of that ratio.
I'm exhausted. Genuinely worn down. But I keep reading pages and thinking — this is the version. This is the book I meant to write the whole time.

That feeling — exhausted and certain at the same time — is about as close as this work gets to confirmation that something went right. The 3-week sprint asked a real price: you made hard structural moves, you pushed back on a cut that would have cost the book something true, and you ended up with a manuscript that is leaner and more itself than what you started with. One more week. The book is already there.

Good evening. I want to use today's session to talk through something that's been on my mind for a while — the HR side of the business. We've grown a lot since we opened, and I'm realizing that the way I've been managing people is not going to scale. It was fine when it was just me, Petrelli, and two or three part-timers, but we're at a different place now. We're running 7 full-time staff and 4 part-time staff as of this month, and the informal way I've been handling things — verbal agreements, ad hoc scheduling, no written policies — is starting to create friction. I had a minor dispute with one of the part-timers last week about overtime expectations that made me realize I need to get serious about formalizing how we do things.

That's exactly the right moment to be having this conversation. The inflection point you're describing — where the informal systems that worked for a small team start generating friction as headcount grows — is predictable and well-documented. Moving from three or four people to a team of 7 full-time staff and 4 part-time staff is not just a headcount increase; it's a qualitative shift in the kind of management infrastructure you need. Verbal agreements and ad hoc arrangements work when everyone has direct daily contact with the owner and disputes can be resolved through conversation. At your current scale, you have people who may not interact with you every shift, who have different contract types, different expectations about their role, and different understandings of what was promised. The overtime dispute you mentioned is a symptom — what it's really telling you is that you don't have a shared reference document that both you and the part-timer can point to when there's ambiguity. Before we get into specifics, I want to understand the current state a bit more clearly. When you say you've been managing things informally — what does that actually look like in practice? Are there written employment contracts in place for anyone, or is it all verbal? And what's the split in role types across your full-time and part-time staff?

So the honest answer is that the full-time staff all have written employment contracts — I insisted on that from the start because I knew it was a legal requirement. But the contracts are pretty bare-bones. They cover the basics: position, compensation, hours, and the termination clause. They don't say anything about performance expectations, escalation procedures, or how disputes get handled. On the part-time side, it's even thinner — I have letters of agreement for three of the four, and the fourth person came on through a referral from Petrelli and we've been operating entirely on a handshake. On the social insurance side, this is where I've been cutting corners that I need to fix. My full-time staff were eligible for social insurance enrollment from the beginning, but I made it voluntary because I was worried about the employer contribution costs in our first year. Now that we're more stable, I know I need to mandate social insurance enrollment for all FT — that's a change I've been putting off and I need to stop putting it off.

I appreciate you being direct about that, because the social insurance situation is the most legally urgent item on your list and it's important to be clear-eyed about it. Under Japanese labor law, social insurance enrollment — specifically shakai hoken covering health insurance and pension — is mandatory for employees who work three-quarters or more of the hours of a standard full-time employee. If your full-time staff are working full-time hours, making social insurance enrollment voluntary is not compliant with the law; it means you've been operating outside the legal requirement, not simply taking a business risk. The good news is that this is a fixable problem, and addressing it proactively — mandating social insurance enrollment for all FT — is the right call. The less good news is that you may have a retroactive liability exposure depending on how long the non-enrollment has been in place, which is something you'll want a qualified professional to assess. Have you engaged a labor consultant or labor attorney at any point, or has this all been managed internally up to now? And do you have a sense of how many of your full-time staff are actually currently enrolled versus not enrolled?

That's exactly why I finally made the call to bring in a specialist. I've been in conversations with a labor consultant — his name is Mr. Endo — and we met for the first time in person two weeks ago. He came recommended by another restaurant owner I know in Roppongi. His read on the social insurance situation was consistent with what you're saying: technically I've been out of compliance, but there's a pathway to regularize it without major penalties if we move proactively and document our intent clearly. He said the key is to move now, before any employee raises a complaint or a labor inspection surfaces the gap. So we're treating that as urgent. The other big deliverable he's scoping out is an employee handbook — a proper written policy document that covers everything from conduct standards to leave policies to grievance procedures. His fee for drafting that document is 280,000 yen, which is not nothing, but he made a compelling case that it's far cheaper than the cost of even one labor dispute if we don't have documented policies in place.

The decision to bring in Mr. Endo is the right move, and his framing on the social insurance regularization — act now, document intent, move before a complaint surfaces — is standard professional advice in this situation. The proactive posture is genuinely important: the labor standards inspection system in Japan tends to treat employers who self-correct more favorably than those who are caught. On the 280,000 yen fee for the employee handbook drafting, I think his argument holds. A well-drafted employee handbook is not just a compliance document; it's an operational tool that reduces ambiguity in exactly the situations that generate conflict — overtime disputes like the one you had last week, questions about leave entitlement, conduct expectations, what happens if someone no-shows. The cost of one labor tribunal case, even a relatively minor one, typically starts well above that figure when you account for attorney fees, management time, and the distraction cost. So 280,000 yen for Mr. Endo's handbook drafting is reasonable if the quality is there. I do want to make sure you're getting a document that's tailored to your actual operation, though, not a generic template with your name inserted. Does Mr. Endo have restaurant-sector experience specifically, or is he a generalist labor consultant? And what's his timeline for delivering a draft?

He does have some restaurant and hospitality experience — he mentioned that about a third of his clients are in food service, which is partly why my contact in Roppongi recommended him specifically. His timeline is six weeks for a full draft, which he says will then go through a review cycle with me before he finalizes it. That feels reasonable. The other thing we discussed in the meeting is something I've been meaning to introduce anyway: formal performance reviews. I've never done structured reviews here — it's always been informal feedback in the moment, a catch-up conversation every few months, that kind of thing. Mr. Endo recommended we get something on the calendar as part of the formalization push. We've agreed that the first formal performance reviews are scheduled for July 1, which gives me about six weeks to prepare the framework and have enough of the handbook in place to reference during the reviews.

Scheduling the first formal performance reviews for July 1 is a good anchor. Six weeks is tight for both the handbook completion and the review framework design, so I'd encourage you to be realistic with Mr. Endo about sequencing — ideally the handbook draft would be substantially complete before July 1, because you want to be able to reference the written policies during the reviews, not just reference them in principle. If the timing slips and the handbook isn't ready, you may end up having conversations where you're telling employees what the policy is going to be rather than what it already is, which weakens the credibility of the process. On the review framework itself: what outcomes are you hoping the performance reviews will drive? The design of the framework depends a lot on what you're trying to accomplish. Are you primarily trying to document performance for legal defensibility — so that you have a paper trail if you need to take action on a problem employee? Are you trying to create a development conversation that helps people grow in their roles? Are you trying to link performance to compensation? Or some combination? Each of those goals pulls the framework design in different directions, and it's worth being explicit about which one is primary before you invest time building the forms and process.

All three, honestly, but if I had to rank them: development first, documentation second, compensation linkage third. I want people to feel like there's a real conversation happening about where they're going, not just a box-checking exercise. The documentation piece matters to me now because of everything Mr. Endo flagged about the legal exposure — I realize I've been operating without any formal record of who's performing well and who isn't, and if I ever have to manage someone out, that's a problem. On compensation, I don't want to tie the reviews to automatic pay increases because I can't guarantee the budget will support it, but I want people to know that strong performance is noticed and does factor into decisions over time. There's another dimension to the staffing conversation I wanted to raise today, and it's actually what's been keeping me up at night more than the HR process stuff. It's about Petrelli specifically. He's the core of the kitchen — everyone knows it, I know it, the regulars know it. And I've started thinking seriously about what happens if he decides to leave. He's been with me since day one, he's thirty-one years old, he has real talent, and at some point some larger group or another restaurant is going to make him an offer. I don't have a succession plan. That feels like a serious vulnerability.

You're right to be thinking about this, and the fact that it's keeping you up at night is appropriate — not because the scenario is imminent, but because key-person dependency in a small restaurant is a genuine operational and financial risk, and the time to build mitigation is before you need it, not after. Let me ask a few questions that will help clarify the actual risk exposure. First, how much of what Petrelli does is truly him and how much has been documented, systematized, or transferred to other kitchen staff? Specifically: are his core preparations written up in any form — recipes, prep sheets, sourcing notes — or does the knowledge live primarily in his head? Second, how is the current kitchen hierarchy structured beneath him? Is there someone on the full-time team who has meaningful exposure to his decision-making and could, under pressure, hold the kitchen together at some level of fidelity? And third — and this may be the most important question — what's your honest read on Petrelli's current satisfaction level? Is he engaged and feeling like he's growing at Osteria Morishita, or are there signs of restlessness that you might be reading around?

On the documentation question: we have recipes written up for most dishes, but they're Petrelli's documents — he made them, he controls them, and honestly some of the key techniques are described at a level of detail that assumes you already know what you're doing. A skilled cook could follow them, but not someone without the underlying technical competence. On the kitchen hierarchy: this is actually where I have some good news to report. One of the hires we made in the last three months is a cook named Nakajima, who joined us from a kaiseki restaurant in Kyoto and has been exceptional. He's quiet, precise, technically very strong. Petrelli has taken to him — which is not a small thing, because Petrelli is not easy to impress. Nakajima has started taking on more responsibility during prep and has been observing Petrelli's expediting during service. He doesn't have the creative leadership experience yet, but the technical foundation is there. If Petrelli leaves, I've actually started thinking about Nakajima as the internal candidate I'd build around. On Petrelli's satisfaction: he seems genuinely engaged right now. The Square Plus rollout energized him rather than frustrated him, and the January menu changes — the guinea fowl addition especially — felt like his decision, which I think matters for his ownership. But I'm aware that could change. He hasn't asked about a raise in four months, which could mean he's content or it could mean he's looking.

The picture you're painting is more manageable than many restaurants in your position. The fact that you've already identified a potential internal successor is significant — most owner-operators in a key-person dependency situation haven't thought that far ahead, and when the departure comes, they're reacting from zero. The succession plan is more concrete than you may realize: if Petrelli leaves, you've identified Nakajima as the successor, and by your own assessment he has the technical foundation to build on. The next question is whether you're being deliberate about accelerating that development now, while Petrelli is still in the kitchen, rather than hoping the transfer happens passively. That means thinking about what specific knowledge and capability Nakajima needs to acquire over the next twelve to eighteen months, and whether there are things you can put in place — more formal documentation of Petrelli's preparations, intentional exposure for Nakajima to sourcing decisions and menu planning conversations, perhaps eventually some kind of sous chef title that formalizes his position — that reduce the dependency gap regardless of what Petrelli does. On Petrelli himself: the four-month silence on compensation is worth addressing proactively rather than waiting for him to raise it. A well-structured performance review on July 1 — one of the first formal performance reviews you're now scheduling — is actually the right vehicle for that conversation. It lets you acknowledge his contribution formally, discuss his trajectory at the restaurant, and have an explicit conversation about compensation in a structured context rather than in a reactive one. If he's content, you'll know. If he's quietly looking, a thoughtful review process may be enough to recapture his engagement. Either way, you'll have better information than you do now. The combination of moves you're making — formalizing HR with Mr. Endo's help, mandating social insurance enrollment for all FT, drafting the handbook at 280,000 yen, building Nakajima's readiness deliberately — those aren't separate line items. They're a coherent maturation of the business. You're building the infrastructure for a restaurant that can run at this scale and beyond it, not just the one that existed when it was you and three people. That's the right investment to be making now.

Good afternoon. So I finally got through the last of the performance reviews this week. It's been a process — I've been sitting down with people one-on-one since mid-June, and I finished the last one yesterday. We have 7 FT staff on the regular payroll, not counting part-timers, so it was seven separate conversations, and some of them were more emotionally loaded than I expected going in. I feel like I'm still processing some of what came out of those meetings.

That sounds like a genuinely demanding stretch of work. Seven individual performance conversations, each of which requires you to be present, direct, and fair — and to hold the line on whatever compensation decisions you've already made — is a real management lift, especially when you're also running the restaurant every night. When you say some of the conversations were more emotionally loaded than you expected, can you be more specific about where the weight came from? Was it pushback on the evaluations, surprises that came up during the conversations, or something more interpersonal — people expressing things about the job or the environment that caught you off guard?

Mostly it was a combination of things. Some of it was straightforward — people were grateful, the mood was positive, and those were easy. But a few of the conversations surfaced things I hadn't fully anticipated. One of the front-of-house staff told me they'd been getting feelers from another restaurant in Roppongi — not that they were leaving, but they made sure I knew there were options on the table. And then Nakajima had a real heart-to-heart with me about where he sees his career going. That one lasted almost two hours. He's been my sous chef for coming up on two years now, and I knew he was going to want to talk substance, but the depth of it surprised me. He's thinking about his future in a way that goes well beyond just asking for a raise.

A two-hour conversation with your sous chef tells you something important right away — Nakajima didn't just want a number from you, he wanted to feel seen and to have a genuine discussion about where he fits in the long-term picture of Osteria Morishita. That's actually a healthy sign. The sous chefs who are quietly disengaged don't give you two hours; they give you fifteen minutes and a resignation letter three months later. The Roppongi feeler from the front-of-house staff is a different kind of signal — more transactional, designed to shift your leverage reading before the salary conversation. Both matter, but they call for different responses. Before we get into the specifics of what you decided on compensation, I want to ask: going into these reviews, had you already made your mind up on the numbers for each person, or were the conversations themselves meant to inform those decisions?

I had a set of preliminary numbers going in, but I kept them deliberately soft on a few people because I wanted to hear what they said first. Nakajima was the main case where I left myself room to move. He came in at 380,000 a month, and I'd told myself privately that I could go up to 430,000 if the conversation justified it. After that two-hour session, I actually ended up going higher than my own ceiling. I'm raising Nakajima to 440,000 yen. He made a case that I thought was genuinely well-reasoned — talked about his role in menu development, the fact that he's training the two new kitchen hires, and the market rate for sous chefs at comparable places in the city. I checked what he was saying against a few reference points and he wasn't wrong. So I decided to go above what I'd originally planned.

Raising Nakajima to 440,000 yen represents a 15.8 percent increase over his previous 380,000, which is substantial — well above what you'd call a standard merit adjustment. I want to ask you to examine the decision carefully, not to second-guess it, but because the reasoning matters for how you manage this going forward. You said he made a well-reasoned case about menu development, training, and market rates. Those are legitimate factors, and if his market rate argument held up when you checked it, then the raise may be entirely justified on the merits. But there's a dynamic worth naming: some of what you're paying for now is the implicit cost of retaining someone who just demonstrated they've thought carefully about their own value and know how to advocate for it. That's not a bad thing — but it means you need to think about what the next conversation with Nakajima looks like in twelve months, because the anchor has moved. What did the conversation about his longer-term trajectory look like? Was he asking for more than just the salary adjustment?

Yes, and that's actually the more interesting part of what we landed on. The salary piece was almost the easier conversation once we got into it. What Nakajima really wanted to talk about was his sense of ownership over the kitchen — not equity in the business, he didn't go that far, but more the feeling that he's building something here that's his, not just executing someone else's vision. So we talked about giving him more formal credit for the menu, having his name on the seasonal menus alongside mine, and about what the future structure of the kitchen could look like if we ever expand to a second location. But we also put something concrete on the table that I think addressed his sense of commitment from my side: we set up a Two-year retention bonus of 200,000 yen at 24 months. If he's still with us in two years, he gets 200,000 yen on top of whatever he's earning at that point. It's not a huge number in absolute terms, but I think the signal it sends is important — it says I'm planning for him to be here.

The two-year retention bonus of 200,000 yen at 24 months is a smart structural choice, and I think you read Nakajima's underlying need correctly. He's not looking to be bought; he's looking for evidence that you see a future with him in it. A retention bonus denominated in time — rather than performance milestones, which can feel subjective — creates a simple, legible commitment on both sides. He knows exactly what he's holding and what it requires of him. A few things worth thinking through as you build this out: Is the bonus documented in writing, as an amendment to his employment contract or at minimum a signed letter? In Japan, verbal compensation commitments between an employer and employee can become ambiguous quickly if circumstances change — a new accountant, a restructuring conversation, or even just a gap in institutional memory two years from now. You want the 200,000 yen at 24 months to be unambiguous. Also, how are you thinking about the tax treatment? For Nakajima, that payment will be treated as ordinary income in the year it's paid, which will take a meaningful bite. Some employers gross up retention bonuses to make the net amount hit closer to the intended figure. Is that in scope for you, or is 200,000 yen the gross number?

Good points on the documentation — I'm going to have my accountant draft that as a formal amendment. I hadn't thought about the gross-up question and I should probably run that by him too. But let me shift to the other big outcome from this review cycle, which is the Petrelli conversation, because that one was its own complicated thing. As you know, Petrelli has been our head chef since we opened, and his original contract was running toward its end. He's been at 720,000 a month, which has always been by far our largest single payroll line. The contract question had been sitting in the background for a while — I'd been deliberately not forcing it to a head too early because I didn't want him feeling like I was pressuring him, but I also knew we needed to resolve it before he started getting other approaches. So I timed the performance review to also serve as the formal contract renewal conversation.

Combining the performance review with the contract renewal negotiation is a reasonable tactical choice, though it does compress a lot of stakes into a single conversation. You're simultaneously evaluating his past year, setting expectations for the next period, and closing a deal — those can pull in different directions emotionally for both parties. How did Petrelli receive the framing? Did he come into the meeting understanding it was also going to be a contract conversation, or did that emerge during the discussion? And at the level he's at — 720,000 a month is senior talent by any measure for a restaurant of your size — what was your read going in on how motivated he was to stay versus how much leverage you were each holding? The outcome of a contract renewal negotiation often hinges more on who needs the deal more than on the specifics of what's on the table.

He knew going in. I'd told him two weeks prior that the review meeting would include the contract discussion, so he had time to think about it. And honestly, I think that was the right call — it gave him room to process rather than putting him on the spot. My read on the leverage situation was that it was roughly balanced, maybe slightly in his favor. Petrelli is the culinary identity of this restaurant in a real sense. Guests come back because of his food, the Michelin inspector who visited last year talked specifically about the consistency of the kitchen. Replacing him at that level would be a minimum six-month disruption and would cost me significantly more than whatever premium I'd pay to keep him. At the same time, he's built something at Osteria Morishita that he's proud of, and he knows that moving to a new kitchen resets a lot of what he's spent two years constructing here. So neither of us had a strong reason to walk. What I needed was to land on terms that reflected that balance. In the end, Petrelli signed a two-year extension, taking his contract through to October 2027. And I moved his compensation — to put it plainly: Petrelli new monthly base: 780,000 yen. That's how I'm going to be logging it in the payroll records going forward.

So to summarize the Petrelli outcome: he signed a two-year extension to October 2027, and his new monthly base is 780,000 yen — up 60,000 from the previous 720,000, which is an 8.3 percent increase. That's a much more conservative proportional adjustment than what you gave Nakajima, which is probably the right order of magnitude given the different positions and starting bases. I want to raise one sustainability question directly. Between Nakajima's raise to 440,000 yen and Petrelli's new monthly base of 780,000 yen, those two lines alone represent over 1.2 million yen per month in payroll just for your kitchen leadership, before you count the rest of the 7 FT staff and your part-timers. That's a significant fixed cost base. At the revenue levels Osteria Morishita has been generating, what does the math look like on that ratio? I'm thinking specifically about whether you stress-tested this against a slower-than-expected quarter — not because I expect things to go wrong, but because you've now locked in these cost commitments for two years in both cases, and the buffer you have matters.

That's the question I've been sitting with since Tuesday, and I don't want to pretend I have a clean answer. What I'll say is that when I modeled this out — and I did actually run the numbers before going into these conversations, not after — I concluded that the revenue we've been generating in the stronger months covers this comfortably, and that even in a January-type trough, we're not in structural distress. The Petrelli commitment worries me more than the Nakajima one, purely because of the absolute size of that number over 24 months. But here's the thing: we also have Yui Tachibana on the front-of-house side, and her situation needed addressing too. She's been with us since almost the beginning as a part-timer and she's genuinely excellent — guests know her by name, she handles private dining with almost no supervision. Her previous hourly rate had been sitting in a range that I felt was too low given what she actually contributes. So as part of this review cycle I raised Yui Tachibana to 1,500 yen per hour. That one doesn't move the needle much in absolute terms, but it was the right thing to do, and I think it matters for how she feels about this place. So across the board, I feel like these decisions are defensible — but you're right that I need to keep watching the revenue side with real discipline now, because the cost structure has stepped up and there isn't much margin for a prolonged soft period.

Good afternoon. I have a lot to catch you up on today. The biggest thing is the private room project — Sala Modena construction underway, on schedule, which is a genuine relief because I was worried about timeline slippage after the delays we had with the permit. The contractor confirmed this morning that we're still on track for an early September completion, which gives us just enough lead time to do a proper soft launch before we push into full marketing mode. I've been losing sleep over this project for the better part of three months, so being able to say 'on schedule' feels significant.

That's genuinely good news, Kenta, and I understand why it's a relief — when you're running a capital project inside an operating restaurant, schedule risk is always carrying a multiplier effect on stress. A permit delay that pushes a September completion into October doesn't just cost you the room revenue for those weeks; it destabilizes every piece of downstream planning you've built around that date: marketing timelines, pre-booking commitments, staffing arrangements, the whole stack. So staying on schedule matters more than just the timeline itself. Let's dig in. What does the current state of construction look like inside Sala Modena — where are you physically in the build-out, and what are the remaining milestones between now and the contractor's completion date?

Physically, they've finished the structural work and the acoustic paneling is mostly in. The lighting rig is getting installed this week — we went with the indirect warm system we discussed a few months ago, the one that gives you that almost candlelit quality without actually using candles, which matters for the insurance side of things. The biggest outstanding items are the custom millwork for the wine display cabinet and the upholstered wall sections in the far corners, which are being fabricated off-site and scheduled to arrive in the first week of August. If those come in on time, the contractor thinks we can have a walk-through punch list done by mid-August and hand over to us by August 28th at the latest. That gives us roughly a week for us to do our own finishing and staging before we'd be ready to host the first event. I've been thinking about doing a friends-and-family soft launch in the very first week of September, just to stress-test the room before we open it to paying guests.

The August 28th handover with a first-week-of-September soft launch is a tight but workable sequence, assuming the millwork arrives on schedule. The off-site fabrication items are your single biggest scheduling risk right now — custom millwork and upholstered pieces from fabricators are exactly the kind of items that slip by a week without much warning, and you're operating without a lot of buffer. I'd want to know what the fabricator's current confirmed delivery date is in writing, and whether the contractor has a contingency plan if those pieces arrive late. On the soft launch concept: a friends-and-family event in early September is the right instinct. It lets you discover operational friction in the room — how the service flow works between the kitchen and the private space, whether the acoustics feel right at a full table of twelve or fourteen, whether the lighting is actually doing what you want it to do in practice versus what it looked like in the mock-up — before any of that friction is visible to a paying client. Who are you thinking you'd invite, and what format would you run it as?

I'd probably do two seatings over two nights — one for industry people and a few journalist contacts, one for close personal relationships, long-standing regulars, that sort of thing. But here's where the conversation gets interesting, because the pre-booking situation has actually moved faster than I anticipated. We started very quietly putting the word out about three weeks ago — not a formal launch, just a few conversations, some targeted outreach to a short list of contacts — and we already have 6 private events booked for September. Two of those are corporate, four are private celebrations, one of which is a fiftieth birthday dinner for twenty people that the guest's daughter organized and which I think will be a beautiful event. The September calendar is filling up faster than I expected, and I'm a little nervous that the soft launch window is getting squeezed.

Six private events booked for September before you've even done a formal launch is a strong early signal — it tells you that the concept is landing with the people you reached out to, and that there's genuine pent-up demand for a dedicated private dining option in Higashi-Azabu at this positioning. The fiftieth birthday dinner for twenty is particularly valuable as an early booking because large celebration events tend to be high-spend, high-engagement evenings that generate word-of-mouth in exactly the social circles you want Sala Modena to become associated with. The squeeze on the soft launch window is real, though. If you have 6 private events for September and the handover is August 28th, you have at most a few days of internal use before you're running live events. That changes the risk calculus significantly. The soft launch was supposed to be your error-absorbing buffer. Now that buffer is essentially gone. How are you thinking about handling that? You might need to treat the first one or two paying events themselves as the operational stress test, which means your team needs to be exceptionally well-rehearsed before day one — no learning on the job with a paying guest in the room.

You're right, and that's something I've been wrestling with. My current thinking is that we do one very tight internal dinner — just me, Petrelli, and the full front-of-house team — as a full service rehearsal in the last few days of August. We run it exactly like a real event: full menu, full wine service, timed sequences, the whole thing. Petrelli can be a demanding critic when the shoe is on the other foot, which is actually useful. But I want to tell you about the most significant booking we have, because it's the one that affects my thinking the most. Marubeni booked Sala Modena for October 14 for a 14-person dinner. Former employer. The person who made the booking is a senior director in the corporate strategy division — not someone I worked directly with, but someone who knows my background. This is not a booking I can have any hiccups on.

The Marubeni booking on October 14 for a 14-person dinner is significant on multiple levels and I want to make sure we're thinking about it carefully. First, the obvious one: Marubeni is a major trading company, and a 14-person dinner from the corporate strategy division is almost certainly an entertainment booking — clients, or internal leadership, or both — which means the people in that room are evaluating Sala Modena as a venue they might use again, recommend to peers at other major companies, and potentially build a relationship with. One flawless dinner on October 14 could generate a pipeline of corporate bookings that has compounding value over years. Second, and more personally: the fact that they know your background and chose to book with you anyway is a statement. They're not just buying a dinner; they're signaling something about your transition from Marubeni employee to restaurateur, and that signal goes both ways. How did the booking come through — did they reach out to you, or did you approach that contact proactively?

They reached out. That was the part that genuinely surprised me. I had put Osteria Morishita on their preferred vendor list for corporate dining about a year ago, and it had been quiet on that front. Then about ten days ago I got a message from an assistant to the director saying they were interested in the private room for a fall dinner. I hadn't specifically promoted Sala Modena to Marubeni directly — it was more a case of the word having traveled through some connection I'm not fully aware of. But I was very direct in the response about pricing and the scope of what we offer, because I don't want any ambiguity going into a booking like this. Our pricing for Sala Modena is 18,000 yen per person minimum plus a venue fee of 50,000 yen. I was clear about that up front, and they confirmed without pushback. At 14 people, that's already a meaningful evening at minimum spend, and my expectation is that the actual spend will run considerably above the minimum once you factor in the full dinner format and wine.

The fact that they confirmed the pricing without pushback is itself informative — it tells you that a senior director in corporate strategy at Marubeni is calibrated to fine dining entertainment at that spend level, and that your pricing is not an obstacle for corporate clients in that tier. Let's look at the arithmetic. At 14 people with a 18,000 yen per person minimum plus the venue fee of 50,000 yen, you're looking at a guaranteed floor of 302,000 yen for the evening before a single bottle of wine or supplemental course is ordered. In practice, for a corporate strategy group entertaining in a private room, the expectation is that they'll take a wine pairing and likely upgrade the menu, which puts the realistic ceiling meaningfully higher. Our wine pairings start at 6,500 yen per person, so even if every guest takes the entry-level pairing, that's another 91,000 yen on top of the minimum. The more important question is how you're going to orchestrate the experience itself on October 14 to make sure it converts that group into a repeat corporate account. Have you thought about what specifically you want to do to distinguish that evening — the menu direction, the level of personal attention from you versus Petrelli, whether you introduce yourself at any point during the service?

I've actually started thinking about the menu already. For a group like this I want to do something that's classic in its structure but where every element is clearly a deliberate choice — not a safe menu, but a confident one. Petrelli and I have been discussing a twelve-course progression where the first half leans into the autumn vegetables and game birds that are at peak in mid-October, and the second half builds toward a dry-aged beef course that we're hoping to source from a producer in Tochigi that we've been in conversation with. The wine question is one I want to think through carefully, because a Marubeni group at that level will have people in the room who know wine seriously. I don't want to run a wine pairing that feels like the standard house progression. I'm considering bringing in a sommelier consultant for that specific event — someone outside the regular team who has corporate entertainment experience and can handle a more bespoke conversation with the guests at the table. On the personal touch front: I'll greet them when they arrive, I'll visit the room at the mid-point and again near the end, but I won't hover. That's a dinner where my visibility should feel effortless, not managed.

But I want to broaden the conversation a bit, because the Marubeni booking is one event — I need a marketing approach for Sala Modena that builds a pipeline of bookings like this on a more systematic basis. Right now the 6 private events for September happened through word of mouth and my direct network. That's not a scalable source. I have a few ideas I've been turning over. One is a very targeted direct outreach to HR directors and executive assistant networks at large Tokyo corporations, because they are the people who actually make these reservations, not the executives themselves. The second is creating a Sala Modena-specific page on the website with much more detailed information about the room, the capacity, and the pricing structure — right now the main site just has a brief mention that a private room is available. And the third is thinking about whether to do any press, specifically targeting the corporate entertaining beat in publications that senior businesspeople in Tokyo actually read. What's your read on priority order for those three?

All three are legitimate channels, but the right sequencing depends on what stage of the pipeline problem you're actually trying to solve. Let me give you my read. The Sala Modena website page should be first and it should be done before anything else, because every other marketing action you take — whether it's direct outreach or press coverage — will eventually send someone to the internet to learn more, and right now that search ends in a brief mention on the main site. That's a conversion problem. When a corporate EA or a senior director's assistant is evaluating venues, they need to see capacity, room dimensions, the minimum pricing structure — the 18,000 yen per person minimum and the venue fee of 50,000 yen — photo assets that reflect the room's actual quality, and ideally a way to initiate a booking inquiry directly. The page doesn't need to be elaborate; it needs to be complete and confident. Two to three weeks of work at most, and it's the foundation everything else sits on. The direct outreach to HR directors and EA networks is your highest-leverage activity once the web page is live, because you're reaching the decision-makers, not the figureheads. Executive assistants who manage large entertainment budgets are perpetually looking for a small set of venues they can recommend reliably — places where they know the pricing is consistent, the experience is predictable, and the room is actually available when they need it. If you can get into that mental shortlist for even five or six EAs at major corporations, the compounding value is significant. I'd prioritize this over press, because press is slow, the audience is diffuse, and the conversion path from a reader of a business publication to a Sala Modena booking is long and indirect. Press is worth doing, but I'd treat it as the third play, not the second, and I'd be selective about the publications — you want something read by the people who actually authorize entertainment spend in Tokyo, not something that reaches the general food media audience. The practical sequencing I'd suggest: get the website page built and live in the next three to four weeks while construction is still ongoing, use the September soft bookings and the operational experience from those events to refine your pitch materials and any printed leave-behind you might use, then start direct outreach in earnest in October — ideally in the window just after the Marubeni dinner on October 14, because that event will give you a real reference point and potentially a reference contact. Press outreach can follow in November, positioned around the story of Sala Modena's first full quarter. Does that sequencing make sense to you, or are there constraints on the website work that make it harder to prioritize?

I've been sitting here this morning with a cup of coffee, looking out at Higashi-Azabu, and it hit me that tomorrow is August 1st. It's been just over a year since we opened, and I don't entirely know what to make of that. A year ago I was running on adrenaline and terror. Now I'm just — here. Running a restaurant. Which still feels strange to say. I wanted to talk through where things stand and what comes next, if you're up for that kind of conversation.

I'm absolutely up for it. In fact, I think this kind of reflective pause is exactly the right thing to do at the one-year mark — not just to take stock, but to make sure the decisions you make in year two are informed by what year one actually taught you, rather than what you assumed it would teach you before you opened.

So let's do this properly. Tell me where your head is this morning. Not the business metrics yet — we'll get to those — but emotionally, personally. When you look back to the beginning of this whole journey, what feels different about where you are now versus where you expected to be?

Honestly? The thing that surprises me most is how far back the real beginning feels. When I think about the timeline now, it's astonishing. I first came to you in March 2025 — just an idea, really, sitting at a desk at Marubeni wondering if I was going to spend the rest of my career in the food trading business or actually do something I cared about. And now here I am, running Osteria Morishita at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, and we have regulars who come twice a month, and Petrelli sent me a message last week saying he'd heard good things from people who visited in June. From idea to thriving restaurant in ~17 months. That's not a long time, actually. When I say it out loud it sounds fast. But it also felt like forever while it was happening.

~17 months is fast. I want to sit with that for a moment, because I think it's easy to normalize in hindsight. You resigned from Marubeni, did the staging work in Italian kitchens around Tokyo, found Sawada-san through those kitchen connections, found the space in Higashi-Azabu, navigated the fit-out, built the menu with Sawada-san from scratch, opened, and then survived the first year — all within seventeen months of the initial idea. That's not a small thing.

And Petrelli's message matters. Marco Petrelli's opinion carries weight in the Italian food community in Tokyo, and word-of-mouth from someone at his level is the kind of signal that takes time to generate and can't be manufactured. What specifically did he say?

But before we go further — you said 'thriving.' Is that really how you'd describe it? Or is that the word that came out because it felt right this morning? I want to understand what you mean by it, because thriving can mean a lot of things.

Fair question. Thriving might be slightly generous on the emotional side, but I think it's defensible on the facts. The Tabelog rating is now 3.78 with 91 reviews, which Nakajima-san said when we hit 3.7 would effectively make us self-sustaining on walk-in and organic discovery traffic — and she was right, we've seen exactly that. The cumulative loss we'd been carrying since opening zeroed out in July 2026. We're now operating profitably, not dramatically, but genuinely. When I say thriving I mean we've crossed the threshold from 'will this survive' to 'this is a real restaurant.' That's what I mean.

Then thriving is the right word. Those are not soft metrics — they're structural. Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I want to make sure you feel the weight of it.

A Tabelog rating of 3.78 with 91 reviews puts you in a tier that most restaurants in Tokyo never reach. At that level, the platform does real work for you — discovery, credibility, the social proof that makes a stranger decide to book rather than scroll past. Nakajima-san was right to identify 3.7 as the threshold, and the fact that you're meaningfully above it with a growing review count suggests the trajectory is still positive, not plateauing.

And the cumulative loss zeroing out in July 2026 is a genuine milestone. A lot of restaurants carry pre-profitability losses for two, three years. You cleared yours in roughly twelve months of operation. That reflects well on the cost discipline you and Sawada-san have maintained, on Nakajima-san's financial oversight, and honestly on the pricing decisions you made early on — the ones that felt uncomfortable at the time but were necessary for the margins to work.

How is Sawada-san doing? A year in, with the pressures of a two-seating kitchen at this pace — what's his state of mind?

Sawada-san is tired, but it's a good kind of tired, I think. He told me last month that this is the first kitchen where he's felt ownership over the food in a way that didn't feel like theater. That mattered to me to hear. He and I have settled into something I'd describe as a genuine working partnership — he pushes back on me when I get ideas that aren't grounded in what we can actually execute well, and I hold the line on sourcing standards when there's pressure to cut costs on ingredients. We've had real disagreements. But we haven't had a single one that felt like it damaged the relationship, which I think is something.

Mariko — who I was honestly most nervous about at the beginning — has become the warmest thing about the dining room. Guests ask for her specifically. The way she reads a table, when to be present and when to disappear, has gotten remarkably good. I take zero credit for that. That's entirely her.

Tanabe-san has been the quiet anchor. He comes in twice a week for prep, and his vegetable knowledge is extraordinary. Some of what's ended up on the menu started because Tanabe-san brought something in and said 'try this.' Yamamoto — our weekend sommelier — built the wine program into something I'm proud of. We started with 22 labels and we're at 38 now, and he's curated it in a way that actually reflects the food instead of just being impressive for its own sake.

What you're describing is a functioning team with real culture, which is rarer than the metrics and harder to build. Let me name what I'm hearing in each of those relationships, because I think it matters for how you think about year two.

Sawada-san describing the kitchen as a place where he feels ownership without theater — that's the chef equivalent of saying the concept is real and not a performance. You found someone whose values align with yours, and the year of actual operation has deepened that, not eroded it. That's a fragile thing in restaurant partnerships and you should treat it accordingly.

Mariko growing into the dining room the way she has is a kind of success you can't train for. You can hire someone who has the instincts, and then you can give them the room and the trust to develop them. The fact that guests ask for her specifically tells you she's become part of the identity of the restaurant, not just a member of staff.

And Yamamoto building the wine program from 22 to 38 labels in a way that serves the food rather than impresses independently — that's editorial discipline. A lot of sommeliers build lists to demonstrate their knowledge. What you're describing is someone who subordinated their ego to the concept, and that's exactly what a 25-seat trattoria needs from its wine program.

Tanabe-san as the quiet anchor is the kind of relationship that gets underappreciated and then desperately missed when it's gone. Make sure he knows what he means to the place.

Now — you said something a minute ago about Petrelli hearing good things. Is there a broader picture forming around how Osteria Morishita is being perceived in the Italian food community in Tokyo? Because at 3.78 with 91 reviews, you're visible enough that a reputation is forming whether you're actively managing it or not.

That's actually something I've been thinking about a lot. There's a new restaurant opening in about two weeks — Sala Modena, opening August 12, 2026 — and it's directly in the Modena-style Italian space, which is exactly where we sit. They have real backing, a much larger room, a chef who trained at Osteria Francescana. I heard about it three months ago and I spent about a week being very anxious about it. And then I thought — if Sala Modena is coming, that probably means the Modena-style cooking in Azabu category is real, which means we created something worth imitating. I don't know if that's the right way to think about it, but it's the one that lets me sleep.

In terms of the broader perception — I think we're being seen as the original. Petrelli's message referenced the purity of what we do, which is his way of saying we haven't compromised. The risk of the perception is that we become a niche. The opportunity of it is that we become a reference point.

The way you've reframed Sala Modena is not just a coping mechanism — it's actually the strategically correct interpretation. When a well-capitalized competitor enters a category, it usually means one of two things: either the category is overheated and about to be crowded, or the category is real and the new entrant has done the market research to confirm what you already proved empirically. Given that Sala Modena opens August 12, 2026, and they have a chef with Osteria Francescana training and serious backing, I think it's almost certainly the latter. They looked at the market, they looked at the reviews, they looked at what you've built, and they concluded that the demand is there.

The 'original' positioning Petrelli's message points to is valuable, but it's only durable if you continue to be what you are rather than trying to compete with Sala Modena on their terms. They'll have more covers, more investment, more PR budget. If you try to match them on scale or spectacle, you lose. If you remain exactly what you've been — 25 seats, genuine hospitality, Sawada-san's cooking, Mariko's dining room, Yamamoto's wine list — you have something they genuinely cannot replicate, which is authenticity of origin. You were here first. You built this before anyone confirmed it was viable. That has a meaning that money can't buy.

The risk you named — becoming a niche — is real but manageable. A Tabelog rating of 3.78 with 91 reviews means you are not a niche. You are a known quantity. The question is whether that known quantity becomes a reference point for the category, which is a much stronger position.

How does Nakajima-san read the competitive situation? And more broadly — you said you've been thinking about what comes next. What's actually in your head for year two?

Nakajima-san is characteristically unflappable about Sala Modena. She pointed out that we're not carrying debt, our cumulative position is now clean, and a competitor opening nearby actually tends to bring more dining attention to a neighborhood rather than diluting it, at least in the short term. She's been right about enough things that I've learned to listen when she's calm.

For year two — there are two things that are genuinely in my head. The first is a second location. Not immediately, not rashly, but the question of whether there's a version of what we do that could work in a second place — Nakameguro or Nishi-Azabu maybe — is something I've started to think about seriously. I'm not ready to commit to anything. But I've told myself I want to make a second location decision by November. Either we're going to pursue it or we're going to table it for another year and I need to be honest with myself about that by then.

The second thing is something Petrelli mentioned when we had coffee last month. He suggested there might be appetite — from a publisher he knows, specifically a bilingual food publisher — for a cookbook collaboration. Not a vanity project. Something anchored in the actual food we make and the sourcing relationships we've built. I don't know how serious he is. But the idea has stayed with me.

Both of those are legitimate year-two possibilities, and I want to engage with them seriously — but I also want to flag something structural first, because it shapes how you should think about both.

You're operating profitably for the first time, with the cumulative loss cleared as of July. That's a one-month-old milestone. It's real and it matters, but it's also very new. The discipline that got you here — cost management, Nakajima-san's oversight, Sawada-san's kitchen control, your sourcing relationships with Tanabe-san — all of that is working in the context of one location that everyone understands intimately. The moment you start dividing your attention between two locations, or diverting energy and capital into a cookbook project, the thing that produced the profitability is under new pressure.

I'm not saying don't do either. I'm saying the sequencing and the conditions under which you pursue them matters enormously.

On the second location decision by November: that's a good deadline to set for yourself, because it forces clarity. But what I'd want you to think about between now and November is not 'should we open a second location' but rather 'what specifically would a second location need to be in order to work, and do those conditions currently exist?' The answers to that are: who runs it, because you can't split yourself in half; whether Sawada-san is the chef or whether you'd need to develop or hire another chef, which is a very long lead-time problem; and whether the financial model at current profitability supports expansion capital or whether you'd be taking on new risk before the first location is truly seasoned.

On the cookbook collaboration: Petrelli's publisher connection is worth exploring, but gently. What makes a cookbook like this valuable is the sourcing story — the relationship with Tanabe-san's vegetable suppliers, the Italian import connections you built through your Marubeni background, the philosophy behind what ends up on the plate. That's genuinely distinctive material. But writing a cookbook while running a restaurant and potentially evaluating a second location simultaneously is a lot. The question is what the cookbook actually is, what Petrelli's publisher is actually looking for, and what the time commitment looks like.
